Precision big bang nucleosynthesis with improved Helium-4 predictions

August 24, 2026
Abstract

Primordial nucleosynthesis is one of the three historical evidences for the big bang model, together with the expansion of the universe and the cosmic microwave background. There is a good global agreement between the computed primordial abundances of helium-4, deuterium, helium-3 and their values deduced from observations. Now that the number of neutrino families and the baryonic densities have been fixed by laboratory measurements or CMB observations, the model has no free parameter and its predictions are rigid. Since this is the earliest cosmic process for which we a priori know all the physics involved, departure from its predictions could provide hints or constraints on new physics or astrophysics in the early universe. Precision on primordial abundances deduced from observations has recently been drastically improved and reach the percent level for both deuterium and helium-4. Accordingly, the BBN predictions should reach the same level of precision. For most isotopes, the dominant sources of uncertainty come from those on the laboratory thermonuclear reactions. This article focuses on helium-4 whose predicted primordial abundance depends essentially on weak interactions which control the neutron-proton ratio. The rates of the various weak interaction processes depend on the experimentally measured neutron lifetime, but also includes numerous corrections that we thoroughly investigate here. They are the radiative, zero–temperature, corrections, finite nucleon mass corrections, finite temperature radiative corrections, weak-magnetism, and QED plasma effects, which are for the first time all included and calculated in a self consistent way, allowing to take into account the correlations between them, and verifying that all satisfy detailed balance. Finally, we include the incomplete neutrino decoupling and claim to reach a 10−410^{-4} accuracy on the helium-4 predicted mass fraction of 0.24709±0.000170.24709\pm 0.00017 (when including the uncertainty on the neutron lifetime). In addition, we provide a Mathematica primordial nucleosynthesis code that incorporates, not only these corrections but also a full network of reactions, using the best available thermonuclear reaction rates, allowing the predictions of primordial abundances of helium-4, deuterium, helium-3 and lithium-7 but also of heavier isotopes up to the CNO region.

I Introduction

Besides the universal spatial expansion and the cosmic microwave background (CMB) radiation, the third historical evidence for the hot big bang model comes from primordial, or big bang nucleosynthesis (BBN). During the first ≈\approx20 minutes of the Universe, when it was dense and hot enough for nuclear reactions to take place, BBN describes the production of the so called “light elements”, 4He, D, 3He and 7Li, together with only minute traces of heavier nuclei (see e.g. Olive [143], Steigman [175], Cyburt et al. [55], Patrignani and Particle Data Group [147], Coc and Vangioni [42] for recent reviews). The number of free parameters that entered in standard BBN has now been reduced to zero. Indeed, the number of light neutrino families is now known from the measurement of the Z0Z^{0} width by LEP experiments at CERN: NνN_{\nu} = 2.984±\pm0.008 [147]. The lifetime of the neutron entering in weak reaction rate calculations and many nuclear reaction rates have been measured in nuclear physics laboratories [38, 55, 165, 60]. The last parameter to have been independently determined is the baryonic density of the Universe which is now deduced from the analysis of the anisotropies of the CMB radiation from the Planck satellite data [2]. Hence, there is no more free parameter in standard BBN and the calculated primordial abundances are in principle only affected by the moderate uncertainties in nuclear cross sections. Keeping in mind that abundances span a range of nine orders of magnitude, the agreement between primordial abundances, either deduced from observations, or from primordial nucleosynthesis calculations, is an outstanding support to the hot big bang model [55]. Hence, BBN is an invaluable tool for probing the physics of the early Universe, and it has been very efficient to constrain physics beyond the standard model. When we look back in time, it is the ultimate process for which we a priori know all the physics involved, given that it is very well tested in laboratories, so that departures from its predictions provide hints for new physics or astrophysics [106, 151, 133, 139].

Great progresses have been made in the precision of both observations and laboratory measurements. The precision on deuterium observations have now reached the percent level [49], a precision hardly reached in nuclear physics measurements. The determination of the primordial abundance of He4{}^{4}{\rm He} has been reduced to less than 2% by the inclusion of an additional atomic infrared line [15]. However, there is still a significant discrepancy on lithium, for which predictions are a factor of ≈\approx3 higher than observations. The previous paper Coc et al. [38] investigated the uncertainties on D/H predictions which directly reflects the experimental uncertainties on few reaction rates that have all been re-evaluated [103, 83], leading to a small but significant decrease of the predicted deuterium abundance with reduced uncertainty. This review aims at reducing the uncertainties, this time on the He4{}^{4}{\rm He} abundance prediction which are dominated by theoretical uncertainties on the weak reactions that interconvert neutrons and protons.

To that goal, we implemented the BBN equations into a Mathematica code11 1 PRIMAT : PRImordial MATter, freely available at http://www2.iap.fr/users/pitrou/primat.htm , in addition to the Fortran code, that has been used recently, e.g. in Coc et al. [37], Coc and Vangioni [40], Coc et al. [38]. This Fortran code originates from the model created at IAP by Elisabeth Vangioni [177] and further developed by Alain Coc [43]. Hence, it was possible to cross–check the implementations and after tuning the parameters to reach similar precisions, verify that the results were virtually identical, and next to focus on nuclear reaction rate uncertainties. Leaving aside, the “lithium problem” that has not yet found a fully satisfactory solution [74], it has become essential to improve the precision on deuterium and He4{}^{4}{\rm He} primordial abundances (He3{}^{3}{\rm He} is not pertinent here). As nuclear uncertainties affecting deuterium BBN have already been investigated recently [103, 83, 38], we will just summarize the situation. On the contrary the uncertainties impacting the He4{}^{4}{\rm He} abundance predictions are limited by the experimental value of the neutron lifetime [147, 186] but also by the numerous corrections that have to be introduced in the theoretical weak–interaction reaction rates. The main aim of this article is to calculate in details all these corrections. In our previous works, either only a fraction of them was taken into account [37, 40] or were also supplemented by a final correction to the He4{}^{4}{\rm He} abundance [39], based on other works [62, 123].

With the now precise theoretical and observational determinations of both the deuterium and He4{}^{4}{\rm He} primordial abundances, it is now possible to better constrain the standard models of particle physics and cosmology and eventually provide hints of physics beyond the standard model.

We define nin_{i} as volume density of isotope ii, and nbn_{\rm b}, the baryon or nucleon volume density. The (pseudo-)mass fraction of isotope ii is defined as

Xi≡Ai​ninb,X_{i}\equiv A_{i}\frac{n_{i}}{n_{\rm b}}\,, (1)

where AiA_{i} is the dimensionless mass integer number of nuclear physics, or baryon number of particle physics, (i.e. not the atomic mass). Baryon number conservation requires that ∑iAi​ni=nb\sum_{i}A_{i}n_{i}=n_{\rm b} or ∑iXi=1\sum_{i}X_{i}=1. For He4{}^{4}{\rm He} it is customary to define

YP≡XHe4,Y_{\rm P}\equiv X_{{}^{4}{\rm He}}\,, (2)

and to introduce for convenience

YP(4)≡104​YP.Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\equiv 10^{4}Y_{\rm P}\,. (3)

I.1 Observed abundances

During the galactic evolution, massive stars are the main source of enrichment of the interstellar medium, when they explode as supernovae, out of which next generations of stars are born. In this process, they release matter, enriched in heavy elements that they have synthesized during the various phases of their evolution. Accordingly, the abundance of metals (elements heavier than helium) in star forming gas increases with time. The observed metallicity is therefore an indication of age: the older, the lower the metallicity. Hence, primordial abundances are extracted from observations of objects with low metallicity, but depending on their galactic chemical evolution, pristine abundances have to be derived from different classes of objects as detailed below.

I.1.1 He4{}^{4}{\rm He} observations

After BBN, stars produce also He4{}^{4}{\rm He}  and its primordial abundance can be measured thanks to observations in Hii (ionized hydrogen) regions inside compact blue galaxies. It is thought that galaxies are formed by the merging of such dwarf galaxies, in a hierarchical structure formation paradigm, hence these are considered to be more primitive. First, for each Hii region, the He4{}^{4}{\rm He} abundance has to be determined within a model aiming at reproducing the observed He4{}^{4}{\rm He} emission lines, that also depends on parameters like e.g. the electron density. Then, to account for stellar production, the He4{}^{4}{\rm He} deduced abundances should be extrapolated to zero metallicity. Recently, the observation [109] of an additional atomic infrared line (λ\lambda10830) in 45 low–metallicity Hii regions have allowed to better constrain the thermodynamic conditions that prevail in the emission regions. After selecting 28 object, Izotov et al. [109] obtained YP=0.2551±0.0022Y_{\rm P}=0.2551\pm 0.0022 for the He4{}^{4}{\rm He} mass fraction. However, Aver et al. [15] (see also Cyburt et al. [55]), starting from the same observational data made a stricter selection, based, in particular on goodness of fit for the emission model of each object. For the selected 16 objects, the uncertainties were so reduced that a slope in the YpY_{p} versus metallicity data could be considered. After extrapolation to zero metallicity, Aver et al. [15] obtained,

YP=0.2449±0.0040,Y_{\rm P}=0.2449\pm 0.0040\,, (4)

that we use here.

I.1.2 Deuterium observations

Deuterium is a very fragile isotope. It can only be destroyed after BBN thanks to stellar evolution. The deuterium abundance closest to primordial abundance is determined from the observation of a few cosmological clouds (absorbers) at high redshift on the line of sight of distant quasars (emitters). Figure 1 shows the observed D/H values as a function of the redshift of the absorber. Until recently, the distribution of D/H observations showed a significant scatter (see e.g. Pettini and Cooke [148]). It allowed Olive et al. [144] to adopt a weighted mean of D/H = (3.02±0.23)×10−5(3.02\pm 0.23)\times 10^{-5} without excluding an upper limit of D/H = 4×10−54\times 10^{-5}. This is not possible anymore thanks to the recent new observations or reanalyses of existing data [47, 16, 48, 154, 49] that now display a plateau as a function of redshift (and metallicity) with a very small scatter (Fig. 1). Moreover, in Dvorkin et al. [67], the comparison with the available measurements is consistent with the cosmic merger tree model of structure formation. It is shown that at redshift higher than 2 (see their Fig. 2), the dispersion in the cosmic deuterium abundance is very tiny leading to think that at these redshifts the observation of the D abundance is probably primordial. Hence, we adopt the new recommended value provided by Cooke et al. [49]:

D/H=(2.527±0.030)×10−5,{\rm D}/{\rm H}=(2.527\pm 0.030)\times 10^{-5}\,, (5)

lower and with smaller uncertainties than in previous determinations 22 2 A recent reanalysis and new D/H observations towards the Q1009+2956 quasar [192, 193] provided a new value of D/H = (2.48−0.35+0.41)×10−5(2.48^{+0.41}_{-0.35})\times 10^{-5} with a limited precision (17%). If included, it shifts the abundance downward to D/H= (2.545±0.025)×10−5(2.545\pm 0.025)\times 10^{-5} . If such a precision of ∼\sim1% in observations is confirmed, great care should be paid to nuclear cross sections affecting deuterium nucleosynthesis.

I.1.3 He3{}^{3}{\rm He} observations

Contrary to the case of He4{}^{4}{\rm He}, stars can both produce and destroy He3{}^{3}{\rm He}, so that the evolution of its abundance in time is not known precisely [178]. Since observing helium is difficult, and given the small 3He/4He ratio, He3{}^{3}{\rm He} was only observed in our Galaxy and the bounds obtained are He3/H=(0.9−1.3)×10−5{}^{3}{\rm He}/{\rm H}=(0.9-1.3)\times 10^{-5}, keeping in mind that this is an upper limit extracted from a single object [17]. However, the next generation of 30+ m telescope facilities may allow to extract the 3He/4He ratio from observations of extra-galactic metal poor HII regions [46].

I.1.4 Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} observations

Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} is peculiar because it has three distinct sources: BBN but also spallative nuclear reactions between galactic cosmic rays and the interstellar medium, and a stellar source (Asymptotic giant branch stars and novae) [81]. For instance, recent observations [176, 111] have confirmed Li production by novae, at a level even higher than model predictions [96]. Hence, after BBN, Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} can be produced but can also easily be destroyed in the interior of stars by proton capture at temperatures as low as 2.5 MK.

The life expectancy of stars with masses lower than our Sun is larger than the age of the Universe so that very old such stars can still be observed in the halo of our Galaxy. In this context, lithium can be observed at the surface of these stars and its abundance was found to be independent of metallicity and effective temperature in the ranges -2.4≤\leq[Fe/H]≤\leq-1.433 3 Logarithm of the ratio, relative to its solar value: [X/Y]≡log((X/Y)/(X⊙/Y⊙))X/Y]\equiv\log\left((X/Y)/(X_{\odot}/Y_{\odot})\right). (i.e. between ≈4×10−3\approx 4\times 10^{-3} and 4×10−14\times 10^{-1} of the solar metallicity) and 5700 ≤Teff≤\leq{T_{\mathrm{eff}}}\leq6800 K [81]. This plateau was discovered by François and Monique Spite [171] and this constant Li abundance is interpreted as corresponding to the BBN Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} production. The thinness of the “Spite plateau” has generally been considered as an indication that surface Li depletion may not have been very effective so that it should reflect the primordial value. However, as shown in Fig. 2, there is a discrepancy of a factor ≈\approx3 between the BBN predicted value and the lithium abundance derived in metal-poor main-sequence (MS) stars. This discrepancy could be alleviated if the stars observed today had undergone photospheric depletion of lithium. Different observations in globular clusters (see Gruyters et al. [89]) and stellar scenarios concerning the formation of the early metal poor stars have been developed, [80] trying to follow lithium evolution in metal-poor stars, from pre-main sequence to the Spite plateau. Li evolution could affect its abundance by introducing the effects of convective overshooting, atomic diffusion and mixing [153]. In this context, Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} could be depleted and it could be possible to move closer to the observed Li Spite plateau. Indeed, several globular clusters (NGC 6397, 6752, M30) show that the discrepancy could be reduced by atomic diffusion leading to a factor of 1.6 instead 3 [136]. Finally the pre-MS depletion can be efficient and this is presently an open question. Note that recent lithium observations [101] have been done in the Small Magellanic Cloud which has a quarter of the sun’s metallicity and a Li abundance nearly equal to the BBN predictions.

Recently, Reggiani et al. [152] have constrained cosmic scatter in the galactic halo using a differential analysis of metal poor for several elements. Regarding lithium, they find a very low scatter (0.04 dex) and a mean value 1.86×10−101.86\times 10^{-10} which is compatible with other studies. We adopt here the analysis of Sbordone et al. [158], namely 44 4 All uncertainties are given with one standard deviation.

Li7/H=(1.58±0.3)×10−10.{}^{7}{\rm Li}/{\rm H}=(1.58\pm 0.3)\times 10^{-10}\,. (6)

I.2 Outlook on weak-rates corrections

Given the observational precision on He4{}^{4}{\rm He}, we aim at predictions with a precision better than 0.1%0.1\%. This amounts to considering all effects which affect YP(4)Y_{\rm P}^{(4)} by units, and to treat carefully all effects which modify the abundance by an order 10−410^{-4}. YPY_{\rm P} is almost exclusively controlled by weak reactions, because nearly all neutrons end up in He4{}^{4}{\rm He}. By varying artificially the weak rates (Γ\Gamma) we find the relation55 5 Using Eq. (146) and Γ∝τn−1\Gamma\propto\tau_{\rm n}^{-1} from Eq. (91).

δ​YPYP≃−0.73​δ​ΓΓ.\frac{\delta Y_{\rm P}}{Y_{\rm P}}\simeq-0.73\frac{\delta\Gamma}{\Gamma}\,. (7)

Hence we need to focus on all corrections which affect the weak rates by 10−410^{-4} or more, on top of the experimental uncertainty on the neutron lifetime.

As for H2{}^{2}{\rm H} and He3{}^{3}{\rm He}, we aim at predictions of order 10−310^{-3} if we leave aside the uncertainty in nuclear rates, and of order of a few 10−210^{-2} when including uncertainties in nuclear rates. In all our computations, we must also make sure to maintain numerical errors much below 10−310^{-3}.

There are many effects to take into account for the weak rates and we must also consider their possible couplings since they cannot always be summed linearly. These effects have several origins, namely

  1. 1.

    radiative corrections,

  2. 2.

    finite nucleon mass corrections,

  3. 3.

    finite temperature radiative corrections,

  4. 4.

    weak-magnetism,

  5. 5.

    QED plasma effects,

  6. 6.

    incomplete neutrino decoupling.

Radiative corrections correspond to the contribution of virtual photons in weak reactions, together with the emission of photons in the final state (bremsstrahlung) from the electron line. They are typically order 10−210^{-2} effects (see § V.3) because of the value of the fine-structure constant αFS≃1/137\alpha_{\rm FS}\simeq 1/137. They are well established in the context of neutron beta decay [57], and even with some resummed effects which are higher orders in αFS\alpha_{\rm FS} for increased precision [108]. In the context of BBN, these effects were originally estimated by Dicus et al. [62].

Finite nucleon mass correction correspond to the effect of nucleon recoil and nucleon thermal distribution of velocity in the theoretical computation of the weak rates. These corrections are also of order 10−210^{-2} (see § V.3) even if smaller than radiative corrections. Wilkinson [187] provided a comprehensive list of these effects in the context of neutron beta decay, and Seckel [163] reviewed these corrections in the context of BBN. These were later estimated numerically by Lopez et al. [124] using a Monte-Carlo estimation of multidimensional integrals. We introduce a new efficient method which relies on a Fokker-Planck expansion in the energy transfer, and which relies only on one-dimensional integrals.

Finite temperature radiative corrections correspond to the interactions with the bath of electrons and positrons during weak reactions. They lead to a long subject of controversy in the literature. They were initially computed in Dicus et al. [62] and Cambier et al. [27]. Discrepancies between these approaches were analyzed by Kernan [114] and a numerical estimation was provided by Lopez and Turner [123]. However, Brown and Sawyer [25] pointed incoherences and the lack of detailed balance, and they proposed to set the finite temperature radiative correction on firm ground by providing a comprehensive theoretical computation from finite-temperature quantum field theory. We find, and this is new, that to be complete and satisfy detailed balance, one must also consider corrections to the bremsstrahlung effects and add them to finite temperature corrections. Overall, when finite-temperature corrections and bremsstrahlung corrections are added, they almost perfectly cancel, leaving YP(4)Y_{\rm P}^{(4)} nearly unchanged (see § V.3).

Weak-magnetism which arises from the internal structure of nucleons is part of finite mass corrections and is order 10−310^{-3} (see § V.3).

Quantum Electrodynamics (QED) is responsible for two effects. First the interaction with the plasma modifies the electron mass. However this effect is strictly speaking part of finite temperature radiative corrections in our computations. Second, QED effects modify the thermodynamics of the plasma, that is it modifies the pressure and energy density. We find that this effect, taken alone, results in a negligible modification of YP(4)Y_{\rm P}^{(4)} which is of order 10−510^{-5} (see § V.3). However it affects the number of effective neutrinos for subsequent cosmology such as the physics of cosmic microwave background (CMB).

Incomplete neutrino decoupling corrections occur when electrons and positrons annihilate, because neutrinos are not fully decoupled from the plasma and some annihilations end up heating the neutrino bath. This effect increases the neutrino temperature and produces distortions in their spectrum. In order to track the neutrinos spectral distortions, it is necessary to use the full machinery of coupled Boltzmann equations, especially when considering neutrino oscillations. Since this effect also modifies the effective number of neutrinos for the subsequent cosmology, several authors among which Dolgov et al. [65], Mangano et al. [127], Grohs et al. [88], de Salas and Pastor [155] focused on it. We shall use a fit taken from Pisanti et al. [149] for the heating rate of neutrinos. Eventually we find that this correction is of order 10−310^{-3} (see § V.3).

All these effects are detailed in § III.

I.3 Main eras of BBN

During BBN, one can distinguish different eras depending on the dominant physical processes.

  1. 1.

    For plasma temperatures TT in the range 2​MeV≲T≲GeV2\,{\rm MeV}\lesssim T\lesssim{\rm GeV}, nucleons are formed and their density is only affected by expansion. Neutrinos are still in thermal equilibrium with the plasma (electron-positrons and protons), that is Tγ=TνT_{\gamma}=T_{\nu} and the neutron to proton ratio Xn/XpX_{n}/X_{p} is enforced to be the thermodynamical equilibrium value since weak interactions interconvert efficiently neutrons in protons and vice-versa, through the reactions (68).

  2. 2.

    In the range, 0.8​MeV≲T≲2​MeV0.8\,{\rm MeV}\lesssim T\lesssim 2\,{\rm MeV} neutrinos have essentially decoupled but weak interactions maintain neutrons and proton in thermodynamical equilibrium. However at weak-interactions freeze-out temperature TF≃0.8​MeVT_{F}\simeq 0.8{\rm MeV}, defined by the equality between weak interaction rates and the cosmological expansion rate, the abundance of neutrons are mostly affected by neutron beta decay. In practice, freeze-out is not instantaneous and the neutron abundance is subject only to neutron beta decay around TF≃0.28​MeVT_{F}\simeq 0.28\,{\rm MeV}. The abundance of neutrons is then about Xn≃0.17X_{n}\simeq 0.17 and it is eventually reduced to XnNuc≃0.125X^{\rm Nuc}_{n}\simeq 0.125 by beta decay when nucleosynthesis starts (see Fig. 3).

  3. 3.

    Around 0.5​MeV0.5{\rm MeV}, electrons and positrons annihilate and heat up the photon bath, resulting in a different temperature between photons and neutrinos (Tγ>TνT_{\gamma}>T_{\nu}). This affects directly the expansion history of the Universe since the energy content of massive particles (electrons and positrons) is replaced by massless particles (photons), but it also affects weak-interaction rates since this is concomitant with the freeze-out period.

  4. 4.

    As long as T≳0.078​MeVT\gtrsim 0.078{\rm MeV}, deuterium dissociation is too efficient to allow for deuterium synthesis. Even though the binding energy of deuterium is about 2.2​MeV2.2{\rm MeV}, deuterium is efficiently destroyed by the high-energy tail of the Bose-Einstein distribution of photons, because the ratio between baryon number density and photon number density η\eta is smaller than 10−910^{-9}.

  5. 5.

    Below T≲TNuc=0.078​MeVT\lesssim T_{\rm Nuc}=0.078{\rm MeV}, deuterium can be formed. Then since the binding energy per nucleon of He4{}^{4}{\rm He} is much larger than for deuterium, a network of reactions ends up in producing nearly only He4{}^{4}{\rm He} and very tiny amounts of other light elements. Since He4{}^{4}{\rm He} is made of two neutrons and two protons, the (pseudo-)mass abundance satisfies YP≃2​XnNucY_{\rm P}\simeq 2X^{\rm Nuc}_{n}, hence leading to a final value YP≃0.25Y_{\rm P}\simeq 0.25. Nucleosynthesis is completely over for all elements when T≲0.01​MeVT\lesssim 0.01{\rm MeV} or T≲108​KT\lesssim 10^{8}{\rm K} but for prediction with 10−310^{-3} precision on deuterium, we found that we must wait until T≲6×107​KT\lesssim 6\times 10^{7}{\rm K}.

I.4 Resolution strategy and outline

This outline of nucleosynthesis implies that we do not need to solve jointly the abundance of all species at all times. Indeed, given that the matter-radiation equivalence occurs around T≃3000​KT\simeq 3000{\rm K}, this means that baryonic matter accounts for less than 10−410^{-4} of the total energy density at the end of BBN and even less during freeze-out. In principle, one should account for the fact that neutron abundance evolves even though the nucleonic density (protons and baryons) is only affected by cosmic expansion. Since the mass difference between neutrons and protons is of order 10−310^{-3} of their rest mass energy, we can ignore this effect when evaluating the total energy density of the Universe. Similarly, given that the binding energy in nuclei is around or less than 10−210^{-2} of the rest mass energy, we can also consider to a very good approximation that nuclear reactions do not affect the baryon energy density. Hence it is possible to compute the evolution of the cosmological background, without having to compute in details the abundance of neutrons nor the details of nuclear reactions. In § II we study the thermodynamics of all species and the dynamics of the cosmic expansion. Then in § III we focus on weak interactions and detail all corrections. Since the weak interaction rates depend on the plasma of electrons, positrons and neutrinos only, they can be studied ignoring nuclear reactions. Finally in § IV we focus on nuclear reactions and we present the results obtained when coupling the background dynamics, the weak interactions and the nuclear reactions. Most technical details can be found in the appendices for ease of reading. We use natural units in all expressions, that is we work in units in which

kB=ℏ=c=1,k_{B}=\hbar=c=1\,, (8)

except when we judge instructive to write them explicitly.

II Background thermodynamics

We consider a homogeneous and isotropic cosmology, more precisely a flat Friedmann-Lemaître (FL) spacetime characterized by the scale factor a⁡(t)a(t) where tt is the cosmic time. The Hubble expansion rate is H=a˙/aH=\dot{a}/a, where a dot indicates a derivative with respect to tt. Since cosmological perturbations are of order 10−510^{-5}, it is fully justified to ignore their effect and consider an homogeneous cosmology given our precision goal.

II.1 Thermodynamics in a FL spacetime

II.1.1 Distribution function and Boltzmann equation

Relativistic species, which encompass neutrinos, photons and electrons with positrons during the relevant BBN era, are best described with a distribution function f⁡(t,p)f(t,p) for each species, and where the dependence is only on the magnitude of momenta p=E2−m2p=\sqrt{E^{2}-m^{2}} given the symmetries of the FL spacetime. This description is valid even out of thermodynamical equilibrium. The distribution function satisfies the general Boltzmann equation in a FL spacetime

L⁡[f]≡∂f∂t+p˙​∂f∂p=C⁡[f],p˙=−H​p.L[f]\equiv\frac{\partial f}{\partial t}+\dot{p}\frac{\partial f}{\partial p}=C[f]\,,\qquad\dot{p}=-Hp\,. (9)

We have used that p∝1/ap\propto 1/a because of cosmic expansion and C⁡[f]C[f] is the collision term of the species under scrutiny. In order to relate this description to the fluid description, thermodynamical quantities such as number density nn, energy density ρ\rho and pressure PP, can be formed from the distribution function as summarized in App. A.

II.1.2 Number density evolution

From the definition of thermodynamic quantities (Eqs. 169), considering ∫L⁡[f]​4​π​p2​𝑑p/(2​π)3\int L[f]4\pi p^{2}\mathrm{d}p/(2\pi)^{3} with the Boltzmann equation (9) leads after integration by parts to the number conservation equation

n˙+3​H​n=𝒥,𝒥≡∫C⁡[f]​4​π​p2​d​p(2​π)3.\dot{n}+3Hn={\cal J}\,,\qquad{\cal J}\equiv\int C[f]\frac{4\pi p^{2}\mathrm{d}p}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,. (10)

𝒥{\cal J} is the net creation rate of particles per unit of physical volume. When the collision term vanishes or when it conserves the number of particles because it describes elastic scattering,

n˙+3​H​n=0⇒d⁡(n​a3)d​t=0.\dot{n}+3Hn=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{\mathrm{d}(na^{3})}{\mathrm{d}t}=0\,. (11)

In that case, for a comoving volume a3a^{3}, the total number of particles N≡n​a3N\equiv na^{3} remains constant.

II.1.3 Energy density evolution

Similarly, starting from the definition of thermodynamic quantities (Eqs. 169), and considering ∫L⁡[f]​E​4​π​p2​𝑑p/(2​π)3\int L[f]E4\pi p^{2}\mathrm{d}p/(2\pi)^{3} with the Boltzmann equation (9), leads after integration by parts (and using E​d​E=p​d​pE\mathrm{d}E=p\mathrm{d}p) to the energy conservation equation

ρ˙+3​H​(ρ+P)=q˙,q˙≡∫C⁡[f]​4​π​E​p2​d​p(2​π)3.\dot{\rho}+3H(\rho+P)=\dot{q}\,,\qquad\dot{q}\equiv\int C[f]\frac{4\pi Ep^{2}\mathrm{d}p}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,. (12)

q˙\dot{q} is the volume heating rate. For massless particles, such as photons or neutrinos (which can be considered massless during the BBN), E=pE=p and P=ρ/3P=\rho/3, implying that when the collision term is vanishing

ρ˙+4​H​ρ=0⇒d⁡(ρ​a4)d​t=0.\dot{\rho}+4H\rho=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad\frac{\mathrm{d}(\rho a^{4})}{\mathrm{d}t}=0\,. (13)

Eqs. (12) and (13) are general and do not rely on a specific distribution function.

II.1.4 Entropy evolution

Volume entropy is defined (see e.g. Grohs et al. [88]) from the distribution function by

s=−∫SB(f)4​π​p2​d​p(2​π)3,s=-\int S_{\rm B}(f)\frac{4\pi p^{2}\mathrm{d}p}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,, (14)

where the Boltzmann entropy is defined as

SB​(f)≡[f​ln⁡f±(1∓f)​ln⁡(1∓f)]S_{\rm B}(f)\equiv\left[f\ln f\pm(1\mp f)\ln(1\mp f)\right] (15)

with upper (lower) sign for fermions (bosons). Using the identity

∂p[SB​(f)]=ln⁡(f1∓f)​∂pf\partial_{p}[S_{\rm B}(f)]=\ln\left(\frac{f}{1\mp f}\right)\partial_{p}f (16)

and multiplying Eq. (9) by SB​(f)S_{\rm B}(f) we get after integration by parts

s˙+3Hs=−∫C[f]ln(f1∓f)4​π​p2​d​p(2​π)3,\dot{s}+3Hs=-\int C[f]\ln\left(\frac{f}{1\mp f}\right)\frac{4\pi p^{2}\mathrm{d}p}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,, (17)

which dictates the evolution of volume entropy. If there are no collisions, it is only affected by dilution as s∝1/a3s\propto 1/a^{3} such that the total entropy in a given comoving volume, S≡s​a3S\equiv sa^{3}, is conserved (S˙=0\dot{S}=0).

II.1.5 Local thermodynamical equilibrium

In case of local thermodynamical equilibrium (LTE), fermions (bosons) follow a Fermi-Dirac (Bose-Einstein) distribution (171) and

ln⁡(f1∓f)=μ−ET,\ln\left(\frac{f}{1\mp f}\right)=\frac{\mu-E}{T}\,, (18)

where μ\mu is the chemical potential. Hence the evolution of volume entropy for a given species satisfies, using Eqs. (10) and (17),

s˙+3​H​s=q˙T−μT​(n˙+3​H​n),\dot{s}+3Hs=\frac{\dot{q}}{T}-\frac{\mu}{T}(\dot{n}+3Hn)\,, (19)

with q˙\dot{q} defined in Eq. (12). From Eq. (19) multiplied by a3a^{3}, we recover the usual thermodynamical identity

T​S˙=Q˙−μ​N˙T\dot{S}=\dot{Q}-\mu\dot{N} (20)

with Q˙≡q˙​a3\dot{Q}\equiv\dot{q}a^{3}. Hence, the entropy for a given species is conserved if there is no heat exchange, that is no interactions, and either a vanishing chemical potential (in practice μ≪T\mu\ll T) or conservation of the number of particles (i.e. N˙=0\dot{N}=0). From the conservation of the total stress-energy tensor, we must have ∑iq˙i=0\sum_{i}\dot{q}_{i}=0, that is there can be no global production of heat. Hence, in case of local thermodynamical equilibrium, the total entropy is conserved whenever for all species either the chemical potential is negligible μi≪T\mu_{i}\ll T or the number of particles is conserved.

If there is LTE, entropy for a given species ii can then be linked to other thermodynamical quantities thanks to

si=Pi+ρi−μi​niTi.s_{i}=\frac{P_{i}+\rho_{i}-\mu_{i}n_{i}}{T_{i}}\,. (21)

The total entropy is obtained from the extensivity of ρ\rho and nn, given that pressure and temperature of all species are equal at equilibrium

s=∑iPi+ρiT+∑iμi​niT=ρ+PT+∑iμi​niT.s=\sum_{i}\frac{P_{i}+\rho_{i}}{T}+\sum_{i}\frac{\mu_{i}n_{i}}{T}=\frac{\rho+P}{T}+\sum_{i}\frac{\mu_{i}n_{i}}{T}\,. (22)

During nucleosynthesis, given the very low value of the baryon-to-photon ratio η\eta (see § II.3 below), we can totally ignore the entropy of protons and neutrons. This amounts to neglecting the electrons, positrons and neutrinos created and destroyed in weak interactions, and any energy exchange with these particles and the photons. Hence we can focus only on the thermodynamics of electrons, positrons, photons and neutrinos. During nucleosynthesis, neutrinos are nearly fully decoupled from other species and their entropy is separately conserved if we can assume that they are totally decoupled. See §II.6 for the small modifications induced by incomplete decoupling (ID).

Conversely, electrons, positrons and photons are tightly coupled by electromagnetic interactions and they behave collectively as a plasma whose common temperature is defined as TT. Photons decouple from electrons only around recombination much later when the CMB is formed and T≲eVT\lesssim{\rm eV}. Due to electron-positron annihilations, the number of particles in the plasma is not conserved, and it is crucial that we can neglect the chemical potential of plasma particles to claim that the plasma entropy is conserved. The chemical potential of photons is always vanishing due to processes which do not conserve the number of photons so we need only to make sure that the chemical potential of electrons and positrons can be neglected. In App. A.2, we evaluate these chemical potentials and show they are completely negligible, implying that we can use entropy conservation.

For convenience we define dimensionless reduced energy density, pressure, number density and entropy as

n¯i≡niTi3P¯i≡PiTi4ρ¯i≡ρiTi4s¯i≡siTi3\bar{n}_{i}\equiv\frac{n_{i}}{T_{i}^{3}}\quad\bar{P}_{i}\equiv\frac{P_{i}}{T_{i}^{4}}\quad\bar{\rho}_{i}\equiv\frac{\rho_{i}}{T_{i}^{4}}\quad\bar{s}_{i}\equiv\frac{s_{i}}{T_{i}^{3}}\, (23)

such that the relation (21) reads simply in case of vanishing chemical potential

s¯i=ρ¯i+P¯i.\bar{s}_{i}=\bar{\rho}_{i}+\bar{P}_{i}\,. (24)

For photons the reduced thermodynamic variables do not depend on temperature and are constants when there is LTE. We find

n¯γ=22​π2​I−(1,1)=2​ζ​(3)π2​ρ¯γ=22​π2​I−(2,1)=π215​P¯γ=26​π2​I−(0,3)=π245​s¯γ=ρ¯γ+P¯γ=4​π245.\bar{n}_{\gamma}&=\frac{2}{2\pi^{2}}I_{-}^{(1,1)}=\frac{2\zeta(3)}{\pi^{2}}\,\\ \bar{\rho}_{\gamma}=\frac{2}{2\pi^{2}}I_{-}^{(2,1)}=\frac{\pi^{2}}{15}\,\\ \bar{P}_{\gamma}=\frac{2}{6\pi^{2}}I_{-}^{(0,3)}=\frac{\pi^{2}}{45}\,\\ \bar{s}_{\gamma}=\bar{\rho}_{\gamma}+\bar{P}_{\gamma}=\frac{4\pi^{2}}{45}\,. (25)

where the definitions for the I±(p,q)I_{\pm}^{(p,q)} are given in App. A.1. Similarly for neutrinos, and assuming that they have a negligible chemical potential, the reduced variables defined in case of LTE, take the constant values

n¯ν=22​π2​I+(1,1)=34​n¯γ​ρ¯ν=22​π2​I+(2,1)=78​ρ¯γ​P¯ν=26​π2​I+(0,3)=78​P¯γ​s¯ν=ρ¯ν+P¯ν=78​s¯γ,\bar{n}_{\nu}&=\frac{2}{2\pi^{2}}I_{+}^{(1,1)}=\frac{3}{4}\bar{n}_{\gamma}\,\\ \bar{\rho}_{\nu}=\frac{2}{2\pi^{2}}I_{+}^{(2,1)}=\frac{7}{8}\bar{\rho}_{\gamma}\,\\ \bar{P}_{\nu}=\frac{2}{6\pi^{2}}I_{+}^{(0,3)}=\frac{7}{8}\bar{P}_{\gamma}\,\\ \bar{s}_{\nu}=\bar{\rho}_{\nu}+\bar{P}_{\nu}=\frac{7}{8}\bar{s}_{\gamma}\,, (26)

where we used gν=1g_{\nu}=1 since only left-handed neutrinos contribute to the relativistic species, but we have multiplied by a factor 22 since conventionally we add together the contributions of neutrinos and antineutrinos66 6 If neutrinos were Majorana particles, neutrinos would be their own antiparticle but they would possess both helicities and one would take g=2g=2, resulting in the same final result. In particular we deduce from Eq. (13) that for photons or (massless) neutrinos in thermodynamical equilibrium

d⁡(a​T)d​t=d⁡(a​Tν)d​t=0,\frac{\mathrm{d}(aT)}{\mathrm{d}t}=\frac{\mathrm{d}(aT_{\nu})}{\mathrm{d}t}=0\,, (27)

if they are completely decoupled from other species. During BBN, a​TaT varies because of electron-positron annihilations. It is customary to define [127, 155]

z≡a⁡(T)​Tzν≡a⁡(Tν)​Tνz\equiv a(T)T\qquad z_{\nu}\equiv a(T_{\nu})T_{\nu} (28)

to characterize this total variation of a​TaT and a​TνaT_{\nu}, with the convention that long before decoupling when all species were coupled together and at the same temperature, that is when T=Tν≫meT=T_{\nu}\gg m_{e}, we had a⁡(T)​T=a⁡(Tν)​Tν=1a(T)T=a(T_{\nu})T_{\nu}=1, that is z=zν=1z=z_{\nu}=1 at early times.

Additionally, in a first approximation, one can also assume that during BBN neutrinos are fully decoupled, implying that a​TνaT_{\nu} is constant and zν=1z_{\nu}=1 remains always true. The tiny effect of incomplete decoupling induces in fact a small variation of zνz_{\nu} that we shall take into account in § II.6. Ignoring it, the neutrino temperature scales simply as

Tν=a0​T0a​z0z0≡z⁡(T≪me),T_{\nu}=\frac{a_{0}T_{0}}{a\,z_{0}}\qquad z_{0}\equiv z(T\ll m_{e})\,, (29)

where T0T_{0} is the photons temperature today and z0z_{0} is the value of zz long after BBN is finished.

II.2 Plasma temperature

Since for the plasma S=s​a3S=sa^{3} is conserved, we can obtain the relation between temperature and scale factor. From Eq. (24) and expressions in App. A, we find that the ratio between plasma entropy at a given time of BBN and photons entropy today is given by

ss0=T3T03​𝒮​(T)​𝒮​(T)≡s¯pls¯γ=s¯γ+s¯e+​(T)+s¯e−​(T)s¯γ=1+2π2​s¯γ​[13​I+(0,3)​(x)+I+(2,1)​(x)]\frac{s}{s_{0}}&=\frac{T^{3}}{T_{0}^{3}}{\cal S}(T)\\ {\cal S}(T)\equiv\frac{\bar{s}_{\rm pl}}{\bar{s}_{\gamma}}=\frac{\bar{s}_{\gamma}+\bar{s}_{e^{+}}(T)+\bar{s}_{e^{-}}(T)}{\bar{s}_{\gamma}}\\ =1+\frac{2}{\pi^{2}\bar{s}_{\gamma}}\left[\frac{1}{3}I_{+}^{(0,3)}(x)+I_{+}^{(2,1)}(x)\right] (30)

z0stand=S1/3​(T≫me)=(114)1/3≃1.40102.z_{0}^{\rm stand}=S^{1/3}(T\gg m_{e})=\left(\frac{11}{4}\right)^{1/3}\simeq 1.40102\,. (32)

From Eqs. (31) and (29) the ratio between neutrino and plasma temperatures is given by

TνT=𝒮1/3​(T)z0stand,\frac{T_{\nu}}{T}=\frac{{\cal S}^{1/3}(T)}{z_{0}^{\rm stand}}\,, (33)

and tends to 1/z0stand=(4/11)1/31/z_{0}^{\rm stand}=(4/11)^{1/3} at low temperatures, which is the celebrated result of instantaneous decoupling.

II.3 Baryon density

In order to obtain the energy density of baryons, it is sufficient to use that for non-relativistic and cold species ρ∝1/a3\rho\propto 1/a^{3}. Hence

ρb=(a0a)3​ρ0crit​Ωb=(a0a)3​ρ100crit×(Ωb​h2)\rho_{\rm b}=\left(\frac{a_{0}}{a}\right)^{3}\rho_{0}^{\rm crit}\Omega_{\rm b}=\left(\frac{a_{0}}{a}\right)^{3}\rho_{100}^{\rm crit}\times\left(\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}\right) (34)

where we defined the critical densities ρ0crit≡3​H02/(8​π​G)\rho_{0}^{\rm crit}\equiv 3H_{0}^{2}/(8\pi G) and ρ100crit≡3​H1002/(8​π​G)\rho_{100}^{\rm crit}\equiv 3H_{100}^{2}/(8\pi G), with the reduced Hubble rate h≡H0/H100h\equiv H_{0}/H_{100} (with the standard definition H100≡100​km/s/MpcH_{100}\equiv 100\,{\rm km}/{\rm s}/{\rm Mpc}). The numerical value of ρ100crit\rho_{100}^{\rm crit} can be found in appendix D. The baryon energy density can be converted into a number density by estimating the average mass of nucleons

nb=ρbmb.n_{\rm b}=\frac{\rho_{\rm b}}{m_{\rm b}}\,. (35)

More details about the definition of mbm_{\rm b} are given in App. C. We define the ratio between baryons and photons by

η≡nbnγ.\eta\equiv\frac{n_{\rm b}}{n_{\gamma}}\,. (36)

Since nb∝1/a3n_{\rm b}\propto 1/a^{3} and nγ∝T3n_{\gamma}\propto T^{3} it can be rewritten in the form

η=η0​(z0z)3.\eta=\eta_{0}\left(\frac{z_{0}}{z}\right)^{3}\,. (37)

Using Eq. (254), the value today is approximately found to be

η0\displaystyle\eta_{0} ≃\displaystyle\simeq 6.0913×10−10​(Ωb​h20.02225)​(2.7255T0)3\displaystyle 6.0913\times 10^{-10}\left(\frac{\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}}{0.02225}\right)\left(\frac{2.7255}{T_{0}}\right)^{3} (38)
×(1−1.759×10−31−1.759×10−3​YP0.24709).\displaystyle\times\left(\frac{1-1.759\times 10^{-3}}{1-1.759\times 10^{-3}\frac{Y_{\rm P}}{0.24709}}\right)\,.

Finally, note that we can safely ignore the thermal energy of baryons since its ratio with the energy density of photons is of order

thus justifying the use of the scaling (34) which is the one of cold particles.

II.4 Cosmology and scale factor

The evolution of the scale factor is dictated by the Friedmann equation

H2=8​π​G3​ρ.H^{2}=\frac{8\pi G}{3}\rho\,. (40)

It determines the evolution of the scale factor a⁡(t)a(t), and to solve it we need the expressions of the total energy density as a function of aa. Since we already have found the relations a⁡(T)a(T), it is sufficient to express the energy density in terms of temperature. This is fortunate, because the energy density of the plasma depends only on temperature as it is always in local thermodynamical equilibrium. From App. A, we find that for the plasma

ρpl=ℰ⁡(T)​ρ¯γ​T4,ℰ⁡(T)≡ρ¯γ+ρ¯e++ρ¯e−ρ¯γ=1+30π4​I+(2,1)​(x),\rho_{\rm pl}&={\cal E}(T)\bar{\rho}_{\gamma}T^{4}\,,\\ {\cal E}(T)\equiv\frac{\bar{\rho}_{\gamma}+\bar{\rho}_{e^{+}}+\bar{\rho}_{e^{-}}}{\bar{\rho}_{\gamma}}=1+\frac{30}{\pi^{4}}I_{+}^{(2,1)}(x)\,, (41)

where we use the definitions (173)-(175). The function ℰ{\cal E} is plotted in Fig. 4 and in the limit T≫meT\gg m_{e} it also tends to 11/411/4. The energy density of the NνN_{\nu} generations of (massless) neutrinos is

ρν=Nν​ρ¯ν​Tν4.\rho_{\nu}=N_{\nu}\bar{\rho}_{\nu}T_{\nu}^{4}\,. (42)

As for the energy density of baryons, we use the simple dilution relation (34) which amounts to neglecting their thermal energy. Hence a similar scaling can be used for cold dark matter.

Using that77 7 The effect of the cosmological constant is also totally negligible as it accounts for less than 10−3010^{-30} of the energy content during BBN even if it dominates today.

ρ=ρν+ρpl+ρb+ρcdm,\rho=\rho_{\nu}+\rho_{\rm pl}+\rho_{\rm b}+\rho_{\rm cdm}, (43)

we obtain ρ⁡(T)\rho(T) that we combine with the relation T⁡(a)T(a) obtained in section II.2 to get ρ⁡(a)\rho(a), such that the Friedmann equation (40) is in the form of an ordinary differential equation for the function a⁡(t)a(t) that we can solve numerically. The relation t⁡(a)t(a) is then deduced by numerical inversion.

II.5 QED corrections for the plasma thermodynamics

The thermal bath of electrons and positrons has electromagnetic interactions with the bath of photons. Using QED, this leads to a modification of the plasma thermodynamics which depend on its temperature. First this leads to an effective modification of the electron and photon masses, which come from the diagrams 5 and 6.

The electron mass is shifted by (see Mangano et al. [126, Eq. 12], Lopez and Turner [123, Eq. 35] or Heckler [95], Fornengo et al. [77] for further details on its derivation)

δ​me2​(p,T)T2\displaystyle\frac{\delta m_{e}^{2}(p,T)}{T^{2}} =\displaystyle= 4​απ​[I−(0,1)+I+(0,1)​(x)]\displaystyle\frac{4\alpha}{\pi}\left[I_{-}^{(0,1)}+I_{+}^{(0,1)}(x)\right] (44)
−\displaystyle- 2​m¯e2​απ​p¯​∫0∞d​q¯​q¯ℰq¯​ln⁡|p¯+q¯p¯−q¯|​g+​(ℰq¯)\displaystyle\frac{2\bar{m}_{e}^{2}\alpha}{\pi\bar{p}}\int_{0}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}\bar{q}\frac{\bar{q}}{{\cal E}_{\bar{q}}}\ln\left|\frac{\bar{p}+\bar{q}}{\bar{p}-\bar{q}}\right|g^{+}\left({\cal E}_{\bar{q}}\right)

where we used the definitions (173)-(175). In this expression, ℰq¯≡q¯2+x2{\cal E}_{\bar{q}}\equiv\sqrt{\bar{q}^{2}+x^{2}}, m¯e=x=me/T\bar{m}_{e}=x=m_{e}/T p¯≡p/T\bar{p}\equiv p/T and g±​(ℰq¯)≡1/(eℰq¯±1)g^{\pm}({\cal E}_{\bar{q}})\equiv 1/({\rm e}^{{\cal E}_{\bar{q}}}\pm 1). The second contribution, which depends explicitly on the e±e^{\pm} momentum, accounts for less than 10%10\% to the total mass shift (see  Mangano et al. [126], Lopez and Turner [123]). The mass shift (44) can be further simplified using

I−(0,1)≡∫0∞g−​(k¯)​k¯​𝑑k¯=π26.I_{-}^{(0,1)}\equiv\int_{0}^{\infty}g^{-}\left(\bar{k}\right)\bar{k}\mathrm{d}\bar{k}=\frac{\pi^{2}}{6}\,. (45)

The photon mass shift is instead given by

δ​mγ2T2=8​απ​I+(0,1)​(x).\frac{\delta m_{\gamma}^{2}}{T^{2}}=\frac{8\alpha}{\pi}I_{+}^{(0,1)}(x)\,. (46)

These mass shifts induce a change in the pressure of the plasma whose expression is given by Heckler [95, Eq. 13] or Mangano et al. [126, Eq. 16]. The pressure shift reads

Hence from the expressions of the mass shifts we get

δ​P¯=δ​P¯d+δ​P¯s,\overline{\delta P}=\overline{\delta P}_{\rm d}+\overline{\delta P}_{\rm s}\,, (48)

where the dominant and subdominant terms are respectively

These pressure modifications are plotted in Fig. 7. We can check that the subdominant contribution is indeed negligible since QED plasma corrections are already very small (see § V.3), but we include it anyway for completeness.

The modification of the plasma energy density is then obtained from the thermodynamic identity88 8 Choosing TT and VV to describe the state of a system, then PP and ρ\rho are functions of TT only since they are intensive quantities. It follows from T​d​S=d⁡(ρ​V)+P​d​VT\mathrm{d}S=\mathrm{d}(\rho V)+P\mathrm{d}V that d​S=(P+ρ)/T​d​V+V/T⁡(d​ρ/d​T)​d​T\mathrm{d}S=(P+\rho)/T\mathrm{d}V+V/T(\mathrm{d}\rho/\mathrm{d}T)\mathrm{d}T. From the integrability conditions we then get ∂T[(ρ+P)/T]=∂V(V/T​d​ρ/d​T)\partial_{T}[(\rho+P)/T]=\partial_{V}(V/T\mathrm{d}\rho/\mathrm{d}T) and the identity (50) follows.

ρ=−P+T​d​Pd​T,\rho=-P+T\frac{\mathrm{d}P}{\mathrm{d}T}\,, (50)

so that we get immediately

δ​ρ¯≡δ​ρT4=3​δ​P¯+∂δ​P¯∂ln⁡T.\overline{\delta\rho}\equiv\frac{\delta\rho}{T^{4}}=3\overline{\delta P}+\frac{\partial\overline{\delta P}}{\partial\ln T}\,. (51)

Lopez and Turner [123] defined corrected relativistic degrees of freedom by

δ​gρ≡2​δ​ρ¯ρ¯γ=30π2​δ​ρ¯,δ​gP≡2​δ​P¯P¯γ=90π2​δ​P¯.\delta g_{\rho}\equiv 2\frac{\overline{\delta\rho}}{\bar{\rho}_{\gamma}}=\frac{30}{\pi^{2}}\overline{\delta\rho}\,,\quad\delta g_{P}\equiv 2\frac{\overline{\delta P}}{\bar{P}_{\gamma}}=\frac{90}{\pi^{2}}\overline{\delta P}\,. (52)

At high temperatures, that is for T≫meT\gg m_{e}, we obtain using I+(0,1)​(x=0)=π2/12I_{+}^{(0,1)}(x=0)=\pi^{2}/12 (see table 9 in appendix A.1) the limits

δ​ρ¯≃−596​(4​π​α),δ​P¯≃13​δ​ρ¯,\overline{\delta\rho}\simeq-\frac{5}{96}(4\pi\alpha)\,,\qquad\overline{\delta P}\simeq\frac{1}{3}\overline{\delta\rho}\,, (53)

which expressed in terms of corrected relativistic degrees of freedom read

δ​gρ≃δ​gP≃−25​α4​π≃0.01452.\delta g_{\rho}\simeq\delta g_{P}\simeq-\frac{25\alpha}{4\pi}\simeq 0.01452\,. (54)

These corrections are plotted in Fig. 8 together with the high temperature limit.

The QED plasma corrections enter in four places.

  • •

    First they imply that the entropy of the plasma as given in Eq. (30) must be modified and we must use

    𝒮QED=𝒮+ρ¯γs¯γ​δ​gρ2+P¯γs¯γ​δ​gP2=𝒮+δ​gP+3​δ​gρ8{\cal S}^{\rm QED}={\cal S}+\frac{\bar{\rho}_{\gamma}}{\bar{s}_{\gamma}}\frac{\delta g_{\rho}}{2}+\frac{\bar{P}_{\gamma}}{\bar{s}_{\gamma}}\frac{\delta g_{P}}{2}={\cal S}+\frac{\delta g_{P}+3\delta g_{\rho}}{8} (55)

    where the last equality follows from Eqs. (25). 𝒮QED{\cal S}^{\rm QED} must be used instead of 𝒮{\cal S} in Eq. (31) in order to obtain a⁡(T)a(T).

  • •

    Second, this entropy modification also affects the evolution of zz and we find

    (z0QED)3=SQED​(T≫me)=114​(1−411​25​α8​π),(z_{0}^{\rm QED})^{3}=S^{\rm QED}(T\gg m_{e})=\frac{11}{4}\left(1-\frac{4}{11}\frac{25\alpha}{8\pi}\right)\,, (56)

    that is z0QED≃1.39979z_{0}^{\rm QED}\simeq 1.39979. This affects the neutrino temperature scaling which then becomes

    TνQED=a0​T0a​z0QED.T^{\rm QED}_{\nu}=\frac{a_{0}T_{0}}{a\,z_{0}^{\rm QED}}\,. (57)

    This neutrino temperature must be used in Eq. (42) when computing the energy density of neutrinos for the Friedmann equation (40).

  • •

    Third, the plasma QED correction must also be incorporated in the energy density of the plasma when solving the Friedmann equation (40), meaning that we must modify Eqs. (41) and use instead

    ℰQED=ℰ+δ​gρ2,{\cal E}^{\rm QED}={\cal E}+\frac{\delta g_{\rho}}{2}\,, (58)

    when computing ρpl\rho_{\rm pl} for the Friedmann equation (40).

  • •

    Finally, the electron mass shifts modifies the statistics of electrons and positrons in the weak-interactions.

An important comment is in order here on the last effect. Since the mass shift (44) is exactly Eq. (5.12) of [25] (that is 2​E​Δ​E=δ​me22E\Delta E=\delta m_{e}^{2}), the effect of the electron mass shift is one of the several effects involved in finite-temperature radiative corrections for the weak rates. Hence, following Brown and Sawyer [25], we consider that the modification of the statistics through the mass shift is part of the finite-temperature corrections and we do not consider that it is part of the QED plasma corrections. This point of view is similar to Esposito et al. [70], Serpico et al. [165] but different from Lopez and Turner [123]. Hence comparisons on the magnitude of the correction must take into account the point of view on the effect of mass shifts, since either they are reported as QED effects or finite-temperature radiative corrections.

It turns out that the QED plasma corrections (that is without the effect of the mass shift on the weak-interaction rates), coming from the modifications (55),(57) and (58), are very small since they modify the Helium production by approximately Δ​YP(4)=−0.1\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=-0.1 (see § V.3).

II.6 Incomplete neutrino decoupling

The effect of incomplete neutrino decoupling has been studied in details in Dodelson and Turner [63], Fields et al. [75], Hannestad and Madsen [94], Gnedin and Gnedin [82], Dolgov et al. [65], Dolgov et al. [66], Esposito et al. [71], Mangano et al. [126], Hannestad [93], Mangano et al. [127], Mangano et al. [128], Birrell et al. [21], Grohs et al. [88], de Salas and Pastor [155]. Electron-positron annihilations lead to a small reheating of the neutrino bath which must be studied in the context of coupled Boltzmann equations since it also leads to spectral distortions in the neutrino spectrum. Furthermore the complete study, that we do not reproduce here, requires to consider neutrino flavor oscillations.

Let us first study the effect of incomplete neutrino decoupling (ID) on the plasma. If there is heat exchange, that is energy exchange between the plasma and the neutrinos, then the evolution of the plasma entropy is dictated by Eq. (20) with the chemical potential neglected, that is

S˙pl=Q˙plT.\dot{S}_{\rm pl}=\frac{\dot{Q}_{\rm pl}}{T}\,. (59)

This is always true for the plasma because it is always at local thermodynamic equilibrium, but not necessarily true for the neutrinos for which we should rely on Eq. (17) if we were to compute the evolution of their entropy. The numerical studies of the effect of incomplete neutrino decoupling gives a fit to the heating rate of the plasma in Pisanti et al. [149]. More precisely, we define the dimensionless function 𝒩⁡(T){\cal N}(T) related to the heating rate as

q˙plH​T=−T3​𝒩​(T),\frac{\dot{q}_{\rm pl}}{HT}=-T^{3}{\cal N}(T)\,, (60)

where we remind Q˙=a3​q˙\dot{Q}=a^{3}\dot{q}. The function T4​𝒩T^{4}{\cal N} can be viewed as the volume heating rate in units of the Hubble rate HH. The fit given in Pisanti et al. [149, Eqs. A24-A25] is a 1313-order polynomial in x=me/Tx=m_{e}/T valid for x<4x<4, and we plot it in Fig. 9.

From Eqs. (59) and (60), the evolution of the plasma reduced entropy is dictated by

1(a​T)3​d⁡[s¯pl​(a​T)3]d​ln⁡a=−𝒩.\frac{1}{(aT)^{3}}\frac{\mathrm{d}[\bar{s}_{\rm pl}(aT)^{3}]}{\mathrm{d}\ln a}=-{\cal N}\,. (61)

From the definition (30) we obtain

d​ln⁡(a​T)d​ln⁡T=𝒩−d​𝒮d​ln⁡T𝒩+3​𝒮\frac{\mathrm{d}\ln(aT)}{\mathrm{d}\ln T}=\frac{{\cal N}-\frac{\mathrm{d}{\cal S}}{\mathrm{d}\ln T}}{{\cal N}+3{\cal S}} (62)

where 𝒮{\cal S} must be replaced by 𝒮QED{\cal S}^{\rm QED} when including plasma QED effects. We recover when 𝒩=0{\cal N}=0, that is for complete neutrino decoupling, that z=aT∝𝒮−1/3z=aT\propto{\cal S}^{-1/3}. This equation can be integrated numerically to obtain a⁡(T)a(T) in the case of incomplete neutrino decoupling, and a numerical inversion allows to obtain subsequently T⁡(a)T(a). zz is modified because of the non-conservation of plasma entropy, and we get z0ID≃1.39911z^{\rm ID}_{0}\simeq 1.39911 if QED plasma effects are not included and z0ID,QED≃1.39788z^{\rm ID,QED}_{0}\simeq 1.39788 if they are also included, in agreement (except for the last digit) with table 1 of de Salas and Pastor [155]. Our results are summarized in table 1.

Let us now focus on the effect of incomplete neutrino decoupling on neutrinos. Since the energy taken from the plasma is gained by the neutrinos, we have necessarily qpl=−qνq_{\rm pl}=-q_{\nu}. Hence we can solve for the evolution of the neutrino energy density from Eq. (12) which is

1a4​d⁡(a4​ρν)d​ln⁡a=−q˙plH=T4​𝒩.\frac{1}{a^{4}}\frac{\mathrm{d}(a^{4}\rho_{\nu})}{\mathrm{d}\ln a}=-\frac{\dot{q}_{\rm pl}}{H}=T^{4}{\cal N}\,. (63)

Since T4​𝒩T^{4}{\cal N} is a function of TT it can be considered as a function of aa using the T⁡(a)T(a) previously obtained. Solving numerically this differential equation gives ρν​(a)\rho_{\nu}(a). Together with the previously solved T⁡(a)T(a) [which allows to get ρpl​(a)\rho_{\rm pl}(a) from Eq. (41)] and the QED correction (58), we obtain ρ⁡(a)\rho(a) and thus the relation a⁡(t)a(t) and its inverse t⁡(a)t(a) from numerically solving the Friedmann equation (40).

This approach to compute the variation of the neutrino energy density from Eq. (63) is correct even if incomplete neutrino decoupling and neutrino reheating by electron-positron annihilations create spectral distortions in the neutrino spectra. That is, the gravitational effect of incomplete neutrino decoupling is taken into account correctly with our approach. However it cannot fully take into account the effect on the weak rates which we discuss further in § III.9 and V.3.5.

II.7 Effective description of neutrinos

Neutrinos are not in local thermodynamical equilibrium and their temperature is not well defined. Indeed, the full characterization of the neutrinos requires to solve the coupled Boltzmann equations dictating the evolution of neutrino distribution functions, and we must in principle build a temperature definition from the energy spectrum (see e.g. Pitrou and Stebbins [150]). In the BBN context it is convenient to define a brightness temperature, being the temperature of the Fermi-Dirac distribution with no chemical potential that would have the same energy density. Hence we define TνT_{\nu} as in Eq. (42) by

ρν=Nν​ρ¯ν​Tν4⇒ρν​a4=Nν​ρ¯ν​zν4,\rho_{\nu}=N_{\nu}\bar{\rho}_{\nu}T_{\nu}^{4}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\rho_{\nu}a^{4}=N_{\nu}\bar{\rho}_{\nu}z^{4}_{\nu}\,, (64)

where ρν\rho_{\nu} results from the integration of Eq. (63). zνz_{\nu}99 9 Note that we still define zνz_{\nu} as in the LTE case [Eq. (28)]. is deduced from the value of ρν​a4\rho_{\nu}a^{4} obtained numerically, and we find zν,0=1.00144z_{\nu,0}=1.00144. It corresponds to a neutrino energy density increase of a factor zν,04=1.00576z^{4}_{\nu,0}=1.00576 compared to the complete decoupling scenario.

The ratio between neutrino and photon temperature is simply

TνT=zνz.\frac{T_{\nu}}{T}=\frac{z_{\nu}}{z}\,. (65)

Using this ratio, Eq. (64) can be rewritten to define an effective number of neutrinos as

ρν=Neff​ρ¯ν​(Tzstand)4Neff≡Nν​(zν​zstandz)4.\rho_{\nu}=N_{\rm eff}\bar{\rho}_{\nu}\left(\frac{T}{z^{\rm stand}}\right)^{4}\quad N_{\rm eff}\equiv N_{\nu}\left(\frac{z_{\nu}z^{\rm stand}}{z}\right)^{4}\,. (66)

This is the number of neutrinos that would be required to have the same energy density if the ratio Tν/TT_{\nu}/T was taken from the complete decoupling result without QED correction, that is 1/zstand1/z^{\rm stand}. NeffN_{\rm eff} today is completely determined by the values of z0z_{0} and zν,0z_{\nu,0}. Its evolution is plotted in Fig. 10.

We find NeffID=3.0337N^{\rm ID}_{\rm eff}=3.0337 today if QED plasma effects are ignored [zz obtained from Eq. (62) and zνz_{\nu} from Eqs. (63) and (65)] but non-instantaneous decoupling is taken into account. We find NeffQED=3.0106N^{\rm QED}_{\rm eff}=3.0106 for the reverse situation (zν=1z_{\nu}=1 but z=zQEDz=z^{\rm QED}). If both effects are taken into account [zz obtained from Eq. (62) with 𝒮QED{\cal S}^{\rm QED} instead of 𝒮{\cal S}, and zνz_{\nu} from Eqs. (63) and (65)], we find NeffID,QED=3.0444N^{\rm ID,QED}_{\rm eff}=3.0444, in very close agreement with the last results of de Salas and Pastor [155].

After BBN, e.g. for the evolution of initial perturbations through baryon acoustic oscillations, only the energy density of neutrinos is important through its gravitational effect. Distortions in the neutrino spectra can have in principle an effect on CMB and structure formation when considering its joint effect with neutrino masses at late times. However this effect is expected to be extremely small and it is enough to assume that after BBN neutrinos follow a Fermi-Dirac distribution. Hence NeffN_{\rm eff} is used in CMB codes such as CAMB [119, 120] and CLASS [118, 22] to take into account the effect of incomplete decoupling during BBN. From the definition (66) the total energy density of radiation after BBN is

ρR=ρν+ργ=ργ​(1+78​Neff​(411)4/3)\rho_{\rm R}=\rho_{\nu}+\rho_{\gamma}=\rho_{\gamma}\left(1+\frac{7}{8}N_{\rm eff}\left(\frac{4}{11}\right)^{4/3}\right)\, (67)

meaning that we can forget about the QED plasma corrections and the incomplete neutrino decoupling during BBN if we use NeffN_{\rm eff} instead of Nν=3N_{\nu}=3.

The values of z0z_{0}, zν,0z_{\nu,0} and NeffN_{\rm eff} for the various cases are reported in table 1. Let us comment on the value Neff≃3.02N_{\rm eff}\simeq 3.02 found in Grohs et al. [88] for the effect of QED alone. It is important to realize that we must be careful not to replace the mass shifts (44) and (46) directly in the distribution function inside the general expression (170) for pressure to obtain the pressure shift (47), since this would overestimate it by a factor 22. This subtlety is detailed in Heckler [95] and is correctly taken into account in Mangano et al. [126]. Since this is what has been done in Grohs et al. [88], it explains why the effect of QED on the plasma as measured by NeffN_{\rm eff} found in this reference is around 3.023.02 instead of 3.013.01.

III Weak Interactions

Once the dynamics of the background has been solved, it is possible to study the evolution of the abundance of neutrons. This determines the final amount of chemical species since atomic nuclei form from the fusion of neutrons and protons. Throughout we assume that all particles are in local thermodynamical equilibrium. If this is certainly true for the plasma of photons strongly coupled with electrons and positrons, this is not exactly true for neutrinos. Indeed, as we have seen in § II.6, neutrinos are not fully decoupled when BBN takes place and there is a residual heating of neutrinos which cannot be fully described as an increased neutrino temperature, since it also leads to a distorted neutrino spectrum.

III.1 General formulation

The weak interaction reactions correspond to a set of reactions which are all related by crossing symmetry. These are the six reactions

n+ν↔p+e−​n↔p+e−+ν¯​n+e+↔p+ν¯n+\nu&\leftrightarrow p+e^{-}\\ n\leftrightarrow p+e^{-}+\bar{\nu}\\ n+e^{+}\leftrightarrow p+\bar{\nu} (68)

where nn (pp) stands for neutrons (protons). The two reactions n+e++ν↔pn+e^{+}+\nu\leftrightarrow p are not possible energetically since mn>mpm_{n}>m_{p}, as can be seen considering the reaction in the proton rest mass frame. However it can exist if there is a photon in the final state of the forward reaction, see appendix § B.7.

It follows that the number density of neutrons and protons is not just diluted by expansion, but varies according to the reaction rates. The general form for the neutron-proton density evolution is

n˙n+3​H​nn=−nn​Γn→p+np​Γp→n​n˙p+3​H​np=−np​Γp→n+nn​Γn→p\dot{n}_{n}+3Hn_{n}&=-n_{n}\Gamma_{n\to p}+n_{p}\Gamma_{p\to n}\\ \dot{n}_{p}+3Hn_{p}=-n_{p}\Gamma_{p\to n}+n_{n}\Gamma_{n\to p} (69)

where the reaction rates Γ\Gamma are associated to the corresponding collision terms in the Boltzmann equation. Here we have gathered the rates according to

Γn→p=Γn+ν→p+e+Γn→p+e+ν¯+Γn+e→p+ν¯​Γp→n=Γp+e→n+ν+Γp+e+ν¯→n+Γp+ν¯→n+e.\Gamma_{n\to p}&=\Gamma_{n+\nu\to p+e}+\Gamma_{n\to p+e+\bar{\nu}}+\Gamma_{n+e\to p+\bar{\nu}}\\ \Gamma_{p\to n}=\Gamma_{p+e\to n+\nu}+\Gamma_{p+e+\bar{\nu}\to n}+\Gamma_{p+\bar{\nu}\to n+e}. (70)

The general expression for these reaction rates is detailed in App. B. For all rates with the nucleon aa in the initial state and nucleon bb in the final state, they take the form

na​Γa→b=∫d3​𝐩a​d3​𝐩e​d3​𝐩ν24​(2​π)8​δ​(Ea−Eb+αe​Ee+αν​Eν)​|M|a→b2En​Ep​Ee​Eν​fa​(Ea)​fν​(αν​Eν)​fe​(αe​Ee)n_{a}\Gamma_{a\to b}=\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}_{a}\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}_{e}\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}_{\nu}}{2^{4}(2\pi)^{8}}\delta\left({E}_{a}-E_{b}+\alpha_{e}E_{e}+\alpha_{\nu}E_{\nu}\right)\frac{\left|M\right|^{2}_{a\to b}}{{E}_{n}{E}_{p}{E}_{e}{E}_{\nu}}f_{a}(E_{a})f_{\nu}(\alpha_{\nu}{E}_{\nu})f_{e}(\alpha_{e}{E}_{e}) (71)

where αν=1\alpha_{\nu}=1 if the neutrino is in the initial state and αν=−1\alpha_{\nu}=-1 if it is in the final state, and a similar definition for αe\alpha_{e} according to the e±{\rm e}^{\pm} position. These coefficients appear obviously in the Dirac delta function ensuring energy conservation in reactions, and they are also used to express the final nucleon momentum as pb=pa+αν​pν+αe​pep_{b}=p_{a}+\alpha_{\nu}p_{\nu}+\alpha_{e}p_{e}. They also appear in the distribution functions of the electrons and neutrinos, because either the particle is in the initial state and the corresponding distribution function appears in the expression, or it is in the final state and it becomes a Pauli-blocking factor thanks to the relation

f⁡(−E)=1−f⁡(E),f(-E)=1-f(E)\,, (72)

valid for a Fermi-Dirac distribution with vanishing chemical potential. For a given reaction, |M|a→b2\left|M\right|^{2}_{a\to b} is the corresponding matrix-element of the weak interaction summed over all initial and final states. For weak interactions in the Fermi theory, it is of the form [73]

|M|227​GF2=cL​L​ℳL​L+cR​R​ℳR​R+cL​R​ℳL​R,\frac{|M|^{2}}{2^{7}G_{F}^{2}}=c_{LL}{\cal M}_{LL}+c_{RR}{\cal M}_{RR}+c_{LR}{\cal M}_{LR}\,, (73)

with the coupling factors c..c_{..} given in Eqs. (203). The expressions for ℳL​L,ℳR​R,ℳL​R{\cal M}_{LL},{\cal M}_{RR},{\cal M}_{LR} are reported in Eqs. (204). The L​LLL term (resp. R​RRR) corresponds to purely left-chiral (resp. right-chiral) couplings, and the L​RLR term is an interference term.

III.2 Infinite nucleon mass approximation

Let us define the energy gap

Δ≡mn−mp≃1.29333​MeV.\Delta\equiv m_{n}-m_{p}\simeq 1.29333\,\,{\rm MeV}\,. (74)

Throughout we use g⁡(E)g(E) for the Fermi-Dirac distribution at temperature of electrons TT and gν​(E)g_{\nu}(E) for the Fermi-Dirac distribution at the neutrino temperature TνT_{\nu}.

g⁡(E)≡1(eET+1)gν​(E)≡1(eETν+1).g(E)\equiv\frac{1}{\left({\rm e}^{\frac{E}{T}}+1\right)}\qquad g_{\nu}(E)\equiv\frac{1}{\left({\rm e}^{\frac{E}{T_{\nu}}}+1\right)}\,. (75)

In § II, details are given on how these temperatures can be computed in function of the scale factor aa and the time tt.

In the infinite nucleon mass limit (but keeping Δ\Delta constant), also called the Born approximation, the reaction rates take simple forms (see App. B). First, the factors entering the matrix element (73) are in that limit simply

ℳL​LEn​Ep​Eν​Ee=ℳR​REn​Ep​Eν​Ee=ℳL​REn​Ep​Eν​Ee=1.\frac{{\cal M}_{LL}}{E_{n}E_{p}E_{\nu}E_{e}}=\frac{{\cal M}_{RR}}{E_{n}E_{p}E_{\nu}E_{e}}=\frac{{\cal M}_{LR}}{E_{n}E_{p}E_{\nu}E_{e}}=1\,. (76)

The last equality is correct only if it is understood that an angular average either on electrons momentum or neutrino momentum is performed1010 10 The LR coupling is at the origin of the asymmetry (214) in the decay product of neutron beta decay [108] from which the value of gAg_{A} is inferred. (see the detailed explanation at the end of § B.2). Hence from Eq. (71), we find the Born rates [25, 123, 184, 20]

Γ¯n→p\displaystyle\overline{\Gamma}_{n\to p} =\displaystyle= Γ¯n→p+e+Γ¯n+e→p\displaystyle\overline{\Gamma}_{n\to p+e}+\overline{\Gamma}_{n+e\to p} (77)
=\displaystyle= K​∫0∞p2​𝑑p​[χ+​(E)+χ+​(−E)],\displaystyle K\int_{0}^{\infty}p^{2}\mathrm{d}p[\chi_{+}(E)+\chi_{+}(-E)]\,, (78)

with E=p2+me2E=\sqrt{p^{2}+m_{e}^{2}} and

χ±​(E)\displaystyle\chi_{\pm}(E) ≡\displaystyle\equiv (Eν∓)2​gν​(Eν∓)​g​(−E),\displaystyle(E_{\nu}^{\mp})^{2}g_{\nu}(E^{\mp}_{\nu})g(-E)\,, (79)
Eν∓\displaystyle E^{\mp}_{\nu} ≡\displaystyle\equiv E∓Δ,\displaystyle E\mp\Delta\,, (80)
K\displaystyle K ≡\displaystyle\equiv 4​GW2​(1+3​gA2)(2​π)3.\displaystyle\frac{4G_{W}^{2}(1+3g_{A}^{2})}{(2\pi)^{3}}\,. (81)

The first contribution in Eq. (77) corresponds to the n→pn\to p processes (68) and (68) added, that is for all processes where the electron is in the final state. It can be checked indeed that the electron distribution is evaluated as g⁡(−E)=1−g⁡(E)g(-E)=1-g(E). Furthermore, if the neutrino is in the initial state (when E>ΔE>\Delta) its energy is Eν=E−ΔE_{\nu}=E-\Delta and its distribution function appears as gν​(Eν)g_{\nu}(E_{\nu}), but if it is in the final state (when E<ΔE<\Delta) its energy is Eν=Δ−EE_{\nu}=\Delta-E and the neutrino distribution function is evaluated as gν​(E−Δ)=1−gν​(Δ−E)g_{\nu}(E-\Delta)=1-g_{\nu}(\Delta-E).

The second term of Eq. (77) corresponds to the reaction (68), that is to the process where the positron is in the initial state. The energy of the positron is EE and its distribution function appears as an initial state [g⁡(E)g(E)], whereas the neutrinos in the final state have energy Eν=Δ+EE_{\nu}=\Delta+E and their distribution function appear thus as Pauli-blocking factor gν​(−E−Δ)=1−gν​(E+Δ)g_{\nu}(-E-\Delta)=1-g_{\nu}(E+\Delta).

The reaction rate for protons, that is Γp→n\Gamma_{p\to n}, is obtained by the simple replacement Δ→−Δ\Delta\to-\Delta, which amounts to χ+→χ−\chi_{+}\to\chi_{-}. We give it for completeness

Γ¯p→n\displaystyle\overline{\Gamma}_{p\to n} =\displaystyle= Γ¯p→n+e+Γ¯p+e→n\displaystyle\overline{\Gamma}_{p\to n+e}+\overline{\Gamma}_{p+e\to n} (82)
=\displaystyle= K​∫0∞p2​𝑑p​[χ−​(E)+χ−​(−E)].\displaystyle K\int_{0}^{\infty}p^{2}\mathrm{d}p[\chi_{-}(E)+\chi_{-}(-E)]\,. (83)

Similarly the second term corresponds to the reverse processes (68) and (68) added since the electron distribution function is always in an initial state [g⁡(E)g(E)], and the neutrino is in the initial or final state depending on the sign of Eν=−E+ΔE_{\nu}=-E+\Delta. The first term corresponds to the reverse process (68) with the positron always in the final state [g⁡(−E)=1−g⁡(E)g(-E)=1-g(E)] and the neutrino always in the initial state [gν​(E+Δ)g_{\nu}(E+\Delta)].

Finally, note that using

g⁡(−E)=1−g⁡(E)=eE/T​g​(E),g(-E)=1-g(E)={\rm e}^{E/T}g(E)\,, (84)

we get in the case of thermal equilibrium between neutrinos and the plasma (that is when Tν=TT_{\nu}=T)

χ+​(E)=eΔ/T​χ−​(−E).\chi_{+}(E)={\rm e}^{\Delta/T}\chi_{-}(-E)\,. (85)

This implies that if neutrinos have the same temperature as the plasma, the reaction rates satisfy the Born approximation detailed balance relation

Γ¯p→n=e−Δ/TΓ¯n→p.\overline{\Gamma}_{p\to n}={\rm e}^{-\Delta/T}\overline{\Gamma}_{n\to p}\,. (86)

It is important that detailed balance be satisfied in our estimation of the weak rates since it is at the origin of the enforcement of the thermodynamical equilibrium between neutrons and protons. When adding corrections to the Born approximation weak rates in the form Γ≡δ​Γ+Γ¯\Gamma\equiv\delta\Gamma+\overline{\Gamma}, then the relative corrections of the forward and reverse rates must be equal, that is

δ​Γp→nΓ¯p→n=δ​Γn→pΓ¯n→p,\frac{\delta\Gamma_{p\to n}}{\overline{\Gamma}_{p\to n}}=\frac{\delta\Gamma_{n\to p}}{\overline{\Gamma}_{n\to p}}\,, (87)

in order that the corrected rates also satisfy the detailed balance property (86). When estimating the corrections to the Born rates, we systematically discuss how this detailed balance is kept valid with the corrections and we highlight our differences on that crucial property with previous literature.

III.3 Calibration from free neutron decay rate

The interaction rates are proportional to the factor KK defined in Eq. (81). It is proportional to

GW2≡GF2​cos2⁡(θC)G_{W}^{2}\equiv G_{F}^{2}\cos^{2}(\theta_{\rm C}) (88)

where GFG_{F} is the Fermi constant and θC\theta_{\rm C} is a CKM angle, and also to 1+3​gA21+3g_{A}^{2} where gAg_{A} is the axial current constant for the nucleons (see App. D for numerical values). Given the uncertainty in these parameters, it is more precise to obtain KK from the free neutron decay1111 11 The relative precision on cos⁡(θC)\cos(\theta_{\rm C}) and gAg_{A} are respectively 2.0×10−42.0\times 10^{-4} and 1.8×10−31.8\times 10^{-3}. If τn\tau_{n} was to be obtained theoretically from these constants, then its uncertainty δ​τn/τn≃2​δ​cos⁡(θC)/cos⁡(θC)+1.66​δ​gA/gA\delta\tau_{n}/\tau_{n}\simeq 2\delta\cos(\theta_{\rm C})/\cos(\theta_{\rm C})+1.66\delta g_{A}/g_{A} would be of order 3×10−33\times 10^{-3} which is larger than the experimental uncertainty which is of order 1.0×10−31.0\times 10^{-3}. However improvements in the measurements of gAg_{A} by a factor 3 would make this direct estimation of τn\tau_{n} competitive.. Indeed, at low temperatures, Γn→p\Gamma_{n\to p} should be equal to the free neutron decay rate 1/τn1/\tau_{n}. The low temperature corresponds to (77) restricted to Eν<0E_{\nu}<0, that is

1τn=Γn→p​(T=0)=K​∫0Δ2−me2p2​Eν2​𝑑p,\frac{1}{\tau_{n}}=\Gamma_{n\to p}(T=0)=K\int_{0}^{\sqrt{\Delta^{2}-m_{e}^{2}}}p^{2}E_{\nu}^{2}\mathrm{d}p\,, (89)

λ¯0\displaystyle\bar{\lambda}_{0} ≡\displaystyle\equiv me−5​∫0Δ2−me2p2​Eν2​𝑑p\displaystyle m_{e}^{-5}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{\Delta^{2}-m_{e}^{2}}}p^{2}E_{\nu}^{2}\mathrm{d}p (92)
=\displaystyle= Δ¯2−1​(−8−9​Δ¯2+2​Δ¯460)+Δ¯4​arccosh⁡Δ¯\displaystyle\sqrt{\bar{\Delta}^{2}-1}\left(\frac{-8-9\bar{\Delta}^{2}+2\bar{\Delta}^{4}}{60}\right)+\frac{\bar{\Delta}}{4}\arccosh\bar{\Delta}
≃\displaystyle\simeq 1.63609,\displaystyle 1.63609,

III.4 Neutron abundance and freeze-out

It is enough to consider the weak rates in the Born approximation to estimate the freeze-out temperature. The Born rates are plotted in Fig. 11 together with the Hubble rate.

A first estimation of the freeze-out temperature consists in noting that expansion overcomes both rates for TF≃8×109​KT_{F}\simeq 8\times 10^{9}{\rm K} which we can take as the freeze-out temperature.

We can justify this estimation by finding an approximate solution for the neutron abundance. Its evolution, in absence of nuclear reactions, is dictated by

X˙n=Xp​Γp→n−Xn​Γn→p.\dot{X}_{n}=X_{p}\Gamma_{p\to n}-X_{n}\Gamma_{n\to p}\,. (93)

Using Xp=1−XnX_{p}=1-X_{n}, we get

Xn=Γp→nΛ−1Λ​X˙n,Λ≡Γp→n+Γn→p.X_{n}=\frac{\Gamma_{p\to n}}{\Lambda}-\frac{1}{\Lambda}\dot{X}_{n}\,,\qquad\Lambda\equiv\Gamma_{p\to n}+\Gamma_{n\to p}\,. (94)

We obtain tight-coupling solutions to order mm by recursive replacement of XnX_{n} and we get

Xn(m)=∑k=0m(−1Λ​dd​t)k​Γp→nΛ.X_{n}^{(m)}=\sum_{k=0}^{m}\left(\frac{-1}{\Lambda}\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\right)^{k}\frac{\Gamma_{p\to n}}{\Lambda}\,. (95)

m=0m=0 corresponds to the pure thermodynamical equilibrium and higher order corrections are due to the fact that the neutron abundance has less and less time to approach this equilibrium value. This expansion is equivalent to Bernstein et al. [20, Eq. 2.8]. We can estimate the freeze-out temperature, that is the temperature at which weak interactions fail to maintain the thermodynamical equilibrium value, by computing the temperature for which the first correction is of order of the equilibrium value, that is when |Xn(1)−Xn(0)|=Xn(0)|X_{n}^{(1)}-X_{n}^{(0)}|=X_{n}^{(0)}. Assuming that the neutrino temperature does not differ significantly from the plasma temperature before freeze-out, we can use Eq. (86) to estimate this condition which reads

H​QT​eQ/T1+eQ/T=Λ.H\frac{Q}{T}\frac{{\rm e}^{Q/T}}{1+{\rm e}^{Q/T}}=\Lambda\,. (96)

We find TF≃8.9×109​K≃0.77​MeVT_{F}\simeq 8.9\times 10^{9}{\rm K}\simeq 0.77\,{\rm MeV} and replacing in the thermodynamical equilibrium abundance we get

XnF≡Xn(0)​(TF)≃0.156.X_{n}^{F}\equiv X_{n}^{(0)}(T_{F})\simeq 0.156\,. (97)

Finally, another estimation consists in determining visually when the neutron abundance is only affected by beta decay. In Fig. 3, this leads to TF≃3.3×109​K≃0.28​MeVT_{F}\simeq 3.3\times 10^{9}\,{\rm K}\simeq 0.28\,{\rm MeV} and XnF≃0.17X_{n}^{F}\simeq 0.17.

After the freeze-out, the neutron abundance is only affected by the neutron beta decay. The nucleosynthesis starts approximately when T<TNuc=0.078​MeVT<T_{\rm Nuc}=0.078\,{\rm MeV}, or 0.9 GK (see § V.2) corresponding to roughly tNuc=200​st_{\rm Nuc}=200\,{\rm s}. The neutron abundance when the nucleosynthesis starts is thus approximately given by

Xn​(TNuc)=XnF​exp​(−tnuc−tFτn)≈0.13.X_{n}(T_{\rm Nuc})=X^{F}_{n}{\rm exp}\left(-\frac{t_{\rm nuc}-t_{F}}{\tau_{n}}\right)\approx 0.13\,. (98)

III.5 Radiative corrections at T=0T=0

III.5.1 Standard computation

Radiative corrections at T=0T=0 correspond to two types of corrections [169, 1, 62, 114]. First the radiative corrections per se, that is for which a virtual photon is emitted and absorbed inside the interaction and which interfere with the lowest order or Born diagram. Hereafter we call these pure radiative corrections and the relevant diagrams in the infinite nucleon mass limit are depicted in Fig. 13 (see also Ivanov et al. [108, App. C]). As shown in the seminal article by Sirlin [169], the other diagrams involving virtual photons1212 12 These extra diagrams correspond first to a virtual photon exchange between the electron and the gauge boson, and between the electron and the neutron [169, Fig. 1], and second to a virtual photon exchange between the proton and the gauge boson and between the proton and the neutron [169, Fig. 3]. can be reabsorbed in the redefinitions of GFG_{F} and gAg_{A}.

Second it also contains the corrections due to the emission of real photon [1, Fig 2e,2f]. These processes are generically called bremsstrahlung (BS), and in the infinite nucleon mass approximation only the emission from the electron line (Fig. 14a) contributes.

It is necessary to handle these two types of corrections simultaneously, because each of these contributions contains an infrared divergence in the photon momentum. But as is well known, when both are considered, these divergences exactly cancel provided they are correctly regularized. The usual procedure consists in letting the photon have a mass for the computation of each type of correction, and then noticing that the log-divergences which appear are exactly opposite, leading to a finite result in the limit mγ→0m_{\gamma}\to 0 [1]; [108, App. B]. These radiative corrections are very well understood for the neutron beta decay [169, 1, 57, 129]. The main result is that radiative corrections can be taken into account by a multiplicative factor whose expression involves Sirlin’s universal function [169, Eq. 20b]. This was subsequently refined mainly to improve the expression of the high energy cut-off which was related to the mass of the vector boson once weak interactions were properly understood, and we use Czarnecki et al. [57] as the most accurate account on this issue.

A careful analysis however indicates that only pure radiative corrections take a universal form which can be used for all the reactions (68). They are given by Abers et al. [1, Eq. 6.2] and depend only on the electron velocity β=p/E\beta=p/E 1313 13 Even though they have been derived for neutron beta decay, they remain formally identical for other reactions because they are related by crossing symmetry under which β\beta is left invariant.. The total corrections for the neutron beta decay include also the bremsstrahlung [1, Eq. 6.6] and these are computed specifically for the neutron beta decay, with a maximum photon energy being Δ−E\Delta-E.

Hence, the radiative corrections for the reactions (68) should in principle be recomputed to take into account the correct bremsstrahlung corrections for each reaction. However it proves much more convenient to temporarily forget about this issue and assume that the radiative corrections computed for the neutron beta decay can be used without modification for all weak reactions. We postpone the correct treatment of bremsstrahlung to the next section.

Note that even for the neutron beta decay this approximation amounts to ignoring the Pauli-blocking effects of the neutrinos which is modified by the energy subtracted from the photon. In this approximation, the maximum energy of emitted photons is chosen to be the maximum energy of the neutrino when in the final state. For the neutron beta decay this is Δ−E\Delta-E, but for reaction (68) this is Δ+E\Delta+E.

Under this assumption, our method to compute the radiative correction at T=0T=0 follows exactly the approach by Dicus et al. [62] and subsequent literature based on it, for which the same assumption was implicitly made. The radiative corrections can be separated between a Coulomb correction, which accounts for the motion of the electron in the Coulomb field of the proton, and the other corrections. It is customary to factorize the Coulomb corrections as they can be taken into account multiplicatively by the Fermi function1414 14 This amounts to including some radiative corrections which are higher order in αFS\alpha_{\rm FS}.. The diagram 13c corresponds to the interaction between the proton and the electron, and since this is accounted for by the Fermi function, its Coulomb part is subtracted so as to avoid double counting.

The non-relativistic Fermi function is

F⁡(E)≡y1−e−y,y≡2​π​αFSββ=pE.F(E)\equiv\frac{y}{1-{\rm e}^{-y}}\,,\qquad y\equiv\frac{2\pi\alpha_{\rm FS}}{\beta}\quad\beta=\frac{p}{E}\,. (99)

The relativistic Fermi function is given by [108, Eq. 5]

F⁡(E)\displaystyle F(E) ≡\displaystyle\equiv 4​(1+γ2)​(2​rp​me​β)2​γΓ2​(3+2​γ)​eπ​αFS/β(1−β2)γ\displaystyle\frac{4\left(1+\tfrac{\gamma}{2}\right)(2r_{p}m_{e}\beta)^{2\gamma}}{\Gamma^{2}(3+2\gamma)}\frac{{\rm e}^{\pi\alpha_{\rm FS}/\beta}}{(1-\beta^{2})^{\gamma}} (100)
×|Γ⁡(1+γ+i​αFSβ)|2\displaystyle\qquad\times\left|\Gamma\left(1+\gamma+\mathrm{i}\frac{\alpha_{\rm FS}}{\beta}\right)\right|^{2}

where γ≡1−αFS2−1\gamma\equiv\sqrt{1-\alpha_{\rm FS}^{2}}-1 and rpr_{p} is the proton radius. In practice the non-relativistic function is enough as long as we do not focus on a precision on YP(4)Y_{\rm P}^{(4)} better than unity.
