The modification on light elements yields is evaluated in § V.3 and we find Δ​YP(4)≃0.3\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 0.3 when using the relativistic Fermi function (see also Smith and Fuller [170] which reports Δ​YP(4)≃0.4\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 0.4). In this work we use the relativistic Fermi function whenever it is not specified differently. The relative difference between the two Fermi functions is plotted in Fig. 15 and it remains smaller than 0.06%0.06\%.

Considering the contributions of Coulomb and other radiative corrections, the Born rates are modified as

Γn→pRC0\displaystyle{\Gamma}^{{{\rm RC}}0}_{n\to p} =\displaystyle= K∫0∞p2dp[ℱ+(E)R(E,|Δ−E|)χ+(E)\displaystyle K\int_{0}^{\infty}p^{2}\mathrm{d}p[{\cal F}_{+}(E)R(E,|\Delta-E|)\chi_{+}(E) (101)
+ℱ+(−E)R(E,Δ+E)χ+(−E)].\displaystyle\qquad+{\cal F}_{+}(-E)R(E,\Delta+E)\chi_{+}(-E)]\,.

The Coulomb corrections occur only if both the electron and the proton are either in the initial or the final state. We have thus defined the compact notation

ℱ±​(x)={F⁡(|x|)if±x>01if±x≤0,{\cal F}_{\pm}(x)=\begin{cases}F(|x|)&{\rm if}\quad\pm x>0\\ 1&{\rm if}\quad\pm x\leq 0\,,\\ \end{cases} (102)

which ensures that this is the case.

The factor R(.,.)R(.,.) takes into account pure radiative corrections and bremsstrahlung (but only in the form of neutron beta decay in vacuum as evoked above) and is of the form

R⁡(E,kmax)≡1+αFS2​π​𝒞​(E,kmax).R(E,k_{\rm max})\equiv 1+\frac{\alpha_{\rm FS}}{2\pi}{\cal C}\left(E,k_{\rm max}\right)\,. (103)

The function 𝒞{\cal C} is given in Eq. (222). However we find it better to use the most recent form (227) for the radiative correction R⁡(E,kkmax)R(E,k_{\rm kmax}) which amounts to resumming higher order corrections, since it is more accurate [69, 57]. We show in § V.3 that it modifies the He4{}^{4}{\rm He} production by Δ​YP(4)≃0.2\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 0.2.

The rate for protons is obtained by the replacement Δ→−Δ\Delta\to-\Delta in (101), that is from χ+→χ−\chi_{+}\to\chi_{-}, together with the replacement ℱ+→ℱ−{\cal F}_{+}\to{\cal F}_{-} to ensure that the Fermi function appears when the proton and the electron are on the same side. Hence it is given by

Γp→nRC0\displaystyle{\Gamma}^{{{\rm RC}}0}_{p\to n} =\displaystyle= K∫0∞p2dp[ℱ−(E)R(E,E+Δ)χ−(E)\displaystyle K\int_{0}^{\infty}p^{2}\mathrm{d}p[{\cal F}_{-}(E)R(E,E+\Delta)\chi_{-}(E) (104)
+ℱ−(−E)R(E,|E−Δ|)χ−(−E)].\displaystyle\quad+{\cal F}_{-}(-E)R(E,|E-\Delta|)\chi_{-}(-E)]\,.

Given our choice to take into account the bremsstrahlung corrections of neutron beta decay for all processes and our choice for the maximum energy of emitted photons kmaxk_{\rm max}, then by construction the detailed balance property (86) is preserved using again the property (85), that is we get by construction

ΓRC0p→n=e−Δ/TΓRC0n→p.{\Gamma}^{\rm RC0}_{p\to n}={\rm e}^{-\Delta/T}{\Gamma}^{\rm RC0}_{n\to p}\,. (105)

The relative variations of the weak rates from radiative corrections are plotted in Fig. 16.

The radiative corrections also affect the free decay rate of neutrons and thus the value of λ0\lambda_{0} which is increased to

λ0RC0\displaystyle\lambda^{{{\rm RC}}0}_{0} ≡\displaystyle\equiv me−5​∫0Δ2−me2F⁡(E)​R​(E,Eν)​p2​Eν2​𝑑p\displaystyle m_{e}^{-5}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{\Delta^{2}-m_{e}^{2}}}F(E)R(E,E_{\nu})p^{2}E_{\nu}^{2}\mathrm{d}p (106)
≃\displaystyle\simeq 1.75767,\displaystyle 1.75767\,,

with Eν=Δ−EE_{\nu}=\Delta-E.

III.5.2 Bremsstrahlung corrections

It was argued in Brown and Sawyer [25] that the detailed balance relation (86) should hold even including radiative corrections at order αFS\alpha_{\rm FS}, as long as we work in the infinite nucleon mass approximation. Hence the derivation of radiative corrections due to interactions with the surrounding bath of particles, which are usually called finite-temperature corrections, must satisfy this detailed balance relation. These corrections correspond to real photon processes which are the absorption diagram 14b together with the stimulated emission part of 14a, and to mass shift effects illustrated by the diagrams 17.

The full computation of the finite temperature radiative corrections was carefully carried out in Brown and Sawyer [25], following the guideline of detailed balance and with a detailed discussion on misconceptions in earlier efforts [62, 27, 157, 31, 70] concerning the so called wave-function renormalization. However the authors of Brown and Sawyer [25] reported that when combining their results with the null-temperature radiative corrections discussed in the previous section, the rates failed to satisfy the detailed balance relation. We argue that this is because bremsstrahlung was inconsistently taken into account. As long as we take into account only null-temperature radiative corrections, it is reasonable to consider that the bremsstrahlung effects are those of the neutron beta decay for all reactions, so as to maintain the detailed balance relation (86). This is what has been done in the previous section.

Strictly speaking it is a mistake because part of the null-temperature corrections are left out. However it is the most reasonable procedure if one ignores the full details of the finite-temperature radiative corrections. Here since we take into account the interactions with the bath of photons and electrons in the finite temperature radiative corrections, we must also correct for this ad-hoc and incorrect treatment of bremsstrahlung in the previous section. The details are reported in appendix B.7 and the result is that we need to add the corrections

δ​Γn→pBS=αFS​K2​π​∫me∞d​E​[g⁡(−E)​ℱ+​(E)​γn→p+eBS+g⁡(E)​ℱ+​(−E)​γn+e→pBS]​δ​Γp→nBS=αFS​K2​π​∫me∞d​E​[g⁡(−E)​ℱ−​(E)​γp→n+eBS+g⁡(E)​ℱ−​(−E)​γp+e→nBS],\delta\Gamma^{\rm BS}_{n\to p}&=\frac{\alpha_{\rm FS}K}{2\pi}\int_{m_{e}}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}E\left[g(-E){\cal F}_{+}(E)\gamma^{\rm BS}_{n\to p+e}\right.\\ \qquad\qquad\left.+g(E){\cal F}_{+}(-E)\gamma^{\rm BS}_{n+e\to p}\right]\\ \delta\Gamma^{\rm BS}_{p\to n}=\frac{\alpha_{\rm FS}K}{2\pi}\int_{m_{e}}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}E\left[g(-E){\cal F}_{-}(E)\gamma^{\rm BS}_{p\to n+e}\right.\\ \qquad\qquad\left.+g(E){\cal F}_{-}(-E)\gamma^{\rm BS}_{p+e\to n}\right]\,, (107)

with the definitions (240-241). Note that we have added the Fermi factor contribution for consistency with the rest of the radiative corrections. Their temperature dependence is plotted in Fig. 18. Even though these BS corrections correspond to null temperature radiative corrections, unless specified we include them as part of the finite temperature radiative corrections discussed in the next section, since they must be added only to maintain consistently the detailed balance relation when finite temperature radiative corrections are included. We report in § V.3 that these BS corrections are responsible for a non-negligible modification of He4{}^{4}{\rm He} production which is Δ​YP(4)≃−3.1\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq-3.1.

III.6 Finite temperature radiative corrections

The finite-temperature corrections can be separated in three parts. Using a notation similar to Brown and Sawyer [25], these three contributions are noted

Γn→pT≡Γn→pγ,T+Γn→pΔ​E,T+Γn→pe​p+e​e,T,\Gamma^{T}_{n\to p}\equiv\Gamma^{\gamma,T}_{n\to p}+\Gamma^{\Delta E,T}_{n\to p}+\Gamma^{ep+ee,T}_{n\to p}\,, (108)

and similar notation for the p→np\to n processes.

The first part is the stimulated emission and absorption of real photons [25, Eq. 5.9], see Fig. 14. When combined with a contribution coming from the diagram 17a it gives

Γn→pγ,T=αFS​K2​π∫0∞d​kk∫me∞dE×{A(E,k)[g(−E)χ~+A(E,k)+g(E)χ~+A(−E,k)]−kB(E,k)[g(−E)χ~+B(E,k)+g(E)χ~+B(−E,k)]}Γp→nγ,T=Γn→pγ,T|χ~+A/B→χ~−A/B&\Gamma^{\gamma,T}_{n\to p}=\frac{\alpha_{\rm FS}K}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{k}\int_{m_{e}}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}E\times\\ \quad\left\{A(E,k)\left[g(-E)\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{A}(E,k)+g(E)\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{A}(-E,k)\right]\right.\\ \qquad-\left.kB(E,k)\left[g(-E)\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{B}(E,k)+g(E)\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{B}(-E,k)\right]\right\}\\ \Gamma^{\gamma,T}_{p\to n}=\left.\Gamma^{\gamma,T}_{n\to p}\right|_{\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{A/B}\to\widetilde{\chi}_{-}^{A/B}} (109)

with

χ~±A​(E,k)\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}^{A}(E,k) ≡\displaystyle\equiv χ~±​(E−k)+χ~±​(E+k)−2​χ~±​(E)\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}(E-k)+\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}(E+k)-2\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}(E) (110)
χ~±B​(E,k)\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}^{B}(E,k) ≡\displaystyle\equiv ±[χ~±​(E−k)−χ~±​(E+k)].\displaystyle\pm\left[\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}(E-k)-\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}(E+k)\right]\,. (111)

It does not satisfy the detailed balance relation. However when the bremsstrahlung corrections (107) are added the sum does satisfy it. This crucial point is detailed in App. B.7.3.

The second part of finite temperature radiative corrections is made of the electron energy shift [25, Eq. 5.13], and it originates partly from the diagrams 17. It reads

Γn→pΔ​E,T=−2​αFS​Kπ∫dp[χ+(E)+χ+(−E)]×[π2​T26+∫me∞dE′p′g(E′)(1−me2E′2−E2)]Γp→nΔ​E,T=Γn→pΔ​E,T|χ+→χ−,\Gamma^{\Delta E,T}_{n\to p}&=-\frac{2\alpha_{\rm FS}K}{\pi}\int\mathrm{d}p\left[\chi_{+}(E)+\chi_{+}(-E)\right]\\ \times\left[\frac{\pi^{2}T^{2}}{6}+\int_{m_{e}}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}E^{\prime}p^{\prime}g(E^{\prime})\left(1-\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{{E^{\prime}}^{2}-E^{2}}\right)\right]\\ \Gamma^{\Delta E,T}_{p\to n}=\left.\Gamma^{\Delta E,T}_{n\to p}\right|_{\chi_{+}\to\chi_{-}}\,, (112)

where E′≡p′2+me2E^{\prime}\equiv\sqrt{{p^{\prime}}^{2}+m_{e}^{2}}.

The third and last part is made of proton-electron interactions, which is a finite temperature correction to the diagram 13c, and electron self-energy and wave-function renormalization [25, Eq. 5.10], which come partly from the diagram 17b. It reads

Γn→pe​p+e​e,T=αFS​K2​π​∫me∞d​E​[χ+​(E)+χ+​(−E)]×∫me∞d​E′​g​(E′)​EE′2−E2×{8​p​p′−(E′2+E2)​ln⁡(p+p′p−p′)2−E′E​(E′2+E2)​ln⁡[(E​E′+p​p′)2−me4(E​E′−p​p′)2−me4]}​Γp→ne​p+e​e,T=Γn→pe​p+e​e,T|χ+→χ−.\Gamma^{ep+ee,T}_{n\to p}&=\frac{\alpha_{\rm FS}K}{2\pi}\int_{m_{e}}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}E\left[\chi_{+}(E)+\chi_{+}(-E)\right]\\ \times\int_{m_{e}}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}E^{\prime}g(E^{\prime})\frac{E}{{E^{\prime}}^{2}-E^{2}}\\ \times\left\{8pp^{\prime}-({E^{\prime}}^{2}+E^{2})\ln\left(\frac{p+p^{\prime}}{p-p^{\prime}}\right)^{2}\right.\\ -\left.\frac{E^{\prime}}{E}({E^{\prime}}^{2}+E^{2})\ln\left[\frac{(EE^{\prime}+pp^{\prime})^{2}-m_{e}^{4}}{(EE^{\prime}-pp^{\prime})^{2}-m_{e}^{4}}\right]\right\}\\ \Gamma^{ep+ee,T}_{p\to n}=\left.\Gamma^{ep+ee,T}_{n\to p}\right|_{\chi_{+}\to\chi_{-}}\,. (113)

The second and third contributions [Eqs. (112) and (113)] satisfy manifestly the detailed balance relation thanks to the property (85). Furthermore, they can be recast in a form which does not involve principal parts of integrals and are thus better suited for numerical integration [25, Eq 5.15]]. We report it in App. B.8.

The modification of the rates from these finite temperature corrections is plotted in Fig. 18. We also show the BS corrections and the sum of the two. By construction for the sum, it can be checked that whenever the neutrinos have the same temperature, that is for T>1010​KT>10^{10}\,{\rm K}, the relative variation of the rates are equal and the detailed balance property (86) is preserved.

III.7 Finite nucleon mass corrections

It is not fully correct to consider that nucleons have an infinite mass. Indeed, the typical energy transfer in weak-interactions to electrons and neutrinos is of the order of the mass gap Δ≃1.29​MeV\Delta\simeq 1.29\,{\rm MeV}, which is 1.4×10−31.4\times 10^{-3} smaller than the nucleon mass. It corresponds to a temperature of 1.5×1010​K1.5\times 10^{10}{\rm K} which is not much larger than the freeze-out temperature. In the infinite nucleon mass approximation, we have thus neglected factors of the type Eν/mNE_{\nu}/m_{N}, Ee/mNE_{e}/m_{N} or Δ/mN\Delta/m_{N} (where mNm_{N} is the average nucleon mass mN≡(mp+mn)/2m_{N}\equiv(m_{p}+m_{n})/2) which represent order 10−310^{-3} corrections with respect to the leading one around 1010​K10^{10}{\rm K} and even larger corrections at higher temperature. Our method consists in expanding the full reaction rate in power of a small parameter ϵ≡T/mN\epsilon\equiv T/m_{N}. Terms of the type Eν/mNE_{\nu}/m_{N} or Ee/mNE_{e}/m_{N} are obviously of order ϵ\epsilon and terms of the type Δ/mN\Delta/m_{N} are also treated as being of order ϵ\epsilon. Our implementation of the finite mass corrections consists in including all the terms up to order ϵ\epsilon, but neglecting terms of order ϵ2\epsilon^{2}. This means that we neglect terms whose importance is of order 10−610^{-6} which is justified given our goal in precision.

If we ignore radiative corrections at null temperature, these corrections take the form

δ​Γn→pFM=K​∫0∞p2​𝑑p×[χ+FM​(E,gA)+χ+FM​(−E,gA)]​δ​Γp→nFM=K​∫0∞p2​𝑑p×[χ−FM​(E,−gA)+χ−FM​(−E,−gA)],\delta\Gamma^{\rm FM}_{n\to p}&=K\int_{0}^{\infty}p^{2}\mathrm{d}p\\ \times[\chi^{\rm FM}_{+}(E,g_{A})+\chi^{\rm FM}_{+}(-E,g_{A})]\\ \delta\Gamma^{\rm FM}_{p\to n}=K\int_{0}^{\infty}p^{2}\mathrm{d}p\\ \times[\chi^{\rm FM}_{-}(E,-g_{A})+\chi^{\rm FM}_{-}(-E,-g_{A})]\,, (114)

and the functions χ±FM\chi^{\rm FM}_{\pm} are reported in App. B.3. However since finite mass effects and radiative corrections can be rather important, they cannot be added linearly and one should also include radiative corrections inside finite nucleon mass corrections1515 15 In principle one should rederive all radiative corrections including consistently all finite nucleon mass effects. This is absent from the literature, and is certainly a daunting task. Our procedure consists in postulating that the multiplicative factor introduced by radiative corrections also multiplies the finite nucleon mass correction as in Cooper et al. [50], Czarnecki et al. [57]. Hence the corrections to the rates are

δ​Γn→pRC+FM=K​∫0∞p2​𝑑p×[ℱ+​(E)​R​(E,|E−Δ|)​χ+FM​(E,gA)+ℱ+​(−E)​R​(E,E+Δ)​χ+FM​(−E,gA)]​δ​Γp→nRC+FM=K​∫0∞p2​𝑑p×[ℱ−​(E)​R​(E,E+Δ)​χ−FM​(E,−gA)+ℱ−​(−E)​R​(E,|E−Δ|)​χ−FM​(−E,−gA)].\delta\Gamma^{\rm RC+FM}_{n\to p}&=K\int_{0}^{\infty}p^{2}\mathrm{d}p\\ \times[{\cal F}_{+}(E)R(E,|E-\Delta|)\chi^{\rm FM}_{+}(E,g_{A})\\ +{\cal F}_{+}(-E)R(E,E+\Delta)\chi^{\rm FM}_{+}(-E,g_{A})]\\ \delta\Gamma^{\rm RC+FM}_{p\to n}=K\int_{0}^{\infty}p^{2}\mathrm{d}p\\ \times[{\cal F}_{-}(E)R(E,E+\Delta)\chi^{\rm FM}_{-}(E,-g_{A})\\ +{\cal F}_{-}(-E)R(E,|E-\Delta|)\chi^{\rm FM}_{-}(-E,-g_{A})]\,. (115)

The expression for χ±FM​(E,gA)\chi^{\rm FM}_{\pm}(E,g_{A}) is given in App. B.3. The relative modifications to the rates are depicted in Fig. 19. It is not obvious that the finite nucleon mass corrections preserve the detailed balance relation. In fact when including these corrections the detailed balance ratio between neutrons and protons is given by Eq. (183). Since this must also be the ratio Γp→n/Γn→p\Gamma_{p\to n}/\Gamma_{n\to p} we define α\alpha following Lopez et al. [124] as

Γ¯p→n+δ​Γp→nFMΓ¯n→p+δ​Γn→pFM≡e−ΔT​[1+(1+α)​3​Δ2​mN].\frac{\overline{\Gamma}_{p\to n}+\delta\Gamma^{\rm FM}_{p\to n}}{\overline{\Gamma}_{n\to p}+\delta\Gamma^{\rm FM}_{n\to p}}\equiv{\rm e}^{-\frac{\Delta}{T}}\left[1+(1+\alpha)\frac{3\Delta}{2m_{N}}\right]\,. (116)

α\alpha characterizes the deviation from the detailed balance equality and must vanish if detailed balance with finite mass corrections is satisfied. It is plotted in Fig. 20. We observe that for T<meT<m_{e} deviations from detailed balance occur because the neutrino temperature is not equal to the plasma temperature. Hence we have also plotted α\alpha with Tν=TT_{\nu}=T artificially enforced. At low temperature, that is below T=meT=m_{e}, detailed balance is very well satisfied because the parameter ϵ=T/mN\epsilon=T/m_{N} is small. At higher temperatures we see deviations, and this comes from the fact that we considered only corrections which are first order in ϵ\epsilon.

Finally, the total neutron rate at null temperature is

Γn→p​(T=0)=Γn→pRC0​(T=0)+δ​Γn→pFM​(T=0),\Gamma_{n\to p}(T=0)=\Gamma_{n\to p}^{{{\rm RC}0}}(T=0)+\delta\Gamma^{\rm FM}_{n\to p}(T=0)\,, (117)

that is there is a correction to λ0\lambda_{0} due to finite nucleon mass effects. If Eq. (114) is used, this is

δ​λ0FM=me−5​∫0Δ2−me2p2​𝑑p​χ+FM​(E,gA)|T=0\delta\lambda_{0}^{\rm FM}=m_{e}^{-5}\int_{0}^{\sqrt{\Delta^{2}-m_{e}^{2}}}p^{2}\mathrm{d}p\,\left.\chi^{\rm FM}_{+}(E,g_{A})\right|_{T=0} (118)

combined with Eq. (218), and we obtain δλFM0≃−3.3828×10−3\delta\lambda^{\rm FM}_{0}\simeq-3.3828\times 10^{-3}, that is δ​λ0FM/λ¯0≃−0.002068\delta\lambda^{\rm FM}_{0}/\bar{\lambda}_{0}\simeq-0.002068. This is in agreement with the result δ​λ0FM/λ¯0≃−0.00206\delta\lambda^{\rm FM}_{0}/\bar{\lambda}_{0}\simeq-0.00206 found in Lopez et al. [124] with an exact method to compute the finite nucleon mass effects. We recomputed this ratio with the method of Lopez et al. [124, Eq. 20] and found it is more precisely given by −0.0020637-0.0020637. The tiny difference with our value δ​λ0FM/λ¯0\delta\lambda^{\rm FM}_{0}/\bar{\lambda}_{0} is only due to the fact that we kept only first order finite nucleon mass corrections, that is we kept terms of order ϵ\epsilon, and ignored terms of higher order ϵ2\epsilon^{2}. Furthermore, if we also include radiative corrections, that is if we use δ​Γn→pRC+FM\delta\Gamma^{\rm RC+FM}_{n\to p} instead of δ​Γn→pFM\delta\Gamma^{\rm FM}_{n\to p} in Eq. (117), hence corresponding to an extra factor F⁡(E)​R​(E,Δ−E)F(E)R(E,\Delta-E) in the integrand of Eq. (118), we get δλFM0≃−3.6201×10−3\delta\lambda^{\rm FM}_{0}\simeq-3.6201\times 10^{-3}. These values are summarized in table 2.

III.8 Weak magnetism

We show in B.4 that the effect of weak magnetism is exactly similar to the finite mass correction which arises from the coupling between the axial current and the vector current. This has been noticed earlier by Seckel [163]. That is, it brings corrections which are exactly of the same type as those proportional to gAg_{A} in Eq. (73). The weak magnetism corrections amount to a simple redefinition of the constant factors (203) as

cL​L≡(1+gA)24+fwm​gA​cR​R≡(1−gA)24−fwm​gA​cL​R≡gA2−14c_{LL}&\equiv\frac{(1+g_{A})^{2}}{4}+f_{\rm wm}g_{A}\\ c_{RR}\equiv\frac{(1-g_{A})^{2}}{4}-f_{\rm wm}g_{A}\\ c_{LR}\equiv\frac{g_{A}^{2}-1}{4} (119)

when computing the finite nucleon mass corrections. The associated couplings (216) must be replaced accordingly.

The weak magnetism, if considered independently of radiative corrections, induces no modification of λ0\lambda_{0}, at least up to the order ϵ\epsilon of our finite nucleon mass expansion, as explained in appendix § B.4. However when this is combined with the radiative corrections, this brings a residual increase to δλFM0≃−3.6333×10−3\delta\lambda^{\rm FM}_{0}\simeq-3.6333\times 10^{-3}. Summing this value of the finite nucleon mass corrections (which includes weak-magnetism and which is coupled to radiative corrections), to the radiative corrections themselves (106) leads to

λ0RC+FM=λ0RC+δ​λ0FM≃1.75474.\lambda_{0}^{{{\rm RC}}+{\rm FM}}=\lambda_{0}^{{{\rm RC}}}+\delta\lambda^{\rm FM}_{0}\simeq 1.75474\,. (120)

This is to be compared with Cooper et al. [50] where it is reported λ0≃1.03887×1.6887≃1.75434\lambda_{0}\simeq 1.03887\times 1.6887\simeq 1.75434, a modest 0.023%0.023\% smaller than the value (120). This close agreement can also be seen by noting that (ℏ​2​π3)/(me5​c10​GF2​λ0RC+FM)≃4907.4​s(\hbar 2\pi^{3})/(m_{e}^{5}c^{10}G_{F}^{2}\lambda_{0}^{\rm RC+FM})\simeq 4907.4\,{\rm s}, which is very close to the value 4908​s4908\,{\rm s} given by Czarnecki et al. [57, Eq. 17] or the refined value 4908.7​s4908.7{\rm s} of Marciano and Sirlin [129, Eq. 18].

III.9 Effect of incomplete neutrino decoupling

Neutrino heating also induces modification of the weak rates. In our thermal approximation of the incomplete neutrino decoupling (see § II.6), this is taken into account by putting the effective neutrino temperature defined in Eq. (64) in all expressions for the weak rates. This amounts to assuming that all neutrinos receive the same share of the heating and ignoring the spectral distortions. We postpone a more detailed discussion on the effect of incomplete neutrino decoupling on the weak rates and thus the He4{}^{4}{\rm He} production in § V.3.5. Briefly, the most notable effect of incomplete neutrino decoupling is to affect the time-temperature relation, and this is also the case from QED corrections in the plasma but the effect is much smaller. Indeed, since for a given plasma temperature, neutrino heating induces an increase of the total energy density, the Hubble rate is increased and so is the rate of variation d​T/d​t\mathrm{d}T/\mathrm{d}t. In practice this means that the Universe is younger when nucleosynthesis starts around TNuc=0.078​MeVT_{\rm Nuc}=0.078{\rm MeV} and the neutron beta decay results in a lower loss of neutrons, and thus a higher production of He4{}^{4}{}\rm He at the end of the BBN. This is the clock effect explained in Fields et al. [75], Dodelson and Turner [63].

III.10 Total correction to the weak rates

The total weak reaction rates are given by summing the various effects [Eqs. (101), (108), (107) and (115)], that is

Γn→p=Γn→pRC0+Γn→pT+δ​Γn→pBS+δ​Γn→pFM,\Gamma_{n\to p}=\Gamma^{\rm RC0}_{n\to p}+\Gamma^{T}_{n\to p}+\delta\Gamma^{\rm BS}_{n\to p}+\delta\Gamma^{\rm FM}_{n\to p}\,, (121)

and a similar sum for p→np\to n processes. The constant KK involved in all contributions is then calibrated on neutron beta decay from λ0\lambda_{0} given by Eq. (120) replaced in Eq. (91). We recall that when including weak-magnetism in finite nucleon mass effects, that is in Eqs. (115), one must use the constants (119) in (216), so as to evaluate the χ±FM\chi^{\rm FM}_{\pm} given by Eqs. (215).

The size of all corrections relative to the Born approximation is plotted in Fig. 21. Around T≃3.3×109​KT\simeq 3.3\times 10^{9}{\rm K} for which the neutron are only subject to beta decay, we find δ​Γn→p/Γ¯n→p≃−0.023\delta\Gamma_{n\to p}/\bar{\Gamma}_{n\to p}\simeq-0.023. From the rule (7) this should lead to Δ​YP(4)≃42\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 42, quite in nice agreement with the total correction Δ​YP(4)≃44.7\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 44.7 that we report in § V.3.

IV Nucleosynthesis

Once the weak interaction rates are determined and computed with great precision, it is possible to solve for the nucleosynthesis by adding the effect of nuclear reactions which form nuclei. Hence we need to build the differential system which rules the evolution of all (neutrons, protons and main isotopes) abundances. We describe how this is performed in this section and turn to report and discuss the numerical results obtained for final abundances in § V.

We remind that, for a general reaction of the type

A+b→C+dA+b\rightarrow C+d (122)

the conventional notation in experimental nuclear physics is A⁡(b,d)​CA(b,d)C to keep in mind that AA is the target nucleus at rest, bb is the projectile from the beam, dd is the outgoing, detected, particle and CC is left generally undetected, possibly not escaping the target. Hence, usually, but not always, AA and CC are the heaviest nuclei. The same notation is used in theoretical nuclear physics, regardless of the experimental details.

IV.1 Thermonuclear reaction rates

We summarize here a few results, to be used in this review, and refer to [102, 8, 122, 33] for a detailed treatment. It is assumed that the medium is in local thermodynamical equilibrium so that the distribution of ion velocities/energies follows a Maxwell–Boltzmann distribution (see § A.3),

ϕMB​(v)​v​d​v=8π​m​1(kB​T)3/2​e−EkB​T​E​d​E.\phi_{\mathrm{MB}}(v)v\mathrm{d}v=\sqrt{8\over{\pi m}}{{1}\over{(k_{B}T)^{3/2}}}e^{-\tfrac{E}{k_{B}T}}E\mathrm{d}E. (123)

It is understood that for the distribution of relative velocities between two reacting nuclei, mm is their reduced mass. In such conditions, one defines the thermonuclear reaction rate by

NA​⟨σ​v⟩=NA​∫0∞σ⁡(v)​ϕMB​(v)​v​𝑑vN_{A}\langle\sigma v\rangle=N_{A}\int_{0}^{\infty}\sigma(v)\phi_{\mathrm{MB}}(v)vdv (124)

in cm3s-1mole-1 units where NAN_{A} is Avogadro’s number (mole-1). For reactions involving charged particles, since the kinetic energies are below the Coulomb barrier, the energy dependence of the cross section is dominated by the tuneling effect through the barrier. The Coulomb plus centrifugal barrier penetration probability is given by

Pℓ​(E)=k​RFℓ2​(η,k​R)+Gℓ2​(η,k​R)P_{\ell}(E)={kR\over{F^{2}_{\ell}(\eta,kR})+G^{2}_{\ell}(\eta,kR)} (125)

where FℓF_{\ell} and GℓG_{\ell} are the Coulomb functions [79], k=2​m​E/ℏk=\sqrt{2mE}/\hbar is the wave number, ℓ\ell the orbital angular momentum and

η≡Z1​Z2​e2ℏ​v\eta\equiv{{\textstyle Z_{1}Z_{2}e^{2}}\over{\textstyle\hbar v}} (126)

the Sommerfeld parameter. To account for this strong energy dependency of the cross section, it is convenient to introduce the astrophysical SS–factor:

σ⁡(E)≡S⁡(E)E​exp⁡(−2​π​η)\sigma(E)\equiv{\textstyle{S(E)}\over{E}}\exp\left(-2\pi\eta\right) (127)

which, in the absence of resonances removes most of the energy dependence. A resonance, associated to a nuclear level in the compound nucleus formed by the fusion of the projectile and target nuclei, induces a strong but localized variation of the SS–factor. Hence, the presence of a resonance can increase by several orders of magnitude a reaction rate.

IV.2 General form

The evolution of abundances, defined in Eq. (1), is deduced from the evolution of number densities found from Eq. (10). Since both nuclear and weak reactions preserve the number of baryons, we obtain

d​nbd​t+3​H​nb=0,\frac{\mathrm{d}n_{\rm b}}{\mathrm{d}t}+3Hn_{\rm b}=0, (128)

that is baryon volume density is only affected by dilution and nb∝1/a3n_{\rm b}\propto 1/a^{3}.

For a given isotope ii, the evolution of the volume density depends on the reaction rates in which it is involved. It is of the form

d​nid​t+3​H​ni=𝒥i,\frac{\mathrm{d}n_{i}}{\mathrm{d}t}+3Hn_{i}={\cal J}_{i}\,, (129)

where 𝒥i{\cal J}_{i} is the net rate of evolution of number density due to all nuclear reactions. A decay of species ii (i→…i\to\dots) and a decay reaction in which species ii is the end product (j→i+…j\to i+\dots) contribute as

𝒥i⊃−ni​Γi→…+nj​Γj→i+…{\cal J}_{i}\supset-n_{i}\Gamma_{i\ \to\dots}+n_{j}\Gamma_{j\to i+\dots} (130)

where the Γ\Gamma are the decay rates (usually given in s−1{\rm s}^{-1}). A two-body reaction of the type i+j↔k+li+j\leftrightarrow k+l contributes instead as

𝒥i⊃nk​nl​γk​l→i​j−ni​nj​γi​j→k​l.{\cal J}_{i}\supset n_{k}n_{l}\gamma_{kl\to ij}-n_{i}n_{j}\gamma_{ij\to kl}\,. (131)

with

γi​j→k​l≡⟨σ​v⟩i​j→k​l.\gamma_{ij\to kl}\equiv\langle\sigma v\rangle_{ij\to kl}\,. (132)

Since both the individual nin_{i} and the total nbn_{\rm b} are affected similarly by expansion, it proves much simpler to study directly the evolution of abundances defined as 1616 16 For neutrons and protons Yn=XnY_{n}=X_{n} and Yp=XpY_{p}=X_{p}.

Yi≡ninb,Y_{i}\equiv\frac{n_{i}}{n_{\rm b}}\,, (133)

since one finds

Y˙i=C⁡[Yi],C⁡[Yi]≡𝒥inb.\dot{Y}_{i}=C[Y_{i}]\,,\qquad C[Y_{i}]\equiv\frac{{\cal J}_{i}}{n_{\rm b}}\,. (134)

Obviously the decay reactions considered in Eq. (130) contribute as

C⁡[Yi]⊃−Yi​Γi→…+Yj​Γj→i+….C[Y_{i}]\supset-Y_{i}\Gamma_{i\ \to\dots}+Y_{j}\Gamma_{j\to i+\dots}\,. (135)

However two-body reactions contribute as

C⁡[Yi]⊃Yk​Yl​Γk​l→i​j−Yi​Yj​Γi​j→k​l,C[Y_{i}]\supset Y_{k}Y_{l}\Gamma_{kl\to ij}-Y_{i}Y_{j}\Gamma_{ij\to kl}\,, (136)

where we related the rates for abundances to those of number densities through

Γi​j→k​l≡nb​γi​j→k​l.\Gamma_{ij\to kl}\equiv n_{\rm b}\gamma_{ij\to kl}\,. (137)

Eq. (131) is straightforwardly generalized to reactions with more bodies. In full generality, and without restricting to decay reactions or two-body reactions, the evolution of abundances takes the form [78, 180]

Y˙i1=∑i2​…​ip,j1​…​jqNi1​(Γj1​…​jq→i1​…​ip​Yj1Nj1​…​YjqNjqNj1!​…​Njq!−Γi1​…​ip→j1​…​jq​Yi1Ni1​…​YipNipNi1!​…​Nip!),\displaystyle\dot{Y}_{i_{1}}=\sum_{i_{2}\dots i_{p},j_{1}\dots j_{q}}N_{i_{1}}\left(\Gamma_{j_{1}\dots j_{q}\to i_{1}\dots i_{p}}\frac{Y_{j_{1}}^{N_{j_{1}}}\dots Y_{j_{q}}^{N_{j_{q}}}}{N_{j_{1}}!\dots N_{j_{q}}!}-\Gamma_{i_{1}\dots i_{p}\to j_{1}\dots j_{q}}\frac{Y_{i_{1}}^{N_{i_{1}}}\dots Y_{i_{p}}^{N_{i_{p}}}}{N_{i_{1}}!\dots N_{i_{p}}!}\right)\,, (138)

where NiN_{i} is the stoichiometric coefficient of species ii in the reaction and with the relation between abundance rates and number density rates given by

Γi1​…​ip→j1​…​jq=nb(Ni1+⋯+Nip)−1​γi1​…​ip→j1​…​jq.\Gamma_{i_{1}\dots i_{p}\to j_{1}\dots j_{q}}=n_{\rm b}^{(N_{i_{1}}+\dots+N_{i_{p}})-1}\gamma_{i_{1}\dots i_{p}\to j_{1}\dots j_{q}}\,. (139)

Note that for a decay reaction Γi→…=γi→…\Gamma_{i\to\dots}=\gamma_{i\to\dots}.

In practice the reaction rates for many-body reactions are given as tables for the quantities NA(Ni1+⋯+Nip)−1​γi1​…​ip→j1​…​jqN_{A}^{(N_{i_{1}}+\dots+N_{i_{p}})-1}\gamma_{i_{1}\dots i_{p}\to j_{1}\dots j_{q}}, as detailed in App. C on the steps required to deduce them from the nuclear physics tables. Furthermore the rates are only given for forward reactions. Indeed, since when there is nuclear statistical equilibrium (NSE) reverse reactions should balance with forward reactions, we can always relate the reverse reactions to the forward reactions from the detailed balance relation

γi1​…​ip→j1​…​jqγj1​…​jq→i1​…​ip=Ni1!​…​Nip!Nj1!​…​Njq!​[nj1Nj1​…​njqNjqni1Ni1​…​nipNip]NSE\frac{\gamma_{i_{1}\dots i_{p}\to j_{1}\dots j_{q}}}{\gamma_{j_{1}\dots j_{q}\to i_{1}\dots i_{p}}}=\frac{N_{i_{1}}!\dots N_{i_{p}}!}{N_{j_{1}}!\dots N_{j_{q}}!}\left[\frac{n_{j_{1}}^{N_{j_{1}}}\dots n_{j_{q}}^{N_{j_{q}}}}{n_{i_{1}}^{N_{i_{1}}}\dots n_{i_{p}}^{N_{i_{p}}}}\right]^{\rm NSE} (140)

where the NSE densities are given in Eq. (190). Since nuclear reactions in many-body reactions do not change the nature of nucleons1717 17 This is not the case for decay reactions but for these we neglect the reverse reactions., that is they conserve the number of protons and neutrons, then using the relation (139) the reverse reactions are related to the forward reactions by

γj1​…​jq→i1​…​ipγi1​…​ip→j1​…​jq\displaystyle\frac{\gamma_{j_{1}\dots j_{q}\to i_{1}\dots i_{p}}}{\gamma_{i_{1}\dots i_{p}\to j_{1}\dots j_{q}}} =\displaystyle= Πi=i1​…​ip​1Ni!​[gi​(mi​T2​π)3/2]NiΠj=j1​…​jq​1Nj!​[gj​(mj​T2​π)3/2]Nj\displaystyle\frac{\Pi_{i=i_{1}\dots i_{p}}\frac{1}{N_{i}!}\left[g_{i}\left(\frac{m_{i}T}{2\pi}\right)^{3/2}\right]^{N_{i}}}{\Pi_{j=j_{1}\dots j_{q}}\frac{1}{N_{j}!}\left[g_{j}\left(\frac{m_{j}T}{2\pi}\right)^{3/2}\right]^{N_{j}}} (141)
×\displaystyle\times exp⁡(∑j=1qmj−∑i=1pmiT).\displaystyle{\rm exp}\left(\frac{\sum_{j=1}^{q}m_{j}-\sum_{i=1}^{p}m_{i}}{T}\right).

We check easily that we recover the particular cases of Fowler et al. [78, Eqs. 15, 18, 25]. Hence the relation between forward and reverse reactions is of the form

γj1​…​jq→i1​…​ipγi1​…​ip→j1​…​jq=α​(T109​K)β​exp​(γ×109​KT),\frac{\gamma_{j_{1}\dots j_{q}\to i_{1}\dots i_{p}}}{\gamma_{i_{1}\dots i_{p}\to j_{1}\dots j_{q}}}=\alpha\left(\frac{T}{10^{9}{\rm K}}\right)^{\beta}{\rm exp}\left(\frac{\gamma\times 10^{9}{\rm K}}{T}\right)\,, (142)

which depends only on 3 constants. In practice, for a given reaction, the forward reaction rate is tabulated for various values of TT or is approximated by an analytic fit, and the constants (α,β,γ)(\alpha,\beta,\gamma) needed to obtain the reverse reaction rate are also computed once for all from Eq. (141) using the tabulated masses and spins of isotopes [we use the table nubase2016.asc described in Audi et al. [14]].

IV.3 Nuclear network and reaction rates uncertainties

The nuclear reaction network used here has been fully described in Coc et al. [35]: it includes 59 nuclides from neutron to 23Na (see table 3), linked by 391 reactions involving neutrons, protons, deuterium, tritium (H3{}^{3}{\rm H}), He3{}^{3}{\rm He} and α\alpha–particles induced reactions, and 33 β\beta-decay processes. The complete list of reactions can be found in Table 4 of Coc et al. [35], together with the references for the values of the reaction rates. Each of these reactions is systematically supplemented (i​j→k​lij{\to}kl) by its reverse (k​l→i​jkl{\to}ij) whose rate is obtained as described above, except for decay reactions whose rates are from Audi et al. [14].

This network is adapted to the prediction of the primordial abundances of the light elements, but also to the calculation of the abundances of the Li6{}^{6}{\rm Li}, 9Be, 10B, 11B and CNO isotopes. As listed in Table 4 of Coc et al. [35], reaction rates and their associated uncertainties were taken primarily from Angulo et al. [8], Descouvemont et al. [60], Iliadis et al. [104], Xu et al. [189] evaluations when available. For many reactions, in the absence of sufficient experimental data, the rates come from theory (TALYS code) [84]. An extensive sensitivity study, performed by Coc et al. [35], identified ten reactions that needed further analyses, and it was followed by their re–evaluations (shown in boldface in Table 4 of Coc et al. [35]). Finally, out of these hundreds of reactions, the most important ones are displayed in Fig. 22. They were identified in sensitivity studies, i.e. [141, 52, 40] for the light elements (4He, D, 3He and 7Li) and Coc et al. [35], Coc et al. [39] for others and correspond to the main nuclear flow.

Experimental uncertainties on YPY_{\rm P} are due to the 1H(n,OPENγ)2\gamma)^{2}H, D(d,n)3He and D(d,p)3H reaction rates and to the neutron lifetime. For these three reactions, one finds [52, 36, e.g.]

Δ​YP≈(1.5×10−3)​Δ​⟨σ​v⟩⟨σ​v⟩,\Delta{Y_{\rm P}}\approx(1.5\times 10^{-3})\frac{\Delta\langle\sigma{v}\rangle}{\langle\sigma{v}\rangle}\,, (143)

and Δ​YP≈0.18​Δ​τn/τn\Delta{Y_{\rm P}}\approx 0.18\Delta\tau_{n}/\tau_{n} from Eq. (7). Since the experimental uncertainties are of the order of 10−210^{-2} for the rates and 10−310^{-3} for the lifetime, they may all contribute to the error budget.

There are basically two methods for the experimental determination of the neutron lifetime: detecting dying neutrons i.e. their decay rate (“beam experiments") or surviving neutrons after being left in a magnetic “bottle" for a certain time. Both methods produce slightly different results [191, see e.g. Fig. 8 in]. This is most probably due to different systematic uncertainties but it might also be real and be explained by an undetected decay into a dark sector [76, see e.g.]. Note that in that case it would be the “bottle" results, corresponding to the surviving neutrons counting, that would be important for BBN. Hence, the value of the neutron lifetime has been revised several times by the Particle Data Group (PDG) from 885.7±\pm0.8 s [5], used, e.g. in Coc and Vangioni [40], to 879.4±\pm0.6 s resulting from an average of “bottle" experiments [58], slightly below the current PDG average [147] which is 880.2±1.0​s880.2\pm 1.0\,{\rm s}. We use the average over post-2000 experiments, 879.5±0.8​s879.5\pm 0.8\,{\rm s} [164], which is extremely close to the average on bottle experiments, but with more conservative errors.

The cross section of the 1H(n,OPENγ)2\gamma)^{2}H reaction is obtained from calculations in the framework of Effective Field Theory whose results are estimated to be reliable to within 1% error [7]. Indeed, the few experimental information available for this cross section at BBN energies are in very good agreement with theory (see Fig. 1 in Coc [34]).

The D(p,OPENγ)3\gamma)^{3}He, D(d,n)3He and D(d,p)3H reactions are the main source of nuclear uncertainty for deuterium nucleosynthesis while the two last one may affect the error budget of YPY_{\rm P}. The relative variations of D/H are related to the variation of these rates [40, see e.g.] by

Δ⁡(D/H)D/H\displaystyle\frac{\Delta{\rm(D/H)}}{\rm D/H} =\displaystyle= −0.32​Δ​⟨σ​v⟩d​(p,γ)3​He⟨σ​v⟩d​(p,γ)3​He\displaystyle-0.32\frac{\Delta\langle\sigma{v}\rangle_{\mathrm{d(p,}\gamma)^{3}\mathrm{He}}}{\langle\sigma{v}\rangle_{\mathrm{d(p,}\gamma)^{3}\mathrm{He}}}
Δ⁡(D/H)D/H\displaystyle\frac{\Delta{\rm(D/H)}}{\rm D/H} =\displaystyle= −0.54​Δ​⟨σ​v⟩d​(d,n)3​He⟨σ​v⟩d​(d,n)3​He−0.46​Δ​⟨σ​v⟩d​(d,p)3​H⟨σ​v⟩d​(d,p)3​H\displaystyle-0.54\frac{\Delta\langle\sigma{v}\rangle_{\mathrm{d(d,n)}^{3}\mathrm{He}}}{\langle\sigma{v}\rangle_{\mathrm{d(d,n)}^{3}\mathrm{He}}}-0.46\frac{\Delta\langle\sigma{v}\rangle_{\mathrm{d(d,p)}^{3}\mathrm{H}}}{\langle\sigma{v}\rangle_{\mathrm{d(d,p)}^{3}\mathrm{H}}}

so that to achieve the ∼\sim1% precision required by observations, one needs a similar precision on reaction rates. None of them are affected by resonances, so that the only questions are to model the slowly varying energy dependence of the SS–factors and precisely determine their absolute scale. There are basically two options: either empirically fit both the energy dependence and scale so as to follow closely the data, or use theoretical energy dependences from nuclear physics models and only determine the absolute normalization. We adopted the rates from the new evaluations of Iliadis et al. [103] and Gómez Iñesta et al. [83] that use both the second option, together with Bayesian methods. The theoretical, ab initio energy dependences were taken from Marcucci et al. [131] for D(p,OPENγ)3\gamma)^{3}He and from Arai et al. [11] for D(d,n)3He and D(d,p)3H. The main difficulty to determine the absolute scale of the SS–factors is that one needs to combine results from different experiments.

Coc et al. [38], using traditional statistics found a normalization factor of 0.9900±\pm0.0368 for the D(p,OPENγ)3\gamma)^{3}He theoretical SS–factor of Marcucci et al. [131], while the Bayesian analysis gives 1.000−0.036+0.038{}^{+0.038}_{-0.036} [103]. This shows that, starting from the same experimental data and theoretical model, different statistical analyses can lead to a, significant, 1% difference. Figure 23 displays the D(p,OPENγ)3\gamma)^{3}He experimental SS–factor normalised to the theoretical model of Marcucci et al. [131]. The solid horizontal line corresponds to the scaling of the theoretical SS–factor adopted by Coc et al. [38]. It is obvious that experimental data are scarce at BBN energies and slightly below the scaled SS–factor (an overall 9% systematic uncertainty is not shown however), while the empirical fit by Adelberger et al. [3] or [60] follows closely, by construction, the experimental data. Note also that Marcucci et al. [130] have included higher order terms in their ab initio model resulting in a ≈\approx10% increase with respect with their previous result [131], this time well above the experimental data (see Fig. 23). Using this new theoretical SS–factor, one would obtain an additional reduction of Δ\Delta(D/H) = -0.072×10−5\times 10^{-5} that nevertheless would vanish if we rescale it (by 0.915) to fit experimental data. This rate is thus a major source of uncertainty for D/H prediction that should be resolved when the new experimental data [90] from LUNA at the Gran Sasso underground facility will be released, supplementing the low energy ones [28].

In a similar way, the D(d,n)3He and D(d,p)3H rates have been evaluated by [38] and later by [83], using the ab initio SS–factor from Arai et al. [11] scaled according to experimental data. They found negligible differences in scaling factors: 0.959±\pm0.010 and 0.955±\pm0.010 for the traditional analysis to be compared with 0.961±\pm0.010 and 0.956±\pm0.010 for the Bayesian one. However, the theoretical work of Arai et al. [11] was focused on low energies and does not correctly reproduce the D(d,n)3He and D(d,p)3H experimental data above ≈\approx600 keV. It is highly desirable that these calculations be extended up to ≈\approx2 MeV, to cover the range of experimental data that encompass BBN energies.

At the CMB deduced density, Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} is produced through the formation of 7Be via the 3He(OPENα,γ)7\alpha,\gamma)^{7}Be reaction as 7Be will decay much later to Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li}. The destruction of 7Be occurs through the 7Be(n,p)7Li(p,OPENα)4\alpha)^{4}He channel which is limited by the scarcity of late time neutron abundance. The most influential reaction rates on Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} nucleosynthesis are [40, e.g. Table 1 in ] 1H(n,OPENγ)2\gamma)^{2}H (indirectly by affecting the neutron abundance) and 3He(OPENα,γ)7\alpha,\gamma)^{7}Be, but large deviations from their nominal cross sections are strongly constrained by experiments. Even though, there has not been new experimental data, since it is the major source of uncertainty on the Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} production, the 3He(OPENα,γ)7\alpha,\gamma)^{7}Be reaction rate has also been recently re-evaluated using Bayesian methods [83] to scale the theoretical SS–factor of Neff [140]. It was known that the 7Be(n,OPENα)4\alpha)^{4}He reaction could not help solve the lithium problem, but its rate was highly uncertain and affected the Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} production at the few percent level. Until recently, the only published rate came from an evaluation by Wagoner [180] based on very scarce data. We used either this rate or the one obtained by TALYS [84] in previous publications [35, 39]. A new re-evaluation [100] and experiments [18, 112] confirmed that the 7Be(n,OPENα)4\alpha)^{4}He rate is approximately, one order of magnitude below the Wagoner one, rendering negligible the effect this reaction. Hence, we now use the rate provided by the n_TOF collaboration [18] that now has no impact on 7Be.

Lithium–6 nucleosynthesis is quite simple given that it is only produced by the D(α,γ)6(\alpha,\gamma)^{6}Li reaction and destroyed by 6Li(p,OPENα)4\alpha)^{4}He. While the rate of the latter has been precisely known for a long time, the rate of the former suffered from large uncertainties [8]. This has now been solved, thanks to experiments [92, 6], and theory [138].

Elements with atomic number above 7 are not expected to be significantly produced in BBN, unless some of the reaction rates involved in their production differ strongly from their current estimates [105, 39]. Indeed, some of them rely on theoretical models not well adapted to low mass nuclei. Figure 22 displays the main reactions producing or destructing the beryllium, boron and C, N and O stable isotopes.

Table 4 displays the few reaction rates that have been updated in Coc et al. [39], Coc et al. [38], and now in this work, with respect to the Table 4 of Coc et al. [35].

V Numerical results

V.1 Overview of PRIMAT

To our knowledge, apart from the Kawano code [113] which is based on the historical code of Wagoner [182, 180, 181], there exist only two public BBN codes, which are PArthENoPE [149, 45] and AlterBBN [12]. The method followed in PRIMAT differs slightly from these two recent implementations, in that we integrate directly differential equations in time, instead of integrating differential equations in the plasma temperature which are obtained by the replacement of d​T/d​t\mathrm{d}T/\mathrm{d}t derived from the Friedmann equation. The code is abundantly commented and refers to equations of the previous sections of this article. Let us summarize the main steps of the code.

  • •

    First we solve for the thermodynamics of the plasma following the details provided in § II. This allows to obtain a⁡(T)a(T) either using entropy conservation (31) if the effect of incomplete neutrino decoupling is neglected, or using the variation of entropy from the heat transfer between the plasma and the neutrinos (62). When QED plasma effects are included we use the corresponding (55). The relation T⁡(a)T(a) is obtained by a numerical inversion. The temperature of neutrinos is either deduced from (29), or (57) when QED plasma effects are included, if we assume they are fully decoupled. If we take into account the incomplete neutrino decoupling, then their effective temperature is obtained from Eqs. (63) and (64). The evolution of baryon energy density follows the simple scaling (34), and similarly for cold dark matter. Then the cosmological expansion is solved using the total energy density (43) [with QED effects included for the plasma energy density (Eq. 58) if the choice is made], inside the Friedmann equation (40), so to obtain a⁡(t)a(t) by numerical resolution of the differential equation. The relation t⁡(a)t(a) is obtained by numerical inversion. Eventually we obtain T⁡(t)T(t) as T⁡(a⁡(t))T(a(t)) that we can use later in the reaction rates since they depend on temperature.

  • •

    Once the thermodynamics and the cosmological expansion are known, we compute the weak rates for a grid of plasma temperatures so as to interpolate them. The total rates are obtained by considering all relevant corrections discussed in § III, which are added as in Eq. (121). The constant KK involved in all rates is obtained from Eq. (91) with λ0\lambda_{0} given by the value (120). Since the weak rates computation can be very long, especially when including finite temperature radiative corrections which involve two-dimensional integrals, we store them on hard disk for later use. An option allows to recompute them when desired and various options allow to switch on or off the various corrections.

  • •

    Finally we build the system of equations for the nuclear network, that is the system of Eqs. (138) including the weak rates. The nuclear reaction rates are read from tabulated values in function of temperature, or from analytical fits and the reverse rates are obtained from (141). The evolution of the nuclides abundances is numerically solved in three periods.

    1. 1.

      For 1011​K≥T≥1010​K10^{11}{\rm K}\geq T\geq 10^{10}{\rm K} we solve only for the abundance of neutrons and protons and totally ignore the nuclear reactions. Photodissociation reactions are too strong for this period and only the abundance of neutrons and protons is relevant at this stage. Nuclear reactions are anyway not tabulated above 1010​K10^{10}{\rm K}.

    2. 2.

      Then for ​1010 K≥T≥1.25×109 K${10}^{10}\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$\geq T\geq$1.25\text{\times}{10}^{9}\text{\,}\mathrm{K}$ we solve for a small nuclear network, made of light elements only (protons, neutron, H2{}^{2}{\rm H}, H3{}^{3}{\rm H}, He3{}^{3}{\rm He}, He4{}^{4}{\rm He}, Li6{}^{6}{\rm Li}, Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} and Be7{}^{7}{\rm Be}) and starting from the NSE abundance, apart for neutrons and protons which are taken from the previously solved period. For this period the system is very stiff and we use a first order BDF scheme (backward differentiation formula), which is equivalent to a backward Euler method.

    3. 3.

      Finally for 1.25×109​K≥T≥6×107​K1.25\times 10^{9}{\rm K}\geq T\geq 6\times 10^{7}{\rm K} we solve numerically for all nuclides, using the full network of reactions. The system is less stiff and it is possible to fasten the numerical integration by using a second order BDF scheme.

V.2 Temperature of nucleosynthesis

One can estimate the temperature of nucleosynthesis as the temperature for which the NSE value of deuterium is equal to the abundance of neutrons found from the simple freeze-out plus beta decay model (98). At this temperature deuterium would have gobbled up all free neutrons and this definition corresponds essentially to the end of nucleosynthesis. Hence TNucT_{\rm Nuc} is defined by

Yn​(TNuc)≡YdNSE​(TNuc).Y_{n}(T_{\rm Nuc})\equiv Y_{d}^{\rm NSE}(T_{\rm Nuc})\,. (144)

These two abundances are plotted in Fig. 24 and we find numerically TNuc≃7.7×108​K≃0.066​MeVT_{\rm Nuc}\simeq 7.7\times 10^{8}{\rm K}\simeq 0.066\,{\rm MeV} and a corresponding tNuc≃300​st_{\rm Nuc}\simeq 300\,{\rm s}. On Fig. 3, we see that nearly all neutrons are hidden in He4{}^{4}{\rm He} which is energetically more favored than deuterium. Overall the deuterium is only a catalytic agent, necessary to convert free neutrons in He4{}^{4}{\rm He}, and we find only traces of it at the end of BBN. The nucleosynthesis of all rare light elements is over when the temperature is around 6×107​K6\times 10^{7}{\rm K}, corresponding to tend≃5×104​st_{\rm end}\simeq 5\times 10^{4}\,{\rm s}. In our code, the decay reactions of elements whose half-life is much longer than tendt_{\rm end} are not included. However when reporting the final abundances of elements, it is customary to consider that these elements have been fully converted into stable elements. For instance the half-life of Be7{}^{7}{\rm Be} is 53.2253.22 days, as it decays into Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li}. Hence when reporting the latter abundances, we add the former ones. Similarly, tritium (H3{}^{3}{\rm H}) decays in He3{}^{3}{\rm He} in 12.3212.32 years and the former is added to the latter in the final abundances reported. The evolution of the isotopes as a function of time is depicted in Fig. 251818 18 The time evolution of 14C in Fig. 25, left panel, strongly differs from the one in Fig. 13 of Coc et al. [35]. This was due to an error in the 14C(OPENα,γ)18\alpha,\gamma)^{18}O and 14C(p,OPENγ)15\gamma)^{15}N reaction rates that are now fixed. It has, however no consequences on the total CNO production..

V.3 Effect of corrections on abundances

The effects of the various corrections in the weak rates have been estimated numerically and are reported in table 5. We have assessed the importance of individual corrections as well as the interplay of some corrections when they do not add simply linearly. Let us now comment in details the effect of these corrections.

V.3.1 Radiative corrections

Using the non-relativistic Fermi function and Sirlin’s function (222) without resummation of higher order corrections, we find Δ​YP(4)=31.0\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=31.0, exactly as in Lopez and Turner [123, Table V, line 2]. With the resummed radiative corrections (227) and using the relativistic Fermi function brings an extra Δ​YP(4)=0.5\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=0.5, worth being considered for precise predictions.

V.3.2 Finite nucleon mass corrections

We find that the cumulated effect of finite nucleon mass corrections and weak-magnetism brings Δ​YP(4)=12.8\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=12.8 corresponding to +0.53%+0.53\% This is slightly more than found by Lopez and Turner [123, Table V, line 3] which is Δ​YP(4)=12\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=12 corresponding to +0.50%+0.50\%, also evoked in Lopez et al. [124]. Given the smallness of the difference we consider that our results are in agreement with these references. Note that weak-magnetism accounts for around 12%12\% of the finite nucleon mass corrections.

It is worth commenting that when finite nucleon mass effects are considered together with incomplete neutrino decoupling, the total effect is less than the sum of the effects taken individually and there is a reduction Δ​YP(4)≃−0.6\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq-0.6. We found that this is because finite nucleon mass corrections are very sensitive to the neutrino temperature (see Fig. 20). Hence we advocate that a correct treatment of neutrino decoupling needs not only to be performed with the full machinery of the Boltzmann equation, with the inclusion of neutrino oscillations, but it should also be performed jointly with the inclusion of finite nucleon mass corrections. So far this joint treatment is lacking in the literature.

V.3.3 Finite temperature radiative corrections

In table 5, we report that the finite radiative corrections bring Δ​YP(4)≃3.1\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 3.1, reduced to Δ​YP(4)≃0\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 0 when bremsstrahlung corrections are added to obtain a consistent detailed balance of weak rates. Indeed in Fig. (18) we check that around freeze-out, finite radiative corrections and bremsstrahlung corrections are almost opposite. In both cases this is very different from the modification computed in Esposito et al. [70] where Δ​YP(4)≃−4\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq-4 is reported.

It is important to realize that the electron mass shift (44) is part of the finite-temperature corrections when it comes to considering the corrections to the weak rates. Hence we adopt the point of view of Brown and Sawyer [25] which is different from Lopez and Turner [123]. In order to allow a comparison with that reference, we evaluated independently the effect of the electron mass shift following their method, that is replacing the electron mass shift directly in the distribution functions, and we found a modification Δ​YP(4)≃+1.4\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq+1.4. Hence from the estimation of Lopez and Turner [123] for finite-temperature radiative corrections Δ​YP(4)≃3\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 3 one should instead use Δ​YP(4)≃4.4\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 4.4 to compare with our results. This is slightly larger than our value Δ​YP(4)≃3.1\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 3.1 without BS corrections but certainly larger than our value Δ​YP(4)≃0\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 0 with BS corrections.

In general, an enhancement of the rates induces a decrease of YPY_{\rm P} thanks to Eq. (7). In Lopez and Turner [123] the rates are increased by the finite temperature radiative corrections, and one would expect a decrease YPY_{\rm P}. However since the corrected rates no longer satisfy the detailed balance relation (86) as they should, Eq. (7) cannot be used and the effect is not opposite. In our case this can be seen when using the radiative corrections, without the BS corrections added. The weak rates are increased (see Fig. 18) and still it leads to Δ​YP(4)≃3.1\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 3.1. This highlights the extreme importance of constructing corrections which respect the detailed balance, in order to obtain meaningful results. Any corrections added which does not satisfy the correct detailed balance relation Eq. (7) is somehow equivalent to a modification of the value of the mass gap Δ\Delta, modifying artificially the thermal equilibrium value. Stated more directly, it is obvious that an overestimated enhancement of Γp→n\Gamma_{p\to n} as in Lopez and Turner [123] leads to an artificial increase of YnY_{n} and thus of YPY_{\rm P}. When a correction does not satisfy the detailed balance relation, the primary effect is no more a delayed or advanced freeze-out, that is a lower or larger freeze-out temperature, but an artificially different freeze-out abundance for the same freeze-out temperature since one rate is overestimated and the thermal equilibrium is artificially displaced.

V.3.4 QED effects on plasma thermodynamics

The effect of QED corrections on YPY_{\rm P} is negligible. In Lopez and Turner [123], it is estimated to be around Δ​YP(4)≃1\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 1 only because it is also cumulated with the electron mass shift effects which are part of finite temperature corrections of the weak rates in our terminology. We find Δ​YP(4)≃1.4\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 1.4 when computing it with the same method.

V.3.5 Incomplete neutrino decoupling

The pure clock effect evoked at the end of § III.9 is not the only effect, because one must also consider the effect of incomplete neutrino decoupling on the weak rates. In our approximate description, we have implicitly assumed in § II.7 that all neutrino flavors share the same ratio of heating, that is we assume that δ​ρνe/ρνe=δ​ρνμ/ρνμ=δ​ρντ/ρντ\delta\rho_{\nu_{e}}/\rho_{\nu_{e}}=\delta\rho_{\nu_{\mu}}/\rho_{\nu_{\mu}}=\delta\rho_{\nu_{\tau}}/\rho_{\nu_{\tau}} so that it is meaningful to define a common effective temperature. It is certainly not correct since there is more energy gained by electronic neutrino than other types of neutrino. Indeed electronic neutrinos couple to electrons and positron with charged and neutral currents whereas the other flavors of neutrinos couple only through neutral currents. However, first this is less the case when considering neutrino flavor mixing [127], and second in the early stage of neutrino heating by electron-positron annihilations, the heating is more efficiently redistributed among the three species. Hence it is not a too bad approximation to assume that the heating is distributed in the same ratio among flavors when considering the effect on weak rates. This means that we assume that all neutrino flavors share always 1/Nν1/N_{\nu} of the total energy density. Even though we know that they have distorted spectra, we still defined an effective neutrino temperature from their energy density. That is we still use Eq. (42) to define the neutrino temperature TνT_{\nu}, and by construction it is the temperature for thermalized neutrino distributions that would have the same energy density.

Apart from the clock effect mentioned earlier, there are two competing effects in the weak rates which nearly fully cancel [75, 63, 127]. First the higher energy density in neutrinos results in an increase of the weak rates, inducing a freeze-out which happens later, with less neutrons and thus producing less He4{}^{4}{\rm He}. However the energy gained by neutrinos is lost from the plasma, and the reduction in electrons-positrons energy density results in lower weak rates, inducing an earlier freeze-out which results in more neutrons and then more He4{}^{4}{\rm He} production. It has been shown in Fields et al. [75] that both effects level off when the freeze out is complete, that is around T=3.3×109​KT=3.3\times 10^{9}{\rm K}. Indeed we find that in our simple thermal approximation, the relative variation in the neutron fraction at that temperature is a modest relative increase of 2×10−52\times 10^{-5}. Without the clock effect this would result in a negligible Δ​YP(4)≃0.05\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 0.05. It is only the clock effect (see § V.3), that is the fact that neutrons have slightly less time to beta decay, which results in Δ​YP(4)≃1.2\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 1.2. When taking more carefully into account the fact that neutrinos do not get the same share of the heating, and that furthermore there are spectral distortions which affect the neutrino distribution functions entering the weak-rates, it is found a slightly larger increase in YP(4)Y_{\rm P}^{(4)} [127].

However note that our variations for YPY_{\rm P}, D/H{\rm D}/{\rm H}, He3/H{}^{3}{\rm He}/{\rm H} and Li7/H{}^{7}{\rm Li}/{\rm H} are in very close agreement with those found in Grohs et al. [88] (Table IV, second line), where these spectral distortions effects (but not the flavor oscillations) have been fully taken into account. It is puzzling that with our thermal approximation based on a heating rate found from Pisanti et al. [149], that is from the result of Mangano et al. [127], we do not recover the results of table 3 in Mangano et al. [127] but we recover with very good agreement the results of Grohs et al. [88]. We found that the argument presented in Grohs et al. [88] for the variations of D/H{\rm D}/{\rm H}, He3/H{}^{3}{\rm He}/{\rm H} and Li7/H{}^{7}{\rm Li}/{\rm H} are very convincing and we recover them in our numerics. Indeed the clock effect results in less time to destroy deuterium through D(d,n)3He, D(p,OPENγ)3\gamma)^{3}He and D(d,p)3H, ending up in more deuterium being left out at the end of BBN. Since two of these deuterium destroying reactions are producing He3{}^{3}{\rm He} [namely D(d,n)3He and D(p,OPENγ)3\gamma)^{3}He], this results in more He3{}^{3}{\rm He}. As for Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} it is reduced only because the production of Be7{}^{7}{\rm Be} has less time to proceed, but we found that the Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} (without Be7{}^{7}{\rm Be} added) is increased since it has also less time to be destroyed down from its peak value during BBN. Hence the signs of variations for D/H{\rm D}/{\rm H}, He3/H{}^{3}{\rm He}/{\rm H} and Li7/H{}^{7}{\rm Li}/{\rm H} have a clear physical origin, when incomplete neutrino decoupling is taken into account, and these signs are opposite to those reported in table 3 of Mangano et al. [127].

V.4 Dependence on main parameters

The variations of the yields for small variations of the main parameters can be given with expansions of the type

Δ​YPYP¯=∑p​q​rCp​q​r​(Δ​Ωb​h2Ωb​h2¯)p​(Δ​NνNν¯)q​(Δ​τnτn¯)r\frac{\Delta Y_{\rm P}}{\overline{Y_{\rm P}}}=\sum_{pqr}C_{pqr}\left(\frac{\Delta\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}}{\overline{\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}}}\right)^{p}\left(\frac{\Delta N_{\nu}}{\overline{N_{\nu}}}\right)^{q}\left(\frac{\Delta\tau_{n}}{\overline{\tau_{n}}}\right)^{r} (145)

with similar expansions for the other abundances (D/H,He3{}^{3}{\rm He}/H,Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li}/H). The reference abundances are given by the last line of table 5 and the reference parameters are Ωb​h2¯=0.02225\overline{\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}}=0.02225, τn¯=879.5​s\overline{\tau_{n}}=879.5\,{\rm s} and Nν¯=3\overline{N_{\nu}}=3. The meaning of varying the number of neutrinos is further discussed in § VI.4. The first coefficients of these expansions are given in table 6.

Leaving aside the non-standard BBN physics which corresponds to a variation of the number of neutrinos, we can restrict this expansion to the linear behaviour to estimate rapidly the variations of the abundances in function of changes in the baryon abundance or the neutron lifetime. Hence if these parameters are slightly modified in the future, our results can be transposed easily. We find

Δ​YPYP¯=0.0390​Δ​Ωb​h2Ωb​h2¯+0.732​Δ​τnτn¯​Δ​D/HD/H¯=−1.65​Δ​Ωb​h2Ωb​h2¯+0.422​Δ​τnτn¯​Δ​He3/HHe3/H¯=−0.567​Δ​Ωb​h2Ωb​h2¯+0.141​Δ​τnτn¯​Δ​Li7/HLi7/H¯=2.08​Δ​Ωb​h2Ωb​h2¯+0.438​Δ​τnτn¯.\frac{\Delta Y_{\rm P}}{\overline{Y_{\rm P}}}&=0.0390\frac{\Delta\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}}{\overline{\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}}}+0.732\frac{\Delta\tau_{n}}{\overline{\tau_{n}}}\\ \frac{\Delta{\rm D}/{\rm H}}{\overline{{\rm D}/{\rm H}}}=-1.65\frac{\Delta\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}}{\overline{\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}}}+0.422\frac{\Delta\tau_{n}}{\overline{\tau_{n}}}\\ \frac{\Delta{}^{3}{\rm He}/{\rm H}}{\overline{{}^{3}{\rm He}/{\rm H}}}=-0.567\frac{\Delta\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}}{\overline{\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}}}+0.141\frac{\Delta\tau_{n}}{\overline{\tau_{n}}}\\ \frac{\Delta{}^{7}{\rm Li}/{\rm H}}{\overline{{}^{7}{\rm Li}/{\rm H}}}=2.08\frac{\Delta\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}}{\overline{\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}}}+0.438\frac{\Delta\tau_{n}}{\overline{\tau_{n}}}\,. (146)

As expected, YPY_{\rm P} is very sensitive to the weak rates and thus to τn\tau_{n} but not to the baryon abundance. Hence even though uncertainty is larger in baryon abundance, the theoretical uncertainty of YPY_{\rm P} is dominated by the uncertainty in the determination of the neutron lifetime. From the measured value of τn\tau_{n} reported in appendix D, this corresponds to a 0.068%0.068\,\% uncertainty in YPY_{\rm P} or σ⁡(YP)≃0.00017\sigma(Y_{\rm P})\simeq 0.00017 which is lower than the value σ⁡(YP)≃0.0003\sigma(Y_{\rm P})\simeq 0.0003 used in Ade et al. [2, p47], implying that we find errors approximately 40%40\% smaller in YPY_{\rm P}. The predicted and observed abundances as functions of η\eta are plotted in Fig. 26.

V.5 Distribution of abundance predictions

We use the method described in Coc et al. [39] to estimate the uncertainty in light elements productions during BBN due to uncertainty in nuclear rates and weak-rates (that is the uncertainty on τn\tau_{n} that we assume to follow a normal distribution). It has been found [122], that probability density functions of reaction rates can be well approximated by lognormal distributions

f(x)=1σ​2​π1xe−(lnx−μ)2/(2σ2)f(x)=\frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{1}{x}e^{-(\ln x-\mu)^{2}/(2\sigma^{2})} (147)

(with x≡NA​⟨σ​v⟩x\equiv{N_{A}}\langle\sigma{v}\rangle for short is the rate). This is equivalent to the assumption that ln⁡(x)\ln(x) is Gaussian distributed with expectation value μ\mu and variance σ2\sigma^{2} (both functions of temperature). The lognormal distribution allows to cope with large uncertainty factors (≡eσ{\equiv}e^{\sigma}) together with ensuring that the rates remain positive. If these parameters are tabulated as a function of the temperature, they can be used to perform subsequent Monte-Carlo nucleosynthesis calculations. The quantile of the distributions of the abundances obtained by such a method are reported in table 7 for which we used 20 00020\,000 Monte-Carlo points.

The variations of YPY_{\rm P} are nearly entirely due to the uncertainty on τn\tau_{n} because it is almost completely controlled by weak rates which set the abundance of free neutrons before nucleosynthesis starts. This Monte-Carlo method allows to construct the probability P⁡(Yi|ωb)P(Y_{i}|\omega_{\rm b}) for each species, where ωb≡Ωb​h2\omega_{\rm b}\equiv\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}. This probability reflects the uncertainty in all parameters affecting the reaction rates, independently of cosmology and it is used to plot the ±σ\pm\sigma width of curved in Fig. 26 by computing the quantiles {0.15865,0.84135}\{0.15865,0.84135\}.

For elements for which the uncertainty is small, it proves useful to approximate these probabilities by a normal distribution as

P⁡(Yi|ωb)≃𝒩⁡[Y¯i​(ωb),σith​(ωb)]​(Yi)P(Y_{i}|\omega_{\rm b})\simeq{\cal N}\left[\bar{Y}_{i}\left(\omega_{\rm b}\right),\sigma^{\rm th}_{i}\left(\omega_{\rm b}\right)\right](Y_{i}) (148)

where the normal distribution is noted

𝒩⁡[μ,σ]​(x)≡12​π​σ​exp​[−(x−μ)22​σ2].{\cal N}[\mu,\sigma](x)\equiv\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}{\rm exp}\left[-\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\right]\,. (149)

If we use the CMB to obtain a prior distribution on ωb\omega_{\rm b} that we assume to follow a normal distribution (the mean and standard deviation are reported in appendix D), then we can build the joint probability

P⁡(Yi,ωb|CMB)=P⁡(Yi|ωb)​P​(ωb|CMB),P(Y_{i},\omega_{\rm b}|{\rm CMB})=P(Y_{i}|\omega_{\rm b})P(\omega_{\rm b}|{\rm CMB})\,, (150)

and marginalizing over ωb\omega_{\rm b} we get probabilities in predicted abundances

P⁡(Yi|CMB)=∫P⁡(Yi,ωb|CMB)​d​ωb.P(Y_{i}|{\rm CMB})=\int P(Y_{i},\omega_{\rm b}|{\rm CMB})\mathrm{d}\omega_{\rm b}\,. (151)

In practice we use also a Monte-Carlo method to obtain directly P⁡(Yi|CMB)P(Y_{i}|{\rm CMB}). We only need to vary ωb\omega_{\rm b}, according to its normal distribution, in addition to varying the reaction rates. With this method we can predict the underlying abundances that are reported in table 8. The predicted abundance for deuterium is noticeably lower than the one in Ade et al. [2, Eq. 74] which uses PArthENoPE [149], and this has consequences when inferring the chemical potential of neutrinos (see § VI.3).

V.6 Comparison with observations

Except for He4{}^{4}{\rm He}, and the weak rates, the predicted abundances, displayed in Table 8, do not differ significantly from those of Coc et al. [38]. As can be seen in Table 4, very few reaction rates have been updated, and if so, either the rate changes are tiny or the reactions have, in any case, a negligible effect. On the contrary, there are significative differences with the results of Cyburt et al. [55] which are mostly, and probably entirely, due to the different choice of reaction rates. Apparently, Cyburt et al. [55] use for some of the most important reactions, D(p,OPENγ)3\gamma)^{3}He, D(d,n)3He, D(d,p)3H, and 3He(OPENα,γ)7\alpha,\gamma)^{7}Be, the rates from NACRE ii [189], now superseded for these reactions by Coc et al. [38], Iliadis et al. [103], Gómez Iñesta et al. [83]. This is clearly the origin of the differences concerning D and Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li}. There is an even greater difference with the D/H value reported by Planck [2, 61] using the PArthENoPE code [149]. This is again, probably due to a different choice of reaction rates for deuterium destruction.

Since the results for deuterium and lithium are not significantly different from our earlier works [39, 38] the comparison with observations is very similar. As explained in § I.1.3 we do not consider He3{}^{3}{\rm He} as a constraint.

V.6.1 Helium

Thanks to the re–evaluation of the corrections to the weak rates, we claim a precision of a few 10−410^{-4} on YPY_{\rm P} i.e. smaller than one unit on YP(4)Y_{\rm P}^{(4)} before taking into account the experimental uncertainty on the neutron lifetime and a few reaction rates (§ IV.3). We finally obtained YP=0.24705±Y_{\rm P}=0.24705\pm0.00019, fully consistent with the value YP=0.2449±0.0040Y_{\rm P}=0.2449\pm 0.0040 deduced from Izotov et al. [109] observations by Aver et al. [15] (see Fig. 26), without the need for extra relativistic degrees of freedom as in [109].

Since this work is focused on He4{}^{4}{\rm He} and is an improved continuation of previous works it is worthwhile tracking the evolution of our calculation of YPY_{\rm P}. In our earliest works (e.g. Coc et al. [44]), since the observational uncertainties on YPY_{\rm P} were large, we neglected some of the corrections discussed here because we were unable to calculate them (e.g. including six–fold integrals). The corrections that we took into account corresponds to line RCa line in Table 5 and our (Fortran) calculated corrections did amount to δ​YP(4)=31.6\delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=31.6 [39]. When the observational uncertainties were reduced, it become important to include the neglected corrections, by artificially increasing YP(4)Y_{\rm P}^{(4)} by 18 at the the very end of the calculation. It corresponded to the finite-nucleon mass correction (δ​YP(4)=12\delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=12 [123]), finite-temperature radiative correction (δ​YP(4)=3\delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=3) [123]), QED plasma (δ​YP(4)=1\delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=1 [123]) and neutrino decoupling (δ​YP(4)=2\delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=2 [127]), for a total of δ​YP(4)=18\delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=18, that we could not easily directly re-calculate. Hence, before this final correction, the YPY_{\rm P} value from Coc et al. [38] was 0.2466 (i.e. 0.2484 minus 0.0018) to be compared to 0.245720.24572 (RCa in Table 5). This difference of δ​YP(4)=9\delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=9, which is in fact only δ​YP(4)=7\delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=7 if we account for the different τn\tau_{n} used, was reduced to δ​YP(4)≃0.5\delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\simeq 0.5 by improving the Fortran code (time steps, temperature grid,...) at the expense of execution time1919 19 Details to appear elsewhere..

V.6.2 Deuterium

Our present result differs by less than 3%, and agrees within error bars with the latest value inferred from Cooke et al. [49] observations. Since the theoretical value lies on the lower bound of the observational one, this leaves only little room for models of lithium (i.e. 7Be) destruction that byproduct extra deuterium (see below). Tiny differences with previous results [38] come in part from the corrections to the weak rates (see Table 5), to the re-evaluation of the three nuclear reaction rates [103, 83] that govern deuterium destruction and improvements in the numerical method. With the high precision reached by D/H observations, these reaction rates [D(p,OPENγ)3\gamma)^{3}He, D(d,n)3He and D(d,p)3H] need to be known at the percent level! This demands accurate measurement at BBN energies where data are scarce and theoretical improvement to better constrain the energy dependence of the SS–factors.

V.6.3 Lithium

There remains a factor of 3.6 between the predicted and observed Li/H values. This discrepancy has not yet found a fully satisfactory solution. On the contrary, the problem had worsened because of an updated reaction rate [53, 54] and because many solutions have been ruled out by the improved precision on D/H observations [49]. We present below the kinds of solutions that have been considered so far.

  • •

    There is no nuclear solution to the lithium problem. Extensive sensitivity studies [44, 35] have not identified reactions, beyond those already known, that could have a strong impact on lithium nucleosynthesis. The most promising was 7Be(d,p)2​α2\alpha [44, 56]: an increase of its rate by a factor of ≈\approx100 would have solved the problem. However, measurements of its average cross section [9] or properties of candidate resonances [145, 161, 115] ruled out this possibility. More generally, other destruction channels have recently been proposed [30] : 7Be+n, p, d, t, He3{}^{3}{\rm He} and He4{}^{4}{\rm He}. In particular, the existence of a relatively narrow state around 15 MeV in the compound nucleus 10C formed by 7Be+3He or the existence of a state close to 8 MeV in the compound nucleus 11C formed by 7Be+4He could help reduce the 7Be production. However, a recent search [91] for missing levels in the relevant excitation energy regions of 10C and 11C, via the reactions 10B(3He,t)10C and 11B(3He,t)11C, respectively, did not find any new level, whose corresponding resonances, in any case, would have too low strengths [24] because of the Coulomb barrier. It seems now that all extra 7Be destructing reactions have been considered and found inefficient.

  • •

    The effect of electron screening or modification of decay lifetime is negligible. For reactions of interest to BBN, screening affects the laboratory cross sections at too low energies [e.g. ≲\lesssim 20 keV for D(d,p)3H [86] or 3He(d,p)4He [4]] to affect measurement at BBN energies [≈\approx100 keV], on the one hand. On the other hand, the effect of screening during BBN is completely negligible [183, 72]. It is well known that the lifetime of 7Be that decays by electron capture depends on the probability of presence of an electron (from an atomic ss orbital or from a plasma) inside the nucleus; for instance it is increased to ∼100\sim 100 days at the center of the Sun [3]. To have an impact on lithium prediction, the 7Be lifetime must be reduced to a value of ∼103\sim 10^{3} s. However, because of the Boltzmann suppression factor, at T<T<0.5 GK, when 7Be is present, the electron density becomes smaller than in the Sun so that one can expect an even longer lifetime. This can be confirmed if one extrapolates the results of Simonucci et al. [168, Fig. 1], to T≲500×106T\lesssim 500\times 10^{6}K and ρ≲10−5\rho\lesssim 10^{-5} g/cm3.

  • •

    Many exotic solutions to the lithium problem have been investigated (e.g. Yamazaki et al. [190]), but most rely on extra neutron sources to boost 7Be destruction through the 7Be(n,p)7Li(p,OPENα)4\alpha)^{4}He channel. However, these extra neutrons, inevitably, also boost the D and 3H production through the 1H(n,OPENγ)2\gamma)^{2}H and 3He(n,p)3H channels, respectively [117, 38]. This is shown in Figs. 1 in Olive et al. [144], 4 in Kusakabe et al. [117], and 14 in Coc et al. [38] that display results of various types of models that succeed in solving the lithium problem, but at the expense of deuterium overproduction to levels now excluded by observations [47, 48, 49]. Very few solutions, even beyond the Standard Model, that do not suffer from this drawback are left, e.g. Goudelis et al. [85].

  • •

    Stellar physics solutions require a uniform reduction of surface lithium over a wide range of effective temperature and metallicity. Some amount of surface lithium destruction is unavoidable, because of atomic diffusion that transport lithium down to deeper and hotter layers where it is destroyed by a factor of 1.5 to 2 [136]. The difficulty comes from the small thickness of the lithium plateau over a wide range of metallicity and temperature and the absence of stars between the plateau and the BBN prediction (Fig. 2). This could possibly be circumvented if an additional mixing process is included in the outer layers of these stars [153]. This is supported by the comparison between lithium observations in the metal–poor globular cluster NGC 6397 with stellar depletion models [116]. Another recent proposition relies on full lithium destruction but followed by a self–regulated re-enrichment of lithium by late time accretion from the interstellar gas [80]. In addition, the Spite plateau does not exist anymore at the metallicity below [Fe/H]=-3, and is replaced by an increased spread of abundances, below the plateau value [158]. This “meltdown” of the Spite plateau is not understood yet. All this suggests that lithium observations cannot be used anymore to constrain BBN models.

  • •

    There is no Li6{}^{6}{\rm Li} problem anymore. A few years ago, observations [13] of Li6{}^{6}{\rm Li} in a few metal poor stars had suggested the presence of a plateau, at typically Li6{}^{6}{\rm Li}/H ≈10−11\approx 10^{-11}, orders of magnitude higher than the BBN predictions of Li6{}^{6}{\rm Li}/H ≈1.3×10−14\approx 1.3\times 10^{-14} [92]. However, later, the observational Li6{}^{6}{\rm Li} plateau has been questioned due to line asymmetries which were neglected in previous abundance analyses. Hence, there is no remaining evidence for a plateau at very low metallicity [121] that can be used to derive a primordial Li6{}^{6}{\rm Li} abundance.

V.6.4 Other elements

Leaving aside the 9Be, 10B and 11B isotopes for which no primordial abundance can be inferred from observations [39], it is worth mentioning the CNO abundance. Here, we call CNO all isotopes with masses larger than 12 (11C mostly decays to 11B). Even though, there are no primordial CNO abundance either, it is of peculiar interest since it may affect the evolution of the first stars (Population III) within the first structures of the Universe. Hydrogen burning in the first generation of stars proceeds through the slow pp–chains until enough carbon is produced (through the triple-alpha reaction) to activate the CNO cycle. The minimum value of the initial CNO mass fraction that would affect Population III stellar evolution is estimated to be 10-11 [29] or even as low as 10-13 (in number of atoms relative to hydrogen, CNO/H) for the less massive stars [68]. Table 7 shows that the median abundance (0.5 quantile) is in agreement with previous works [105, 35], if taking into account that the distribution is not Gaussian [39, 41]. As a result, the 0.97725 quantile corresponds to CNO/H≈0.7×10−13\approx 0.7\times 10^{-13}, close to the limit to have an impact on some first stars. As this is explained in Coc et al. [39], this value, much larger than the median comes from the simultaneous variations, during the Monte Carlo, of a few reaction rates around 10Be. Since very few or no experimental data are available for these reactions, the actual rates may differ by a few orders of magnitudes, from the TALYS [84] theoretical predictions. Experimental efforts are needed to confirm or infirm this possibility.

VI Cosmology with BBN

VI.1 Cosmological perturbations

Cosmological fluctuations are of order 10−510^{-5}, and whatever their effect, we have neglected them given our precision goal. However it is easy to estimate the effect of adiabatic perturbations seeded by inflation. Indeed, since the Hubble radius is extremely small during BBN, most modes can be considered as super-Hubble modes, that is longer than the Hubble radius. In that case their effect can be described by a simple coordinate transformation applied on a homogeneous cosmology [185, 51, 137].

Let us consider a perturbed metric (expressed in conformal time defined by d​t=a​d​η\mathrm{d}t=a\mathrm{d}\eta)

d​s2=a2​(η)​(−(1+2​Φ)​d​η2+(1−2​Ψ)​δi​j​d​xi​d​xj).\mathrm{d}s^{2}=a^{2}(\eta)\left(-(1+2\Phi)\mathrm{d}\eta^{2}+(1-2\Psi)\delta_{ij}\mathrm{d}x^{i}\mathrm{d}x^{j}\right)\,. (152)

It can be put in the homogeneous form using a coordinate transformation. Or conversely the dynamics of a spacetime perturbed by long modes can be deduced from the homogeneous dynamics thanks to a coordinate transformation. Not all such transformations lead to a physical long mode dynamics, and one must ensure some conditions. In the case where the Universe dynamics is dominated by radiation, as is the case for BBN, the relevant coordinate transformation is [51]

η~=η⁡(1−ζ3),x~i=xi​(1+ζ)\tilde{\eta}=\eta\left(1-\frac{\zeta}{3}\right)\,,\qquad\tilde{x}^{i}=x^{i}(1+\zeta) (153)

where ζ\zeta is the comoving curvature perturbation.

It follows using Eq. (10) that the number density in the perturbed universe n~i\tilde{n}_{i} is related to the one of a homogeneous cosmology nin_{i} thanks to

n~i=ni−η​ζ3​∂ηni=(1+ζ)​ni−η​ζ3​a​𝒥i,\tilde{n}_{i}=n_{i}-\frac{\eta\zeta}{3}\partial_{\eta}n_{i}=(1+\zeta)n_{i}-\frac{\eta\zeta}{3}a{\cal J}_{i}\,, (154)

where we used that for radiation domination a∝ηa\propto\eta and ∂ηa/a=1/η\partial_{\eta}a/a=1/\eta.
