At the end of BBN, when all reactions are inefficient, all net creation rates 𝒥i{\cal J}_{i} vanish and we find that all number densities are simply rescaled by 1+ζ1+\zeta. Note that this could have been anticipated because for super-Hubble modes, ζ\zeta is equal to density perturbations on isocurvature surfaces [179]. Since abundances are ratios of number densities, they remain unchanged by the long mode perturbation. Hence, provided we can neglect the effect of modes which are smaller than the Hubble radius during BBN, standard adiabatic cosmological perturbations have no effect on BBN predictions. Intuitively, an adiabatic perturbation enhances baryon and photons number densities in the same proportions, leaving η\eta constant. Since this analysis is based on long modes only, one cannot infer the consequences of fluctuations on scales smaller than the Hubble radius during BBN from the homogeneous cosmology results. For these small scales, only a complete treatment of all perturbed equations dictating the evolution of species can lead to a meaningful result.

Finally, it is worth noting that long modes of entropy perturbation, that is perturbations which do not modify the total energy density (and for which ζ=0\zeta=0) but which modify the ratios ρb/ργ\rho_{\rm b}/\rho_{\gamma} have an effect on abundances. Since during BBN the total energy density is dominated by radiation, and long mode entropy perturbation can be rephrased as a perturbation in ρb\rho_{\rm b} alone, that is a perturbation of η\eta. As a consequence, its effect is directly evaluated by the sensitivity of BBN final abundances on η\eta.

VI.2 Measurement of baryon abundance from BBN

The observed abundances are related to the underlying one by an assumed normal distribution, that is for each isotope observed, the likelihood is

P⁡(Yiobs|Yi)=𝒩⁡[Yi,σiobs]​(Yiobs).P(Y_{i}^{\rm obs}|Y_{i})={\cal N}\left[Y_{i},\sigma^{\rm obs}_{i}\right](Y_{i}^{\rm obs})\,. (155)

The observed values and their standard deviations are reported in § I.1. Then we can consider

P⁡(Yiobs|ωb)≡∫d​Yi​P​(Yiobs|Yi)​P​(Yi|ωb),P(Y_{i}^{\rm obs}|\omega_{\rm b})\equiv\int\mathrm{d}Y_{i}P(Y_{i}^{\rm obs}|Y_{i})P(Y_{i}|\omega_{\rm b})\,,

and we deduce using Eqs. (148) and (155) that it follows approximately a normal distribution

P⁡(Yiobs|ωb)≃𝒩⁡[Y¯i​(ωb),Σi​(ωb)]​(Yiobs)P(Y_{i}^{\rm obs}|\omega_{\rm b})\simeq{\cal N}\left[\bar{Y}_{i}\left(\omega_{\rm b}\right),\Sigma_{i}(\omega_{\rm b})\right](Y_{i}^{\rm obs}) (156)

with Σi2​(ωb)≡(σiobs)2+[σith​(ωb)]2\Sigma^{2}_{i}(\omega_{\rm b})\equiv(\sigma^{\rm obs}_{i})^{2}+\left[\sigma^{\rm th}_{i}\left(\omega_{\rm b}\right)\right]^{2}. In practice we do not use the approximation (148) and use instead the full result of our Monte-Carlo method to estimate the distribution of abundances due to reaction rates uncertainties. However, the results obtained are extremely similar given that (148) is a very good approximation.

If we then use an uniform prior on ωb\omega_{\rm b}, that is if we do not use our knowledge from CMB observations, the posterior distribution for ωb\omega_{\rm b} is immediately given from P⁡(ωb|Yiobs)∝P⁡(Yiobs|ωb)P(\omega_{\rm b}|Y_{i}^{\rm obs})\propto P(Y_{i}^{\rm obs}|\omega_{\rm b}). Otherwise we use the CMB prior to build the posterior distribution for ωb\omega_{\rm b} as

P⁡(ωb|Yiobs,CMB)\displaystyle P(\omega_{\rm b}|Y_{i}^{\rm obs},{\rm CMB}) ∝\displaystyle\propto P⁡(Yiobs,ωb|CMB)\displaystyle P(Y_{i}^{\rm obs},\omega_{\rm b}|{\rm CMB}) (157)
=\displaystyle= P⁡(Yiobs|ωb)​P​(ωb|CMB).\displaystyle P(Y_{i}^{\rm obs}|\omega_{\rm b})P(\omega_{\rm b}|{\rm CMB}).

When including all observed abundances, we use that the total probability is the product of individual ones. In practice, only He4{}^{4}{\rm He} and H2{}^{2}{\rm H} are determined with enough precise experimental precision to be taken into account.

The CMB prior distribution and the posterior distribution from the observations of BBN are plotted in Fig. 27. The posterior bounds from BBN and CMB are Ωb​h2=0.02215±0.00014\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}=0.02215\pm 0.00014, whereas from BBN alone on gets Ωb​h2=0.02190±0.00025\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}=0.02190\pm 0.00025. Note that if we had used a code which predicts D/H≃2.61×10−5{\rm D}/{\rm H}\simeq 2.61\times 10^{-5} instead of D/H≃2.46×10−5{\rm D}/{\rm H}\simeq 2.46\times 10^{-5} for the Planck parameters, we would have obtained the constraint Ωb​h2=0.02271±0.00025\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}=0.02271\pm 0.00025 from BBN alone, having exactly the same central value than found in Consiglio et al. [45], using PArthENoPE.

VI.3 Neutrino chemical potential from BBN

If there is a neutrino asymmetry, that is a non-vanishing neutrino chemical potential, then for each flavor we have necessarily

μν+μν¯=0\mu_{\nu}+\mu_{\bar{\nu}}=0 (158)

because of processes like ν+ν¯↔e−+e+↔2​γ\nu+\bar{\nu}\leftrightarrow e^{-}+e^{+}\leftrightarrow 2\gamma and photons have a vanishing chemical potential. Furthermore cosmological expansion affects only the particle momenta and ξν≡μν/Tν\xi_{\nu}\equiv\mu_{\nu}/T_{\nu} is frozen at its initial value, whose consequences on BBN can be investigated [166, 106, 167].

The neutrino asymmetry (defined for each neutrino flavor) is defined by the excess of neutrinos over antineutrinos as

ην≡nν−nν¯nγ\displaystyle\eta_{\nu}\equiv\frac{n_{\nu}-n_{\bar{\nu}}}{n_{\gamma}} =\displaystyle= I+(1,1)​(0,ξν)−I+(1,1)​(0,−ξν)2​I−(1,1)\displaystyle\frac{I_{+}^{(1,1)}(0,\xi_{\nu})-I_{+}^{(1,1)}(0,-\xi_{\nu})}{2I_{-}^{(1,1)}} (159)
≃\displaystyle\simeq 112​ζ​(3)​(TνT)3​(π2​ξν+ξν3).\displaystyle\frac{1}{12\zeta(3)}\left(\frac{T_{\nu}}{T}\right)^{3}\left(\pi^{2}\xi_{\nu}+\xi_{\nu}^{3}\right).

The neutrino oscillations imply that the various flavors must reach an equilibrium for which the chemical potentials are equal [188, 64]. Assuming accordingly that the asymmetry is the same for all flavors, the first modification of the neutrino asymmetry is an excess of energy densities stored in neutrinos which can be absorbed by a redefinition of the number of neutrino generations NνN_{\nu} as

N~ν\displaystyle\tilde{N}_{\nu} =\displaystyle= Nν​(1+I+(2,1)​(0,ξν)+I+(2,1)​(0,−ξν)2​I+(2,1))\displaystyle N_{\nu}\left(1+\frac{I_{+}^{(2,1)}(0,\xi_{\nu})+I_{+}^{(2,1)}(0,-\xi_{\nu})}{2I_{+}^{(2,1)}}\right) (160)
≃\displaystyle\simeq Nν​(1+30​ξν27​π2+15​ξν47​π4).\displaystyle N_{\nu}\left(1+\frac{30\xi_{\nu}^{2}}{7\pi^{2}}+\frac{15\xi_{\nu}^{4}}{7\pi^{4}}\right)\,.

This effect is very small for small values of ξν\xi_{\nu} since it is at least quadratic in ξν\xi_{\nu}.

There is a second modification for the weak-interaction rates in which one must use instead of Eq. (75)

gν​(E)≡{gν+​(E)≡1e(E/Tν−ξν)+1n→p​ratesgν−​(E)≡1e(E/Tν+ξν)+1p→n​rates.g_{\nu}(E)\equiv\begin{cases}g^{+}_{\nu}(E)\equiv\frac{1}{{\rm e}^{\left(E/T_{\nu}-\xi_{\nu}\right)}+1}&n\to p\,\,{\rm rates}\\ g^{-}_{\nu}(E)\equiv\frac{1}{{\rm e}^{\left(E/T_{\nu}+\xi_{\nu}\right)}+1}&p\to n\,\,{\rm rates}\,.\\ \end{cases} (161)

For instance in the definition (79) of χ±\chi_{\pm}, one must use gν±g_{\nu}^{\pm} instead of gνg_{\nu}. To show this we used that the Pauli-blocking factor of the antineutrino (resp. neutrino) is still related to the distribution of the neutrino (resp. antineutrino) according to (72) thanks to the property (158). This modification is the most important one and modifies the thermodynamical equilibrium ratio between neutrons and protons (183) because from Eq. (182) we get μn−μp=−μν\mu_{n}-\mu_{p}=-\mu_{\nu}. We get that at thermodynamical equilibrium

nnnp=nnnp|ξν=0×e−ξν,\frac{n_{n}}{n_{p}}=\left.\frac{n_{n}}{n_{p}}\right|_{\xi_{\nu}=0}\times{\rm e}^{-\xi_{\nu}}\,, (162)

and one expects a modification of the freeze-out abundance (for small ξν\xi_{\nu}) of order

Δ​YnFYnF≃Δ​YPYP≃−(1−YnF)​ξν.\frac{\Delta Y^{F}_{n}}{Y^{F}_{n}}\simeq\frac{\Delta Y_{\rm P}}{Y_{\rm P}}\simeq-(1-Y_{n}^{F})\xi_{\nu}\,. (163)

Finally there is a third modification when one considers the effect of incomplete neutrino decoupling [87] but this is negligible since the effect without the asymmetry is already very small. For small ξν\xi_{\nu} we find the abundance modifications

Δ​YPYP≃−0.96​ξν​Δ​D/HD/H≃−0.53​ξν​Δ​He3/HHe3/H≃−0.18​ξν​Δ​Li7/HLi7/H≃−0.62​ξν.\frac{\Delta Y_{\rm P}}{Y_{\rm P}}&\simeq-0.96\,\xi_{\nu}\\ \frac{\Delta{\rm D}/{\rm H}}{{\rm D}/{\rm H}}\simeq-0.53\,\xi_{\nu}\\ \frac{\Delta{}^{3}{\rm He}/{\rm H}}{{}^{3}{\rm He}/{\rm H}}\simeq-0.18\,\xi_{\nu}\\ \frac{\Delta{}^{7}{\rm Li}/{\rm H}}{{}^{7}{\rm Li}/{\rm H}}\simeq-0.62\,\xi_{\nu}\,. (164)

The modification of YPY_{\rm P} is in very good agreement with the estimation (163) since (1−YnF)≃0.92(1-Y_{n}^{F})\simeq 0.92. Since BBN has no free parameter when assuming non-degenerate neutrinos (ξν=0\xi_{\nu}=0), the observational constraints on YPY_{\rm P} and D/H{\rm D}/{\rm H} can be used to obtain bounds on the degeneracy parameter ξν\xi_{\nu} if we consider instead that it is unknown.

We repeat the analysis of § VI.2, using the pair of cosmological parameters (ωb,ξν)(\omega_{\rm b},\xi_{\nu}) instead of ωb\omega_{\rm b} alone. However, we still assume that the CMB prior determines only ωb\omega_{\rm b}. Again, for each species the uncertainty from nuclear rates σith​(ωb,ξν)\sigma^{\rm th}_{i}(\omega_{\rm b},\xi_{\nu}) is obtained from a Monte-Carlo method. The posterior distribution for (ωb,ξν)(\omega_{\rm b},\xi_{\nu}) from BBN combined with CMB is plotted in Fig. 28. Once marginalized over baryon abundance we get

ξν=0.001±0.016,\xi_{\nu}=0.001\pm 0.016\,, (165)

which is a much tighter constraint than the constraints from CMB alone [142, ξν=−0.002−0.060+0.053{\xi_{\nu}=-0.002}^{+0.053}_{-0.060}] or than earlier BBN constraints such as Simha and Steigman [167, = ξ ν ± 0.037 0.026 ], thanks to the recent improvement on both deuterium and He4{}^{4}{\rm He} abundance measurements.

Even though the bounds (165) are tighter, they are also surprisingly still highly compatible with a vanishing neutrino chemical potential. Since we find |ξν|<0.016​(68%​CL)|\xi_{\nu}|<0.016\,(68\%\,{\rm CL}), it corresponds to (N~ν−Nν)/Nν<0.011%(\tilde{N}_{\nu}-N_{\nu})/N_{\nu}<0.011\% and ην<4.0×10−3\eta_{\nu}<4.0\times 10^{-3}.

Note that if we had used Parthenope [149], as is the case in Ade et al. [2], which predicts D/H≃2.61×10−5{\rm D}/{\rm H}\simeq 2.61\times 10^{-5} rather than D/H≃2.46×10−5{\rm D}/{\rm H}\simeq 2.46\times 10^{-5} for Planck parameters, we would have found rather ξν=0.021±0.016\xi_{\nu}=0.021\pm 0.016 less compatible with a vanishing neutrino chemical potential. Indeed, in our case the observed value for YPY_{\rm P} (resp. D/H{\rm D}/{\rm H}) is lower (resp. higher) than the averaged value inferred from the CMB measured baryon abundance, and given the linearized dependences (164) which have the same sign, this results in a compensation and a central value very close to zero. However if the prediction for deuterium from a BBN code is also above its observed value, then both YPY_{\rm P} and D/H{\rm D}/{\rm H} tend to favor a positive ξν\xi_{\nu}.

VI.4 Number of neutrinos

We repeat the analysis of § VI.2 but for the pairs of cosmological parameters (Ωb​h2,Nν)(\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2},N_{\nu}) instead of the baryon abundance alone. We use the CMB prior P⁡(Ωb​h2,Nν|CMB)P(\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2},N_{\nu}|{\rm CMB}) obtained from the Monte-Carlo Markov chains base_nnu_plikHM_TTTEEE_lowTEB of Ade et al. [2] (TT+TE+EE+lowP analysis). The constraints from CMB are given directly in terms of NeffN_{\rm eff} (see § II.7) since they are obtained as the model-independent gravitational contribution of relativistic degrees of freedom. However, during BBN the effective number of neutrinos evolves as can be seen in Fig. 10, and this evolution is model-dependent. We assume that if there are extra relativistic degrees of freedom, they do not share any of the energy which is brought to neutrinos by incomplete decoupling. Hence for these extra neutrinos, or what is described phenomenologically as extra neutrinos, zν=1z_{\nu}=1 throughout BBN. Given these assumptions Eq. (66) which was derived for Nν=3N_{\nu}=3 becomes

Neff=3​(zν​zstandz)4+(Nν−3)​(zstandz)4,N_{\rm eff}=3\left(\frac{z_{\nu}z^{\rm stand}}{z}\right)^{4}+(N_{\nu}-3)\left(\frac{z^{\rm stand}}{z}\right)^{4}\,, (166)

from which we deduce in particular that d​Neff/d​Nν=(zstand/z)4≃1.0090\mathrm{d}N_{\rm eff}/\mathrm{d}N_{\nu}=\left(z^{\rm stand}/z\right)^{4}\simeq 1.0090. In fact, this relation is unchanged as long as the energy exchange between the plasma and the neutrino sector remains identical to Eq. (60), that is if the function 𝒩⁡(T){\cal N}(T) is unchanged. More generally the effective number of neutrinos is insensitive to any type of neutrino spectral distortions which leaves the total neutrino energy density unchanged. Hence, as long as the energy transfer with the plasma is the same, we can also assume that the new neutrino degrees of freedom share a part of the energy transfer during the incomplete decoupling phase, and still use Eq. (166). This relation allows to convert the distribution P⁡(Ωb​h2,Neff|CMB)P(\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2},N_{\rm eff}|{\rm CMB}) into P⁡(Ωb​h2,Nν|CMB)P(\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2},N_{\nu}|{\rm CMB}). This approach is different from the one chosen by Cyburt et al. [55] where Eq. (66) is assumed to hold even for Nν≠3N_{\nu}\neq 3. However, given the rather large observational bounds on NνN_{\nu} obtained, and the smallness of zν4z_{\nu}^{4}, this difference in the conversion of neutrino numbers is not crucial.

The posteriors obtained are depicted in Fig. 29. They are to be compared with the plots of Cyburt et al. [55, Fig. 10]. Furthermore, it presents a significant improvement compared to Cooke et al. [49, Fig. 7] thanks to the inclusion of the measured YPY_{\rm P} in the BBN constraint. We used the full results of the chains for the CMB prior, but it can be very well represented by a two-dimensional Gaussian distribution with Ωb​h2=0.022197±0.000245\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}=0.022197\pm 0.000245, Nν=2.945±0.203N_{\nu}=2.945\pm 0.203 and a rather strong correlation coefficient r=0.7699r=0.7699, since this approximation affects only marginally the posteriors obtained. Once marginalized over baryon abundance, the constraints on the numbers of neutrinos are

Nν={2.95±0.20CMB2.88±0.27BBN3.01±0.15BBN+CMB.N_{\nu}=\begin{cases}2.95\pm 0.20&{\rm CMB}\\ 2.88\pm 0.27&{\rm BBN}\\ 3.01\pm 0.15&{\rm BBN+CMB.}\\ \end{cases} (167)

As for the marginalized baryon abundances we get

100×Ωb​h2={2.220±0.025CMB2.168±0.055BBN2.216±0.022BBN+CMB.100\times\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}=\begin{cases}2.220\pm 0.025&{\rm CMB}\\ 2.168\pm 0.055&{\rm BBN}\\ 2.216\pm 0.022&{\rm BBN+CMB}.\\ \end{cases} (168)

Note that if we had used a code which predicts D/H≃2.61×10−5{\rm D}/{\rm H}\simeq 2.61\times 10^{-5} instead of D/H≃2.46×10−5{\rm D}/{\rm H}\simeq 2.46\times 10^{-5} for the Planck parameters, we would have obtained Nν=2.84±0.27N_{\nu}=2.84\pm 0.27 from BBN alone, corresponding to Neff=2.88±0.27N_{\rm eff}=2.88\pm 0.27, whose central value is similar to the one obtained in Consiglio et al. [45, Eq. 26]. Since we use consistently the CMB prior P⁡(Ωb​h2,Nν|CMB)P(\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2},N_{\nu}|{\rm CMB}) when obtaining constraints from BBN and CMB, we cannot compare our results with those of Consiglio et al. [45] in that case, since they use only a CMB prior on Ωb​h2\Omega_{\rm b}h^{2}.

Conclusion

It is widely acknowledged that Cosmology has entered in the "precision era"; this should also apply to big bang nucleosynthesis. For both D and He4{}^{4}{\rm He} isotopes the precision on the abundances deduced from observations have reached the percent level. The precision on primordial D abundance prediction by BBN codes is now limited to a few percents because of the uncertainties on the D(p,OPENγ)3\gamma)^{3}He, D(d,n)3He and D(d,p)3H thermonuclear reaction rates [61, 38]. Ongoing experiments [90] from LUNA at the Gran Sasso underground facility, supplemented by theoretical works [130] are expected to improve the situation. Here, we concentrated on the prediction of He4{}^{4}{\rm He} primordial abundance. Uncertainties on YPY_{\rm P} related to experimental data come from the neutron lifetime 879.5​(±0.8)​s879.5\,(\pm 0.8)\,{\rm s} (but that may be affected by systematic uncertainties [147]), leading to a Δ​YP(4)=1.7\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=1.7 (Eq. 7) uncertainties and from the 1H(n,OPENγ)2\gamma)^{2}H, D(d,n)3He and D(d,p)3H reaction rates (∼\sim1% factor uncertainty [7, 83]) leading to Δ​YP(4)≲\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}\lesssim0.5 in total (Eq. 143). These uncertainties are small, compared with the observational uncertainty of Δ​YP(4)=40\Delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=40 (Eq. 4). However, the predicted He4{}^{4}{\rm He} primordial abundance includes corrections to the "bare" weak rates: zero–temperature radiative corrections, finite nucleon mass corrections, finite temperature radiative corrections, weak-magnetism, QED plasma effects and incomplete neutrino decoupling that, in total, shift the abundance by δ​YP(4)=44.7\delta Y_{\rm P}^{(4)}=44.7 (Table 5), i.e. larger than the uncertainties.

It is thus of the utmost importance to precisely calculate all these corrections, in order to limit theoretical uncertainties. Here, they are for the first time all included and calculated in a self consistent way allowing to take into account the correlations between them. In addition, it was verified that all satisfy detailed balance, a crucial point since it directly affects the neutron/proton number ratio, and hence the He4{}^{4}{\rm He} abundance. Table 5 details the contributions of these corrections to the 4He, D, 3He and 7Li primordial abundance. We did not calculate the effect of incomplete neutrino decoupling, but use the results of Pisanti et al. [149]. This amounts to ignoring the spectral distortions, but this affects YP(4)Y_{\rm P}^{(4)} by approximately less than one unit. However we find results for incomplete neutrino decoupling effects which are very similar to Grohs et al. [88], and most notably we find a coherence on the sign of light element abundances variations which is different from Mangano et al. [127]. Given the coupling we find with finite nucleon mass effect, this is the very last correction which requires careful evaluation to fully settle the weak rates corrections.

In this work, we have been using a network of ≈\approx400 nuclear reactions (and their reverse), from neutron to sodium to encompass the light element big bang nucleosynthesis up to the CNO isotopes [35]. We used the most up to date reaction rates, and in particular those involved in deuterium production [103, 83], but even more important, the weak rates with their carefully calculated corrections. Hence, we claim that our predicted abundances (Table 7) are the most accurate to date, not only for D, He3{}^{3}{\rm He}, Li7{}^{7}{\rm Li} and CNO isotopes but also for He4{}^{4}{\rm He}. Our predicted deuterium and He4{}^{4}{\rm He} primordial abundances are in agreement with observations, within error bars (Fig. 26 and Table 8), and in particular, there is no need for extra relativistic degrees of freedom (i.e. Nν>3N_{\nu}>3). Our predicted lithium abundance remains a factor of ≈\approx3 above the Spite plateau. The solution of this problem probably involves several mechanisms including stellar depletion and possibly some physics beyond the standard model. Finally, our prediction of CNO abundance (Table 7) does not completely rule out the possibility that they may influence the evolution of some of the first, Population III, stars [68].

Last, but not least, we provide at http://www2.iap.fr/users/pitrou/primat.htm, a freely available Mathematica code that includes all the physics discussed in this work. We expect that it will be used and hopefully modified in order to include new physics (see e.g. Iocco et al. [106], Mathews and Kusakabe [132]), or just to update some reaction rates 2020 20 They can be provided in tabular form, in a format similar to the Starlib one [156] at https://starlib.github.io/Rate-Library/, or as (possibly parameter dependent) analytical formulae..

A.1 Thermodynamical quantities

From the distribution function of a given species, it is possible to define macroscopic quantities such as number density nn, energy density ρ\rho, and pressure PP. Due to the isotropy of the FL spacetime, the distribution function depends only on the magnitude of spatial momenta, that is it is of the form f⁡(t,p)f(t,p). Furthermore isotropy implies that there is no anisotropic stress. Omitting the time dependence to alleviate the notation, we define

with E=p2+m2E=\sqrt{p^{2}+m^{2}} and gg the number of spin degrees of freedom of the species considered (g=1g=1 for neutrinos and g=2g=2 for all other species). n=g2​π2​∫f⁡(E)​p​E​𝑑E​ρ=g2​π2​∫f⁡(E)​p​E2​𝑑E​P=g6​π2​∫f⁡(E)​p3​𝑑En&=\frac{g}{2\pi^{2}}\int f(E)pE\mathrm{d}E\\ \rho=\frac{g}{2\pi^{2}}\int f(E)pE^{2}\mathrm{d}E\\ P=\frac{g}{6\pi^{2}}\int f(E)p^{3}\mathrm{d}E (170)

Bose-Einstein and Fermi-Dirac with statistical physics convention for chemical potential are defined as

gT,μ±​(E)≡1eE−μT±1g^{\pm}_{T,\mu}(E)\equiv\frac{1}{{\rm e}^{\frac{E-\mu}{T}}\pm 1} (171)

with upper (lower) sign for fermions (bosons). For these distributions we find from Eqs. (170)

n⁡(t)=g​T32​π2​I±(1,1)​(x,ξ)​ρ​(t)=g​T42​π2​I±(2,1)​(x,ξ)​P​(t)=g​T46​π2​I±(0,3)​(x,ξ)n(t)&=\frac{gT^{3}}{2\pi^{2}}I_{\pm}^{(1,1)}(x,\xi)\\ \rho(t)=\frac{gT^{4}}{2\pi^{2}}I_{\pm}^{(2,1)}(x,\xi)\\ P(t)=\frac{gT^{4}}{6\pi^{2}}I_{\pm}^{(0,3)}(x,\xi) (172)

A.2 Chemical potential of electrons

In chemical equilibrium μe−=−μe+≡μe\mu_{e^{-}}=-\mu_{e^{+}}\equiv\mu_{e} because of reactions 2​γ↔e++e−2\gamma\leftrightarrow e^{+}+e^{-}. Hence the net negative charge density in electrons and positrons is

ne−−ne+=2​T32​π2​[I+(1,1)​(x,ξ)−I+(1,1)​(x,−ξ)]n_{e^{-}}-n_{e^{+}}=\frac{2T^{3}}{2\pi^{2}}\left[I_{+}^{(1,1)}(x,\xi)-I_{+}^{(1,1)}(x,-\xi)\right] (177)

with x≡me/Tx\equiv m_{e}/T and ξ≡μe/T\xi\equiv\mu_{e}/T. The chemical potential of electrons and positrons must adapt to ensure the electric neutrality of the Universe, hence it is constrained by

ne−−ne+=np.n_{e^{-}}-n_{e^{+}}=n_{p}\,. (178)

Let us estimate the chemical potential at the end of BBN for simplicity. Indeed, since ξ\xi increases with time, it is enough to check that its final value at the end of BBN is small. We use therefore the final value of baryon-to-photon ratio η\eta [defined in Eq. (36)] and use that the baryonic matter is essentially in protons and He4{}^{4}{\rm He} nuclei. We find

ne−−ne+=(1−YP/2)​η0​n¯γ​T3.n_{e^{-}}-n_{e^{+}}=(1-Y_{\rm P}/2)\eta_{0}\,\bar{n}_{\gamma}T^{3}\,. (179)

In that limit, the electric charge density of electrons and positrons is given by

ne−−ne+≃4​T3​(x2​π)3/2​e−x​sinh⁡ξ.n_{e^{-}}-n_{e^{+}}\simeq 4T^{3}\left(\frac{x}{2\pi}\right)^{3/2}{\rm e}^{-x}\sinh\xi\,. (180)

Combining these two equations we obtain

ξ≃Arcinsh⁡(η⁡(1−YP/2)​ex​2​ζ​(3)π​x3/2).\xi\simeq{\rm Arcinsh}\left(\frac{\eta(1-Y_{\rm P}/2){\rm e}^{x}\sqrt{2}\zeta(3)}{\sqrt{\pi}x^{3/2}}\right)\,. (181)

The evolution of the electrons chemical potential is depicted in Fig. 30. ξ=μe/T\xi=\mu_{e}/T stays much below 10−510^{-5} whenever T>5×108​KT>5\times 10^{8}{\rm K}. For lower temperatures, ξ\xi rises but it is only because electron-positron annihilations are nearly complete and the chemical potential adapts so that the relic density of electrons is equal to the number of protons. That is, whenever the chemical potential of electrons rises at low temperature, the amount of electrons is insignificant due to the low value of the baryon to photon ratio. Hence for all practical purposes, from Eq. (20) we deduce that whenever there is no heat exchange with the neutrinos, the total entropy of the plasma is conserved, that is S˙pl=d⁡(spl​a3)/d​t=0\dot{S}_{\rm pl}=\mathrm{d}(s_{\rm pl}a^{3})/\mathrm{d}t=0.

A.3 Nucleons at thermodynamical equilibrium

The chemical potential of neutrons and protons are not negligible individually, and they are constrained to give the number density in the low temperature limit (176). However the difference μn−μp\mu_{n}-\mu_{p} is negligible with respect to TT. Indeed we can neglect ξe≡μe/T\xi_{e}\equiv\mu_{e}/T (see § A.2) and assuming it is also the case for neutrinos (see §VI.3 for degenerate neutrinos), and given that at equilibrium we have necessarily

μn+μν=μp+μe⇒μn−μp=μe−μν,\mu_{n}+\mu_{\nu}=\mu_{p}+\mu_{e}\quad\Rightarrow\quad\mu_{n}-\mu_{p}=\mu_{e}-\mu_{\nu}\,, (182)

then we deduce μn−μp≪1\mu_{n}-\mu_{p}\ll 1.

Hence from (176) we obtain that the neutron to proton ratio is

with xp≡mp/Tx_{p}\equiv m_{p}/T and ξp=μp/T\xi_{p}=\mu_{p}/T, which can be used to solve for ξp\xi_{p}. In particular the distribution function of protons is approximately given by

and thus it is approximated by the Maxwellian distribution

fp​(p)\displaystyle f_{p}(p) ≃\displaystyle\simeq np2​(2​πmp​T)3/2​exp​(−p22​mp​T)\displaystyle\frac{n_{p}}{2}\left(\frac{2\pi}{m_{p}T}\right)^{3/2}{\rm exp}\left(-\frac{p^{2}}{2m_{p}T}\right) (186)
≃\displaystyle\simeq Yp​η​ζ​(3)​8π​(Tmp)3/2​exp​(−p22​mp​T).\displaystyle Y_{p}\frac{\eta\zeta(3)\sqrt{8}}{\sqrt{\pi}}\left(\frac{T}{m_{p}}\right)^{3/2}{\rm exp}\left(-\frac{p^{2}}{2m_{p}T}\right)\,.

The distribution function for an isotope ii is exactly similar with the obvious replacement Yp→YiY_{p}\to Y_{i}, np→nin_{p}\to n_{i} and mp→mim_{p}\to m_{i}. The distribution of velocities is defined as (omitting the ii index of the isotope considered)

A.4 Abundances at nuclear statistical equilibrium

At nuclear statistical equilibrium (NSE), a given isotope ii is at chemical equilibrium with its nucleons, hence the relation between chemical potentials

μi=Zi​μp+(Ai−Zi)​μn.\mu_{i}=Z_{i}\mu_{p}+(A_{i}-Z_{i})\mu_{n}\,. (188)

ni=gi​(mi​T2​π)3/2​eξi−xi,gi≡2​si+1,n_{i}=g_{i}\left(\frac{m_{i}T}{2\pi}\right)^{3/2}{\rm e}^{\xi_{i}-x_{i}}\,,\quad g_{i}\equiv 2s_{i}+1\,, (189)

where sis_{i} is the spin of species ii. Using Eq. (188) and (189), we get

niNSE\displaystyle n^{\rm NSE}_{i} =\displaystyle= gi​mi3/22Ai​(npmp3/2)Zi​(nnmn3/2)Ai−Zi\displaystyle\frac{g_{i}m^{3/2}_{i}}{2^{A_{i}}}\left(\frac{n_{p}}{m^{3/2}_{p}}\right)^{Z_{i}}\left(\frac{n_{n}}{m^{3/2}_{n}}\right)^{A_{i}-Z_{i}} (190)
×(2​πT)3​(Ai−1)2​eBi/T\displaystyle\times\left(\frac{2\pi}{T}\right)^{\frac{3(A_{i}-1)}{2}}\,{\rm e}^{B_{i}/T}

where we defined the binding energy

Bi≡Zi​mp+(Ai−Zi)​mn−mi.B_{i}\equiv Z_{i}m_{p}+(A_{i}-Z_{i})m_{n}-m_{i}\,. (191)

Using (36), the abundances are then given at NSE by

YiNSE\displaystyle Y^{\rm NSE}_{i} =\displaystyle= gi​ζ​(3)Ai−1​23​Ai−52​π1−Ai2​(mi​TAi−1mpZi​mnAi−Zi)3/2\displaystyle g_{i}\zeta(3)^{A_{i}-1}2^{\frac{3A_{i}-5}{2}}\pi^{\frac{1-A_{i}}{2}}\left(\frac{m_{i}T^{A_{i}-1}}{m_{p}^{Z_{i}}m_{n}^{A_{i}-Z_{i}}}\right)^{3/2} (192)
×ηAi−1​YpZi​YnAi−Zi​eBi/T.\displaystyle\times\eta^{A_{i}-1}Y_{p}^{Z_{i}}Y_{n}^{A_{i}-Z_{i}}{\rm e}^{B_{i}/T}\,.

We check in particular that for neutrons and protons Bn=Bp=0B_{n}=B_{p}=0 and An=Ap=1A_{n}=A_{p}=1, so we get the tautological relation YnNSE=YnY_{n}^{\rm NSE}=Y_{n} and YpNSE=YpY_{p}^{\rm NSE}=Y_{p}. In order to obtain the NSE values from (192), we use Audi et al. [14] for the masses and spins of nuclear elements. In Fig. 31, we plot jointly the abundances of the main isotopes together with their NSE values to check that they are equal at high temperatures.

Appendix B Weak reactions rates

In this section, we gather all the technicalities required to obtain the theoretical forms of the weak-rates including the most relevant corrections.

B.1 General expressions

Let us consider first the reactions with neutrons in the initial state. Throughout this section we use the mostly minus metric signature since it is the most common in particle physics. The general expression for each of the three reactions involved is of the form [124, 73]

nn​Γ=∫Πi​[d3​𝐩i]​(2​π)4​δ4​(p¯n−p¯p+αν​p¯ν+αe​p¯e)\displaystyle n_{n}\Gamma=\int\Pi_{i}[\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}_{i}](2\pi)^{4}\delta^{4}\left(\underline{p}_{n}-\underline{p}_{p}+\alpha_{\nu}{\underline{p}}_{\nu}+\alpha_{e}\underline{p}_{e}\right)
×|M|2​fn​(En)​[1−fp​(Ep)]​fν​(αν​Eν)​fe​(αe​Ee)\displaystyle\quad\times\left|M\right|^{2}f_{n}({E}_{n})[1-f_{p}({E}_{p})]f_{\nu}(\alpha_{\nu}{E}_{\nu})f_{e}(\alpha_{e}{E}_{e}) (193)

where the p¯i\underline{p}_{i} with i=n,p,e,νi=n,p,e,\nu are the four-momenta of particles, and we used the compact notation for the relativistic volume element

[d3​𝐩]≡d3​𝐩2​E​(2​π)3=4​π​p2​d​p2​E​(2​π3).[\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}]\equiv\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}}{2E(2\pi)^{3}}=\frac{4\pi p^{2}\mathrm{d}p}{2E(2\pi^{3})}\,. (194)

The factor αν\alpha_{\nu} is +1+1 if the neutrino is in the initial state and −1-1 otherwise with a similar definition for αe\alpha_{e} and the electron or positron. In (193), it is apparent that the Dirac function ensures energy and momentum conservation. For a Fermi-Dirac distribution

g⁡(−E)=1−g⁡(E),g(-E)=1-g(E)\,, (195)

implying that the coefficients αe,αν\alpha_{e},\alpha_{\nu} also ensure that either it is the distribution function which appears if the lepton is in the initial state, or the Pauli-blocking factor if it is in the final state.

A first simplification consists in neglecting the Pauli-blocking factor of the final state proton due to the very low value of the baryon-to-photon ratio [see Eq. (186)]. Having no dependence on the distribution function of the final protons, we can simplify Eq. (193) further by performing the integral on spatial momenta of protons, using the spatial part of the Dirac function. The reaction rates reduces to

nn​Γ\displaystyle n_{n}\Gamma =\displaystyle= ∫d3​𝐩n​d3​𝐩e​d3​𝐩ν24​(2​π)8​δ​(En−Ep+αe​Ee+αν​Eν)\displaystyle\int\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}_{n}\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}_{e}\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}_{\nu}}{2^{4}(2\pi)^{8}}\delta\left(E_{n}-E_{p}+\alpha_{e}E_{e}+\alpha_{\nu}E_{\nu}\right) (196)
×|M|2En​Ep​Ee​Eν​fn​(En)​fν​(αν​Eν)​fe​(αe​Ee)\displaystyle\times\frac{\left|M\right|^{2}}{E_{n}E_{p}E_{e}E_{\nu}}f_{n}(E_{n})f_{\nu}(\alpha_{\nu}{E}_{\nu})f_{e}(\alpha_{e}{E}_{e})

where the proton momentum and energies are related by

𝐩p=𝐩n+αν​𝐩ν+αe​𝐩e,Ep=𝐩p⋅𝐩p+mp2.\mathbf{p}_{p}=\mathbf{p}_{n}+\alpha_{\nu}\mathbf{p}_{\nu}+\alpha_{e}\mathbf{p}_{e}\,,\quad E_{p}=\sqrt{\mathbf{p}_{p}\cdot\mathbf{p}_{p}+m_{p}^{2}}\,. (197)

For a given reaction, |M|2\left|M\right|^{2} is the corresponding matrix-element of the weak interaction summed over all initial and final states, computed from the interaction Hamiltonian. For the reactions (68), the relevant part of the interaction Hamiltonian is a coupling of weak currents in the form

ℋI=GF2​Je​νμ​Jp​n,μ{\cal H}_{I}=\frac{G_{F}}{\sqrt{2}}J^{\mu}_{e\nu}J_{pn,\,\mu} (198)

where GFG_{F} is the Fermi constant. The electron-neutron weak current is purely left chiral, and of the form

Je​νμ=𝝂¯​γμ​(1−γ5)​𝐞.J^{\mu}_{e\nu}=\bar{\bm{\nu}}\gamma^{\mu}(1-\gamma^{5})\mathbf{e}\,. (199)

𝐞\mathbf{e} and 𝝂{\bm{\nu}} are the fermionic quantum fields of electrons and neutrinos, and the γμ\gamma^{\mu} are the matrices of the Clifford algebra [we use the conventions of [73]]. The proton-neutron current is of the form [108, Eqs. 1 and A2]

Jp​nμ=cosθC𝐩¯(γμ(1−gAγ5)+ifwmmN2Σμ​νqν)𝐧J^{\mu}_{pn}=\cos\theta_{\rm C}\bar{\mathbf{p}}\left(\gamma^{\mu}(1-g_{A}\gamma^{5})+\mathrm{i}\frac{f_{\rm wm}}{m_{N}}2\Sigma^{\mu\nu}q_{\nu}\right)\mathbf{n} (200)

where 𝐩\mathbf{p} and 𝒏{\bm{n}} are the Fermionic quantum fields of protons and neutrons and 2​Σμ​ν≡i/2​(γμ​γν−γν​γμ)2\Sigma^{\mu\nu}\equiv\mathrm{i}/2(\gamma^{\mu}\gamma^{\nu}-\gamma^{\nu}\gamma^{\mu}). gAg_{A} is the axial current constant for nucleons (also sometimes written CA/CVC_{A}/C_{V} or λ\lambda in the literature), and fwmf_{\rm wm} is the weak magnetism constant whose numerical value is given by [98, 97, 108]

fwm=μp−μn2≃1.793−(−1.913)2≃1.853.f_{\rm wm}=\frac{\mu_{p}-\mu_{n}}{2}\simeq\frac{1.793-(-1.913)}{2}\simeq 1.853\,. (201)

θC\theta_{\rm C} is the Cabbibo-Kobayashi-Maskawa (CKM) angle (cos⁡θC\cos\theta_{\rm C} also noted Vu​dV_{ud} in the literature), qμq^{\mu} is the nucleon four-momentum transfer, that is the difference between the final nucleon four-momentum and the initial one. The most recent numerical values for the constants in weak interactions are gathered in appendix D.

It is possible to show that from Eqs. (198)-(200) the matrix element is of the form [see e.g. [73]]

|M|227​GF2=cL​L​ℳL​L+cR​R​ℳR​R+cL​R​ℳL​R\frac{|M|^{2}}{2^{7}G_{F}^{2}}=c_{LL}{\cal M}_{LL}+c_{RR}{\cal M}_{RR}+c_{LR}{\cal M}_{LR} (202)

with the coupling factors

cL​L≡(1+gA)24​cR​R≡(1−gA)24​cL​R≡gA2−14.c_{LL}&\equiv\frac{(1+g_{A})^{2}}{4}\\ c_{RR}\equiv\frac{(1-g_{A})^{2}}{4}\\ c_{LR}\equiv\frac{g_{A}^{2}-1}{4}\,. (203)

If weak interactions for nucleons were purely left-chiral, that is with gA=1g_{A}=1, only the ℳL​L{\cal M}_{LL} would contribute. ℳR​R{\cal M}_{RR} contains the contribution of the right-chiral part of the interaction, and ℳL​R{\cal M}_{LR} is an interference between left and right chiral contributions.

Let us ignore first the contribution from weak-magnetism that are investigated further in § B.4. We then find

ℳL​L=(p¯n⋅p¯ν)​(p¯p⋅p¯e)​ℳR​R=(p¯n⋅p¯e)​(p¯p⋅p¯ν)​ℳL​R=mp​mn​(p¯ν⋅p¯e).{\cal M}_{LL}&=(\underline{p}_{n}\cdot\underline{p}_{\nu})(\underline{p}_{p}\cdot\underline{p}_{e})\\ {\cal M}_{RR}=(\underline{p}_{n}\cdot\underline{p}_{e})(\underline{p}_{p}\cdot\underline{p}_{\nu})\\ {\cal M}_{LR}=m_{p}m_{n}(\underline{p}_{\nu}\cdot\underline{p}_{e})\,. (204)

It is worth noting that all weak reactions (68) have in fact the same matrix element. First the three reactions with a neutron in the initial state are obtained by crossing symmetry. Crossing symmetry for the electron amounts for instance to the formal replacement p¯e→−p¯e\underline{p}_{e}\to-\underline{p}_{e} with an overall minus sign [73] and it is straightforward to check that this leaves the matrix element invariant. The same property arises obviously for neutrinos. Second, the three reverse reactions (with an initial proton and a final neutron) are obtained by time reversal, and since there is no CP violation at this level, there is also a time-reversal symmetry so as to ensure the CPT symmetry. Hence all reverse rates have exactly the same matrix element.

B.2 Fokker-Planck expansion

The integral in (196) is 88-dimensional when one removes the Dirac function. Due to the isotropy of all distributions, this can be reduced to a 55-dimensional integral. This is the method followed by Lopez et al. [124]. Here we follow a much simpler route by performing a Fokker-planck expansion in the energy transferred in reactions. Even though our method is different from Seckel [163], it follows a method which is similar in spirit. As we shall see, this results in one-dimensional integrals which are much faster to evaluate.

At low temperature, it is enough to assume that nucleons follow an isotropic Maxwellian distribution of velocities at the plasma temperature TT given by Eq. (186). Hence the following integrals are obtained

2​∫fN​(𝐩)​d3​𝐩(2​π)3=nN,2​∫fN​(𝐩)​pimN​d3​𝐩(2​π)3=0,2​∫fN​(𝐩)​pi​pjmN2​d3​𝐩(2​π)3=TmN​δi​j​nN.2\int f_{N}(\mathbf{p})\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}}{(2\pi)^{3}}&=n_{N}\,,\\ 2\int f_{N}(\mathbf{p})\frac{p^{i}}{m_{N}}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}}{(2\pi)^{3}}=0\,,\\ 2\int f_{N}(\mathbf{p})\frac{p^{i}p^{j}}{m_{N}^{2}}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}}{(2\pi)^{3}}=\frac{T}{m_{N}}\delta^{ij}n_{N}\,. (205)

In particular contracting with δi​j\delta_{ij} we recover the expression for the pressure of nucleons in the low temperature limit

PN=2​∫fN​(𝐩)​p23​mN​d3​𝐩(2​π)3=T​nN.P_{N}=2\int f_{N}(\mathbf{p})\frac{p^{2}}{3m_{N}}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}}{(2\pi)^{3}}=Tn_{N}\,. (206)

For electron or neutrino distributions, since we have assumed isotropy, we deduce the property

∫g⁡(E)​pα​Eβ​pi​pj​d3​𝐩(2​π)3=δi​j3​∫g⁡(E)​pα+2​Eβ​d3​𝐩(2​π)3\int g(E)p^{\alpha}E^{\beta}p^{i}p^{j}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}}{(2\pi)^{3}}=\frac{\delta^{ij}}{3}\int g(E)p^{\alpha+2}E^{\beta}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}}{(2\pi)^{3}} (207)

where α\alpha and β\beta are some numbers. From isotropy we also find that

∫g⁡(E)​pα​Eβ​pi​d3​𝐩(2​π)3=0.\int g(E)p^{\alpha}E^{\beta}p^{i}\frac{\mathrm{d}^{3}\mathbf{p}}{(2\pi)^{3}}=0\,. (208)

Hence for all practical purposes, we can perform the replacements

pi​pj→p2​δi​j/3,pi→0.p^{i}p^{j}\to p^{2}\delta^{ij}/3\,,\qquad p^{i}\to 0\,. (209)

on all species, resulting in great simplifications.

We assess the importance of corrections to the Born approximations as explained in § III.7, that is in powers of ϵ≡T/mN\epsilon\equiv T/m_{N}. To evaluate the order of each term, we consider that the momentum or energies of neutrinos are of order T∼ΔT\sim\Delta, that is factors of the type Ee/mNE_{e}/m_{N} or Eν/mNE_{\nu}/m_{N} are of order ϵ\epsilon. Furthermore, from (205) a factor 𝐩n/mn\mathbf{p}_{n}/m_{n} is of order T/M∼Δ/M\sqrt{T/M}\sim\sqrt{\Delta/M} and thus ϵ\sqrt{\epsilon}. However since only even powers of the spatial momentum of nucleons must appear [see Eqs. (205)], we shall encounter terms of the type |𝐩p/mn2||\mathbf{p}_{p}/m_{n}^{2}| which are of order ϵ\epsilon.

The Fokker-Planck expansion consists in expanding the energy difference between the nucleons, En−EpE_{n}-E_{p} around the lowest order value Δ=mn−mp\Delta=m_{n}-m_{p}. Keeping only the lowest corrections this expansion reads

En−Ep=Δ+δ​Q1+δ​Q2+δ​Q3E_{n}-E_{p}=\Delta+\delta Q_{1}+\delta Q_{2}+\delta Q_{3} (210)
δ​Q1≡−𝐩n⋅𝐪mN​δ​Q2≡−|𝐪|22​mN​δ​Q3≡|𝐩n|22​(1mn−1mp)≃−|𝐩n|2​Δ2​mN2.\delta Q_{1}&\equiv-\frac{\mathbf{p}_{n}\cdot\mathbf{q}}{m_{N}}\\ \delta Q_{2}\equiv-\frac{|\mathbf{q}|^{2}}{2m_{N}}\\ \delta Q_{3}\equiv\frac{|\mathbf{p}_{n}|^{2}}{2}\left(\frac{1}{m_{n}}-\frac{1}{m_{p}}\right)\simeq-\frac{|\mathbf{p}_{n}|^{2}\Delta}{2m_{N}^{2}}\,. (211)

where 𝐪≡𝐩p−𝐩n=αν​𝐩ν+αe​𝐩e\mathbf{q}\equiv\mathbf{p}_{p}-\mathbf{p}_{n}=\alpha_{\nu}\mathbf{p}_{\nu}+\alpha_{e}\mathbf{p}_{e} is the spatial momentum transferred. The first term in (210) is the lowest order, or Born approximation, that is the only appearing when considering the infinite nucleon mass approximation. The second term is an order ϵ\sqrt{\epsilon} correction, and the third term is an order ϵ\epsilon correction. Finally the last term is of order T​Δ/mNT\Delta/m_{N} so it is an order ϵ\epsilon correction as well. It is the only corrective term for which it is crucial to take into account the difference of mass between neutrons and protons. Using Eq. (210), we expand the Dirac delta function on energies as

δ⁡(En−Ep+αe​Ee+αν​Eν)≃\displaystyle\delta\left(E_{n}-E_{p}+\alpha_{e}E_{e}+\alpha_{\nu}E_{\nu}\right)\simeq (212)
δ⁡(Σ)+δ′​(Σ)​(∑i=13δ​Qi)+12​δ′′​(Σ)​(δ​Q1)2,\displaystyle\qquad\delta(\Sigma)+\delta^{\prime}(\Sigma)\left(\sum_{i=1}^{3}\delta Q_{i}\right)+\frac{1}{2}\delta^{\prime\prime}(\Sigma)(\delta Q_{1})^{2}\,,

where Σ≡Δ+αe​Ee+αν​Eν\Sigma\equiv\Delta+\alpha_{e}E_{e}+\alpha_{\nu}E_{\nu}.

We must then expand the matrix element and the energies appearing in Eq. (196). It proves much easier to expand all these contributions together. Furthermore, whenever a term is already of order ϵ\epsilon, we know that it should multiply only the Born term of the expansion (212), so we can apply the simplification rule (209). With this method we find

ℳL​LΠi​Ei→1−𝐩nmN⋅(𝐩eEe+𝐩νEν)−αν​|𝐩ν|2mN​Eν​ℳR​RΠi​Ei→1−𝐩nmN⋅(𝐩eEe+𝐩νEν)−αe​|𝐩e|2mN​Ee​ℳL​RΠi​Ei→(1−|𝐩n|2mN2)​(1−𝐩e⋅𝐩νEe​Eν).\frac{{\cal M}_{LL}}{\Pi_{i}E_{i}}&\to 1-\frac{\mathbf{p}_{n}}{m_{N}}\cdot\left(\frac{\mathbf{p}_{e}}{E_{e}}+\frac{\mathbf{p}_{\nu}}{E_{\nu}}\right)-\frac{\alpha_{\nu}|\mathbf{p}_{\nu}|^{2}}{m_{N}E_{\nu}}\\ \frac{{\cal M}_{RR}}{\Pi_{i}E_{i}}\to 1-\frac{\mathbf{p}_{n}}{m_{N}}\cdot\left(\frac{\mathbf{p}_{e}}{E_{e}}+\frac{\mathbf{p}_{\nu}}{E_{\nu}}\right)-\frac{\alpha_{e}|\mathbf{p}_{e}|^{2}}{m_{N}E_{e}}\\ \frac{{\cal M}_{LR}}{\Pi_{i}E_{i}}\to\left(1-\frac{|\mathbf{p}_{n}|^{2}}{m_{N}^{2}}\right)\left(1-\frac{\mathbf{p}_{e}\cdot\mathbf{p}_{\nu}}{E_{e}E_{\nu}}\right)\,. (213)

The second term in Eqs. (213) and (213) is of order ϵ\sqrt{\epsilon} and the last term in these equations is of order ϵ\epsilon. Hence the second term needs to be coupled with the order ϵ\sqrt{\epsilon} term in the Dirac delta expansion (212) which is δ′​(Σ)​δ​Q1\delta^{\prime}(\Sigma)\delta Q_{1}, and simplified with the rules (209).

There are four steps to complete this Fokker-Planck expansion.

  1. 1.

    First, using Eqs. (213) and (212) in the reaction rates (196) we perform the integral on the initial neutron momentum with the rules (205).

  2. 2.

    Second, we can replace the differential elements for the integral on electron and neutrino momenta with d3​p→4​π​p2​d​p\mathrm{d}^{3}p\to 4\pi p^{2}\mathrm{d}p because we have already performed all angular averages.

  3. 3.

    We are left with a two dimensional integral on the electron and neutrino momentum magnitudes pe=|𝐩e|p_{e}=|\mathbf{p}_{e}| and pν=|𝐩ν|p_{\nu}=|\mathbf{p}_{\nu}|. Let us note Eν=pνE_{\nu}=p_{\nu} in order to write the result in a easily readable form. Third, we perform the integral on EνE_{\nu} using the Dirac delta and their derivatives. Whenever a Dirac delta derivative appears, it means that we have to perform integration by parts to convert it into a normal Dirac delta. This will introduce derivatives with respect to the EνE_{\nu} applied on the neutrino distribution function or Pauli-blocking factor. Also for a given reaction it might appear that the value of EνE_{\nu} constrained by the Dirac delta is not physical for that reaction if αν=1\alpha_{\nu}=1 and physical if αν=−1\alpha_{\nu}=-1, or vice-versa. This is the reason why we consider the total reaction rate of the reactions (68) and (68). Once their rates are added, the Dirac delta automatically selects either the neutrino in the initial state, with the corresponding distribution function, or the neutrino in the final state, with the associated Pauli-blocking factor. Eventually once the rates (68) and (68) are added, we might forget about αν\alpha_{\nu}, that is about the position of the neutrino. We need only to compute two rates, one where the electrons is in the initial state [reaction (68)], and one where it is a positron which is in the final state [the sum of reactions (68) and (68)].

  4. 4.

    Finally, we need to determine the procedure to convert the rate with a neutron in the initial state into the reverse rate with a proton in the initial state. Even if the matrix element is the same for all reactions, as explained in § B.1, the method to perform a finite mass expansion is not symmetric under the interchange p↔np\leftrightarrow n. Indeed we chose to expand the momentum of the final nucleon around the initial one, and we remove the integral on the final nucleon momenta. It is apparent on Eqs. (204) that the electron (resp. neutrino) momentum is contracted with the neutron (resp. proton) in the L​LLL term but this is the opposite in the R​RRR term. Since the coupling factors of these terms are interchanged by the replacement gA→−gAg_{A}\to-g_{A}, we can deduce the rates with an initial proton from those with an initial neutron using the rule gA→−gAg_{A}\to-g_{A}. Obviously the argument of the Dirac delta contains now Ep−En=−Δ+…E_{p}-E_{n}=-\Delta+\dots instead of En−Ep=Δ+…E_{n}-E_{p}=\Delta+\dots so we must also apply the rule Δ→−Δ\Delta\to-\Delta. Finally when considering a reverse reaction, the electron in the initial state turns into a positron in the final state so we must also apply the rule Ee→−EeE_{e}\to-E_{e}, that is change the electron distribution function to a Pauli-blocking factor or vice-versa. These are the rules used extensively in § III to deduce the reverse rates.

Having sketched the details of the procedure, we are in position to give the results. The Born approximation results are obvious under this expansion. From Eqs. (213) we obtain in the limit

ℳL​LΠi​Ei≃ℳR​RΠi​Ei≃1,ℳL​RΠi​Ei≃(1−𝐩e⋅𝐩νEe​Eν).\frac{{\cal M}_{LL}}{\Pi_{i}E_{i}}&\simeq\frac{{\cal M}_{RR}}{\Pi_{i}E_{i}}\simeq 1\,,\\ \frac{{\cal M}_{LR}}{\Pi_{i}E_{i}}\simeq\left(1-\frac{\mathbf{p}_{e}\cdot\mathbf{p}_{\nu}}{E_{e}E_{\nu}}\right)\,. (214)

Furthermore in the Dirac expansion (212) we keep only δ⁡(Σ)\delta(\Sigma), and the average over electrons and neutrino spatial momenta removes the momentum dependent part of Eq. (214). The Born rates are gathered and commented in § III.2.

The first corrections in this Fokker-Planck expansion, and which are due to finite nucleon mass, are reported in the next section.

B.3 Finite nucleon mass corrections

The finite nucleon mass corrections take the form (114) [or (115) if radiative corrections are added]. The function χ±FM\chi^{\rm FM}_{\pm} is

χ±FM​(E,gA)\displaystyle\chi^{\rm FM}_{\pm}(E,g_{A}) =\displaystyle= c~L​L​p2mN​E​gν​(Eν∓)​g​(−E)−c~R​R​Eν∓mN​gν(2,0)​(Eν∓)​g​(−E)\displaystyle\tilde{c}_{LL}\frac{p^{2}}{m_{N}E}g_{\nu}(E_{\nu}^{\mp})g(-E)-\tilde{c}_{RR}\frac{E_{\nu}^{\mp}}{m_{N}}g^{(2,0)}_{\nu}(E_{\nu}^{\mp})g(-E) (215)
+(c~L​L+c~R​R)​TmN​(gν(2,1)​(Eν∓)​g​(−E)​p2E−gν(3,1)​(Eν∓)​g​(−E))\displaystyle+\left(\tilde{c}_{LL}+\tilde{c}_{RR}\right)\frac{T}{m_{N}}\left(g^{(2,1)}_{\nu}(E_{\nu}^{\mp})g(-E)\frac{p^{2}}{E}-g^{(3,1)}_{\nu}(E_{\nu}^{\mp})g(-E)\right)
+(c~L​L+c~R​R+c~L​R)[T2​mN(gν(4,2)(Eν∓)g(−E)+gν(2,2)(Eν∓)g(−E)p2)\displaystyle+\left(\tilde{c}_{LL}+\tilde{c}_{RR}+\tilde{c}_{LR}\right)\left[\frac{T}{2m_{N}}\left(g^{(4,2)}_{\nu}(E_{\nu}^{\mp})g(-E)+g^{(2,2)}_{\nu}(E_{\nu}^{\mp})g(-E)p^{2}\right)\right.
+12​mN(gν(4,1)(Eν∓)g(−E)+gν(2,1)(Eν∓)g(−E)p2)]\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\left.+\frac{1}{2m_{N}}\left(g^{(4,1)}_{\nu}(E_{\nu}^{\mp})g(-E)+g^{(2,1)}_{\nu}(E_{\nu}^{\mp})g(-E)p^{2}\right)\right]
−(c~L​L+c~R​R+c~L​R)​3​T2​(1−mnmp)​gν(2,1)​(Eν∓)​g​(−E)\displaystyle-\left(\tilde{c}_{LL}+\tilde{c}_{RR}+\tilde{c}_{LR}\right)\frac{3T}{2}\left(1-\frac{m_{n}}{m_{p}}\right)g^{(2,1)}_{\nu}(E_{\nu}^{\mp})g(-E)
+c~L​R​[−3​TmN​gν(2,0)​(Eν∓)​g​(−E)+p23​mN​E​gν(3,1)​(Eν∓)​g​(−E)+p2​T3​mN​E​gν(3,2)​(Eν∓)​g​(−E)]\displaystyle+\tilde{c}_{LR}\left[-\frac{3T}{m_{N}}g^{(2,0)}_{\nu}(E_{\nu}^{\mp})g(-E)+\frac{p^{2}}{3m_{N}E}g^{(3,1)}_{\nu}(E_{\nu}^{\mp})g(-E)+\frac{p^{2}T}{3m_{N}E}g^{(3,2)}_{\nu}(E_{\nu}^{\mp})g(-E)\right]

where p=E2−me2p=\sqrt{E^{2}-m_{e}^{2}}, Eν∓=E∓ΔE_{\nu}^{\mp}=E\mp\Delta. We defined the reduced couplings

and the functions [with the notation (75)]

B.4 Weak-magnetism corrections

Because the weak-magnetic term enters in the current (200) with a factor qν/mNq_{\nu}/m_{N}, with the momentum transfer to nucleon being of the order of TT, it is an order ϵ\epsilon correction and thus vanishes at the Born approximation level. The matrix element is corrected by the addition of

|M|227​GF2\displaystyle\frac{|M|^{2}}{2^{7}G_{F}^{2}} ⊃\displaystyle\supset fwm​gA​mn+mp2​(ℳL​L−ℳR​R)\displaystyle f_{\rm wm}g_{A}\frac{m_{n}+m_{p}}{2}\left({\cal M}_{LL}-{\cal M}_{RR}\right) (219)
+\displaystyle+ fwm2​[mn+mp2​(ℳL​R−ℳL​L−ℳR​R−(p¯n⋅p¯p)​(p¯ν⋅p¯e))+mp​(p¯n⋅p¯e)​(p¯n⋅p¯ν)+mn​(p¯p⋅p¯e)​(p¯p⋅p¯ν)]\displaystyle\frac{f_{\rm wm}}{2}\left[\frac{m_{n}+m_{p}}{2}\left({\cal M}_{LR}-{\cal M}_{LL}-{\cal M}_{RR}-(\underline{p}_{n}\cdot\underline{p}_{p})(\underline{p}_{\nu}\cdot\underline{p}_{e})\right)+m_{p}(\underline{p}_{n}\cdot\underline{p}_{e})(\underline{p}_{n}\cdot\underline{p}_{\nu})+m_{n}(\underline{p}_{p}\cdot\underline{p}_{e})(\underline{p}_{p}\cdot\underline{p}_{\nu})\right]

where we used the expressions (204). It is possible to show, although rather tedious, that the contributions of the second line vanish at first order in ϵ\epsilon. This remarkable simplification has been noticed earlier by Seckel [163]. Hence the weak-magnetism contributes exactly as the axial vector current coupled to the vector current. It is taken into account by changing the coupling constants (203) to the values (119), modifying accordingly the constants (216) appearing in the finite nucleon mass corrections.

Only the first two terms of Eq. (215) can in principle contribute to λ0\lambda_{0} since weak-magnetism does no affect the sum cL​L+cR​Rc_{LL}+c_{RR} nor cL​Rc_{LR}. However, it is straightforward to show that they result in a vanishing contribution since

λ0wm\displaystyle\lambda_{0}^{\rm wm} ∝\displaystyle\propto ∫0Δ2−1d​p​p2​(E−Δ)2​(p2E+(E−Δ))\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\sqrt{\Delta^{2}-1}}\mathrm{d}pp^{2}(E-\Delta)^{2}\left(\frac{p^{2}}{E}+(E-\Delta)\right) (220)
=\displaystyle= 13​∫mΔd​E​∂E[(E−Δ)3​(E2−m2)3/2]\displaystyle\tfrac{1}{3}\int_{m}^{\Delta}\mathrm{d}E\partial_{E}\left[(E-\Delta)^{3}(E^{2}-m^{2})^{3/2}\right]
=\displaystyle= 0.\displaystyle 0\,.

Note that when the weak-magnetism contribution is coupled with radiative corrections, this result is no longer valid and there is a small change in λ0\lambda_{0} that we give in § III.8.

B.5 Mandelstam variables

Let us define the Mandelstam variables for ν+n→e+p\nu+n\to e+p.

s≡(p¯ν+p¯n)2=(p¯e+p¯p)2​t≡(p¯ν−p¯e)2=(p¯n−p¯p)2​u≡(p¯ν−p¯p)2=(p¯n−p¯e)2.s&\equiv(\underline{p}_{\nu}+\underline{p}_{n})^{2}=(\underline{p}_{e}+\underline{p}_{p})^{2}\\ t\equiv(\underline{p}_{\nu}-\underline{p}_{e})^{2}=(\underline{p}_{n}-\underline{p}_{p})^{2}\\ u\equiv(\underline{p}_{\nu}-\underline{p}_{p})^{2}=(\underline{p}_{n}-\underline{p}_{e})^{2}\,. (221)

The total matrix element |M|2|M|^{2} deduced from Eqs. (198)-(200), is the sum of Eqs. (202) and (219), where we use the definitions (204). Once expressed with the Mandelstam variables, we checked that it takes the form given in Lopez et al. [124, App. A] (published version and with m1=mνm_{1}=m_{\nu}, m2=mnm_{2}=m_{n}, m3=mem_{3}=m_{e} and m4=mpm_{4}=m_{p}), except for a few differences. First, we do not include their term t3t_{3} because this is second order in finite nucleon mass effects. Hence, we kept only contributions which are linear in fwmf_{\rm wm}. Second, we find that there is a typo in t5t_{5} of Lopez et al. [124], since there should be a factor gAg_{A} instead of gA2g_{A}^{2}.

We also performed a comparison with Seckel [163] and found that it matches our result and the one of Lopez et al. [124] if we replace its f2f_{2} by 2​fwm2f_{\rm wm} (again ignoring terms which are quadratic in f2f_{2} and the parameter fp​sf_{ps} in Seckel [163]).

B.7 Bremsstrahlung

We review in the next section the bremsstrahlung correction to the neutron decay, also called radiative neutron decay when the photon is detected [50]. We then extend it to the other weak processes during BBN. This allows to find the difference between the correct treatment of bremsstrahlung and how it was partially included in the radiative correction factor detailed above in § B.6. We report subsequently the detailed expression of this bremsstrahlung correction.

B.7.1 Neutron decay

Let us consider first the bremsstrahlung for the decay of neutron. We note the emitted photon momentum k¯\underline{k}. Its spatial part is 𝐤\mathbf{k}, that we decompose into energy kk and direction 𝐤^\hat{\mathbf{k}} as 𝐤=k​𝐤^\mathbf{k}=k\hat{\mathbf{k}}. We note the electron energy EE and its spatial momentum pp for simplicity. In the infinite nucleon mass approximation, the bremsstrahlung differential decay rate is of the form [see e.g. Ivanov et al. [108, Eq. B12], Cooper et al. [50, Eq. 4], Abers et al. [1, Eq. 6.6] or Ivanov et al. [107, Eq. A40]]

d​Γn→BSd​E​d​k​d​μ\displaystyle\frac{\mathrm{d}\Gamma^{\rm BS}_{n\to}}{\mathrm{d}E\mathrm{d}k\mathrm{d}\mu} =\displaystyle= αFS​K2​π​β​Eν2k\displaystyle\frac{\alpha_{\rm FS}K}{2\pi}\frac{\beta E_{\nu}^{2}}{k} (229)
×\displaystyle\times [β2​(1−μ2)(1−β​μ)2​(1+kE)+k2E2​11−β​μ]\displaystyle\left[\frac{\beta^{2}(1-\mu^{2})}{(1-\beta\mu)^{2}}\left(1+\frac{k}{E}\right)+\frac{k^{2}}{E^{2}}\frac{1}{1-\beta\mu}\right]

where

μ≡𝐩e⋅𝐤^\mu\equiv\mathbf{p}_{e}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{k}} (230)

is the (cosinus) of the angle between the photon momentum and the electron momentum. The neutrino energy is constrained from energy conservation to be

Eν=Δ−E−k.E_{\nu}=\Delta-E-k\,. (231)

Performing the integral on μ\mu leads to

d​Γn→BSd​k​d​E=αFS​K2​π​k​Eν2​F+​(E,k).\frac{\mathrm{d}\Gamma^{\rm BS}_{n\to}}{\mathrm{d}k\mathrm{d}E}=\frac{\alpha_{\rm FS}K}{2\pi k}E_{\nu}^{2}F_{+}(E,k)\,. (232)

with

F±​(E,k)\displaystyle F_{\pm}(E,k) ≡\displaystyle\equiv A⁡(E,k)±k​B​(E,k)\displaystyle A(E,k)\pm kB(E,k) (233)
A⁡(E,k)\displaystyle A(E,k) ≡\displaystyle\equiv (2​E2+k2)​ln⁡(E+pE−p)−4​p​E\displaystyle(2E^{2}+k^{2})\ln\left(\frac{E+p}{E-p}\right)-4pE
B⁡(E,k)\displaystyle B(E,k) ≡\displaystyle\equiv 2​E​ln⁡(E+pE−p)−4​p.\displaystyle 2E\ln\left(\frac{E+p}{E-p}\right)-4p\,.

The total decay rate cannot be obtained from a simple integration of the form

Γn→BS=∫meEmaxd​E​∫0Δ−Ed​k​d​ΓBSd​k​d​E.\Gamma^{\rm BS}_{n\to}=\int_{m_{e}}^{E_{\rm max}}\mathrm{d}E\int_{0}^{\Delta-E}\mathrm{d}k\frac{\mathrm{d}\Gamma^{\rm BS}}{\mathrm{d}k\mathrm{d}E}\,. (234)

since there is an infrared divergence. However this divergence cancels a corresponding divergence in the pure radiative corrections. The usual procedure consists in letting the photon having a mass and taking the limit mγ→0m_{\gamma}\to 0 [see e.g. Ivanov et al. [108] or Abers et al. [1]].

B.7.2 Bremsstrahlung for other reactions

The other rates of bremsstrahlung can be deduced from crossing symmetry. Indeed, if one considers the process n+e+→p+ν¯n+e^{+}\to p+\bar{\nu} it is obtained from crossing symmetry of beta decay. A crossing symmetry is performed by inverting the four-momentum of the corresponding particle. Hence changing the position of the final electron to an initial positron amounts to E→−EE\to-E and p→−pp\to-p. This leads to F+→F−F_{+}\to F_{-} in (232). In fact it is simple to check that if the electron (or positron) and the photon are on the same side, one should use F+F_{+} and if they are on opposite sides, we should use F−F_{-}. The contributions of bremsstrahlung to the reaction rates is then straightforward, provided it is clear that we should take the infrared regularized contribution, and they read

Γn→p​γ=αFS​K2​π​∫me∞𝑑E×[g⁡(−E)​χ~++​(E)+g⁡(E)​χ~+−​(−E)]​Γp→n​γ=Γn→p​γ|χ~+s→χ~−s\Gamma_{n\to p\gamma}&=\frac{\alpha_{\rm FS}K}{2\pi}\int_{m_{e}}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}E\\ \times\left[g(-E)\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{+}(E)+g(E)\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{-}(-E)\right]\\ \Gamma_{p\to n\gamma}=\left.\Gamma_{n\to p\gamma}\right|_{\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{s}\to\widetilde{\chi}_{-}^{s}} (235)

with the definitions

χ~±s​(E)\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}^{s}(E) ≡\displaystyle\equiv ∫0∞d​kk​Fs​(E,k)​χ~±​(k+E)\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{k}F_{s}(E,k)\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}(k+E) (236)
χ~±​(E)\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}(E) ≡\displaystyle\equiv (Eν∓)2​gν∓​(Eν),Eν∓=E∓Δ.\displaystyle(E^{\mp}_{\nu})^{2}g^{\mp}_{\nu}(E_{\nu})\,,\quad E^{\mp}_{\nu}=E\mp\Delta\,. (237)

B.7.3 Correction for bremsstrahlung

However, the bremsstrahlung radiative corrections included in § III.5, that is in the factor (103), are those of neutron beta decay. Indeed the radiative correction function RR in Eqs. (101) and (104) is the sum of a pure radiative correction and a bremsstrahlung correction. It is decomposed as

R⁡(E,kmax)=Rpure​(E)+RBS​(E,kmax)R(E,k_{\rm max})=R^{\rm pure}(E)+R^{\rm BS}(E,k_{\rm max}) (238)

with the BS part being

RBS​(E,kmax)≡αFS2​π​∫0kmaxd​kk​(kmax−k)2kmax2​F+​(E,k)E​p.R^{\rm BS}(E,k_{\rm max})\equiv\frac{\alpha_{\rm FS}}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{k_{\rm max}}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{k}\frac{(k_{\rm max}-k)^{2}}{k_{\rm max}^{2}}\frac{F_{+}(E,k)}{Ep}\,. (239)

In Eqs. (101) and (104) the choice was made to take kmaxk_{\rm max} as being the energy of the neutrino because this is the case for neutron beta decay. However the maximum energy of the photon emitted is not the neutrino energy in the other reactions. Furthermore, the distribution function for the neutrino appearing in Eqs. (101) and (104) is incorrectly taken in the limit in which the photon energy is so soft that it does not affect the neutrino energy. These are the two shortcomings that we need to correct for by adding the difference between the correct correction [Eqs. (235)] and the approximate contribution [it is formally Eqs. (101) and (104) with R→RBSR\to R^{\rm BS}]. We write this bremsstrahlung correction in a form which contains explicitly no infrared divergence and this is given by Eqs. (107) with the definitions

δ​Γn→p+eBS\displaystyle\delta\Gamma^{\rm BS}_{n\to p+e} =\displaystyle= ∫0|Δ−E|d​kk​F+​(E,k)​[χ~+​(E+k)−(|Δ−E|−k)2​gν​(E−Δ)]+∫|Δ−E|∞d​kk​F+​(E,k)​χ~+​(E+k)\displaystyle\int_{0}^{|\Delta-E|}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{k}F_{+}(E,k)\left[\widetilde{\chi}_{+}(E+k)-(|\Delta-E|-k)^{2}g_{\nu}(E-\Delta)\right]+\int_{|\Delta-E|}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{k}F_{+}(E,k)\widetilde{\chi}_{+}(E+k)
δ​Γn+e→pBS\displaystyle\delta\Gamma^{\rm BS}_{n+e\to p} =\displaystyle= ∫0Δ+Ed​kk​[F−​(E,k)​χ~+​(k−E)−F+​(E,k)​(|Δ+E|−k)2​gν​(−E−Δ)]\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\Delta+E}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{k}\left[F_{-}(E,k)\widetilde{\chi}_{+}(k-E)-F_{+}(E,k)(|\Delta+E|-k)^{2}g_{\nu}(-E-\Delta)\right] (240)
+\displaystyle+ ∫Δ+E∞d​kk​F−​(E,k)​χ~+​(k−E)\displaystyle\int_{\Delta+E}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{k}F_{-}(E,k)\widetilde{\chi}_{+}(k-E)
δ​Γp→n+eBS\displaystyle\delta\Gamma^{\rm BS}_{p\to n+e} =\displaystyle= ∫0Δ+Ed​kk​F+​(E,k)​[χ~−​(E+k)−(|E+Δ|−k)2​gν​(E+Δ)]+∫Δ+E∞d​kk​F+​(E,k)​χ~−​(E+k)\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\Delta+E}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{k}F_{+}(E,k)\left[\widetilde{\chi}_{-}(E+k)-(|E+\Delta|-k)^{2}g_{\nu}(E+\Delta)\right]+\int_{\Delta+E}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{k}F_{+}(E,k)\widetilde{\chi}_{-}(E+k)
δ​Γp+e→nBS\displaystyle\delta\Gamma^{\rm BS}_{p+e\to n} =\displaystyle= ∫0|Δ−E|d​kk​[F−​(E,k)​χ~−​(k−E)−F+​(E,k)​(|E−Δ|−k)2​gν​(−E+Δ)]\displaystyle\int_{0}^{|\Delta-E|}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{k}\left[F_{-}(E,k)\widetilde{\chi}_{-}(k-E)-F_{+}(E,k)(|E-\Delta|-k)^{2}g_{\nu}(-E+\Delta)\right] (241)
+\displaystyle+ ∫|Δ−E|∞d​kk​F−​(E,k)​χ~−​(k−E).\displaystyle\int_{|\Delta-E|}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{k}F_{-}(E,k)\widetilde{\chi}_{-}(k-E)\,.

With these corrections added to Eqs. (101) and (104), the total effect of bremsstrahlung is taken into account. However, with this new contribution the rates no longer satisfy the detailed balance relation (86). Indeed the emission of a final photon needs to be compensated by the absorption of photons from the thermal bath to lead to a thermodynamical equilibrium. It is only when the finite temperature radiative corrections are taken into account, with stimulated emission and absorption, that the total rates can satisfy detailed balance. This is shown explicitly in Fig. 18.

Note that by construction the bremsstrahlung corrections do not modify the radiative corrections for λ0RC0\lambda^{\rm RC0}_{0} because the neutron beta decay in vacuum, is the only reaction for which bremsstrahlung is fully taken into account already.

Finally note that there was some intuition in Brown and Sawyer [25] about the incorrect treatment of real-photon processes. Indeed in this reference, the authors advocate that one should add the process n+ν¯+e+→p+γn+\bar{\nu}+e^{+}\to p+\gamma, that they call the five-body process, since it cannot be a correction to n+ν¯+e+→pn+\bar{\nu}+e^{+}\to p which is forbidden energetically. This is indeed correct and it corresponds to the last term in δ​Γn+e→pBS\delta\Gamma^{\rm BS}_{n+e\to p}, where the photon emitted must have an energy larger than Δ+E\Delta+E. What we find is that not only this process needs to be added, but all other processes need to be corrected except for the neutron beta decay.

B.8 Finite temperature radiative corrections

The finite temperature radiative corrections are made of Eqs. (109), (112) and (113). These last two contributions involve implicitly principal parts in the apparently divergent part of the integrals. After rearrangement, they can be put in the form [25, Eq. (5.15)]

Γn→pΔ​E,T+Γn→pe​p+e​e,T=αFS​K2​π​∫me∞d​E​[χ+​(E)+χ+​(−E)]​[−2​π2​T2​E3​p+∫me∞d​E′​FT​(E,E′)]​Γp→nΔ​E,T+Γp→ne​p+e​e,T=(Γn→pΔ​E,T+Γn→pe​p+e​e,T)|χ+→χ−\Gamma^{\Delta E,T}_{n\to p}+\Gamma^{ep+ee,T}_{n\to p}&=\frac{\alpha_{\rm FS}K}{2\pi}\int_{m_{e}}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}E[\chi_{+}(E)+\chi_{+}(-E)]\left[-\frac{2\pi^{2}T^{2}E}{3p}+\int_{m_{e}}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}E^{\prime}F^{T}(E,E^{\prime})\right]\\ \Gamma^{\Delta E,T}_{p\to n}+\Gamma^{ep+ee,T}_{p\to n}=\left.\left(\Gamma^{\Delta E,T}_{n\to p}+\Gamma^{ep+ee,T}_{n\to p}\right)\right|_{\chi_{+}\to\chi_{-}} (242)
FT​(E,E′)≡−14​ln2​(p+p′p−p′)2​{g′​(E′)​p′​E2p​E′​(E+E′)+g⁡(E′)​E2p​p′​[E′+me2​EE′2]}−g⁡(E′)​[4​E​p′p+2​E′​L​(E,E′)]+ln⁡(p+p′p−p′)2​{g′​(E′)​[p′2​EE′​(me2p2+2)−E2​p′p​L​[E,E′]]+g⁡(E′)​[E​me2p2​E′2​(E′2+2​p2+me2)−E2+E′2E+E′−E2​E′p​p′​L​(E,E′)]}​L​(E,E′)≡ln⁡(E​E′+p​p′+me2E​E′−p​p′+me2),F^{T}(E,E^{\prime})&\equiv-\frac{1}{4}\ln^{2}\left(\frac{p+p^{\prime}}{p-p^{\prime}}\right)^{2}\left\{g^{\prime}(E^{\prime})\frac{p^{\prime}E^{2}}{pE^{\prime}}(E+E^{\prime})+g(E^{\prime})\frac{E^{2}}{pp^{\prime}}\left[E^{\prime}+\frac{m_{e}^{2}E}{{E^{\prime}}^{2}}\right]\right\}-g(E^{\prime})\left[4E\frac{p^{\prime}}{p}+2E^{\prime}L(E,E^{\prime})\right]\\ +\ln\left(\frac{p+p^{\prime}}{p-p^{\prime}}\right)^{2}\left\{g^{\prime}(E^{\prime})\left[{p^{\prime}}^{2}\frac{E}{E^{\prime}}\left(\frac{m_{e}^{2}}{p^{2}}+2\right)-E^{2}\frac{p^{\prime}}{p}L[E,E^{\prime}]\right]\right.\\ \qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad\left.+g(E^{\prime})\left[\frac{Em_{e}^{2}}{p^{2}{E^{\prime}}^{2}}({E^{\prime}}^{2}+2p^{2}+m_{e}^{2})-\frac{E^{2}+{E^{\prime}}^{2}}{E+E^{\prime}}-\frac{E^{2}{E^{\prime}}}{pp^{\prime}}L(E,E^{\prime})\right]\right\}\\ L(E,E^{\prime})\equiv\ln\left(\frac{EE^{\prime}+pp^{\prime}+m_{e}^{2}}{EE^{\prime}-pp^{\prime}+m_{e}^{2}}\right)\,, (243)

where g′​(E)≡∂Eg⁡(E)g^{\prime}(E)\equiv\partial_{E}g(E).

This form is simpler numerically if the double integration on EE and E′E^{\prime} is performed on the variables EΣ≡E+E′E_{\Sigma}\equiv E+E^{\prime} and EΔ≡E−E′E_{\Delta}\equiv E-E^{\prime} using 2​∫∫d​E​d​E′=∫∫⁡d​EΣ​d​EΔ2\int\int\mathrm{d}E\mathrm{d}E^{\prime}=\int\int\mathrm{d}E_{\Sigma}\mathrm{d}E_{\Delta}.

The first contribution (109) is made of real photon processes, such as absorption and stimulated emission, see Fig. 14, but not simple emission which has been already accounted for as bremsstrahlung (see appendix B.7). To obtain it we start from the real photons processes [25, Eq. B28]

Γn→pγ=αFS​K2​π​∫me∞𝑑E×[g⁡(−E)​χ~+γ,+​(E)+g⁡(E)​χ~+γ,−​(−E)]​Γp→nγ=Γn→pγ|χ~+γ,s→χ~−γ,s\Gamma^{\gamma}_{n\to p}&=\frac{\alpha_{\rm FS}K}{2\pi}\int_{m_{e}}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}E\\ \times\left[g(-E)\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{\gamma,+}(E)+g(E)\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{\gamma,-}(-E)\right]\\ \Gamma^{\gamma}_{p\to n}=\left.\Gamma^{\gamma}_{n\to p}\right|_{\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{\gamma,s}\to\widetilde{\chi}_{-}^{\gamma,s}} (244)

where we defined

χ~±γ,s​(E)\displaystyle\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}^{\gamma,s}(E) ≡\displaystyle\equiv ∫0∞d​kk[(1+f(k))Fs(E,k)χ~±(E+k)\displaystyle\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{k}\left[(1+f(k))F_{s}(E,k)\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}(E+k)\right. (245)
+f(k)F−s(E,k)χ~±(E−k)],\displaystyle\qquad\quad\left.+f(k)F_{-s}(E,k)\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}(E-k)\right],

and f⁡(k)≡g−​(k/T)=1/[exp⁡(k/T)−1]f(k)\equiv g^{-}(k/T)=1/[{\rm exp}(k/T)-1]. Note that from the property

1+f⁡(k)=−f⁡(−k)=ekT​f​(k)1+f(k)=-f(-k)={\rm e}^{\frac{k}{T}}f(k) (246)

combined with the property (84), the detailed balance relation (86) for the real photon processes (244) is automatically satisfied2121 21 At this stage this is only formal since this presents infrared divergences..

Then we replace the factor [1+f⁡(k)][1+f(k)] by f⁡(k)f(k) so as to keep only stimulated emission, since bremsstrahlung processes (235) which are taken into account separately are obtained by f⁡(k)→0f(k)\to 0. A consequence is that the real photon processes without bremsstrahlung do no satisfy formally the detailed balance relation. It is only when all real photon processes are added that it is recovered, as illustrated in Fig. (18).

Finally, in order to obtain the form (109) for which it is apparent that there is no infrared divergence, it is necessary to add an infrared diverging contribution [25, Eq. (B53)] that can be considered as part of the wave-function radiative correction (it is partially coming from the diagram 17a) and which is

Γn→pγ,Z=αFS​K2​π​∫me∞𝑑E×[g⁡(−E)​χ~+γ,Z​(E)+g⁡(E)​χ~+γ,Z​(−E)]​Γp→nγ,Z=Γn→pγ,Z|χ~+γ,Z→χ~−γ,Z\Gamma^{\gamma,Z}_{n\to p}&=\frac{\alpha_{\rm FS}K}{2\pi}\int_{m_{e}}^{\infty}\mathrm{d}E\\ \times\left[g(-E)\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{\gamma,Z}(E)+g(E)\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{\gamma,Z}(-E)\right]\\ \Gamma^{\gamma,Z}_{p\to n}=\left.\Gamma^{\gamma,Z}_{n\to p}\right|_{\widetilde{\chi}_{+}^{\gamma,Z}\to\widetilde{\chi}_{-}^{\gamma,Z}} (247)
χ~±γ,Z(E)≡−2∫0∞d​kkf(k)A(E,k)χ~±(E).\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}^{\gamma,Z}(E)\equiv-2\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{\mathrm{d}k}{k}f(k)A(E,k)\widetilde{\chi}_{\pm}(E)\,. (248)

Again on Eqs. (247) it is apparent using the property (84) that these extra terms formally satisfy the detailed balance relation (86).

Appendix C Nuclear reactions

C.1 Conventions for nuclear reaction rates

Let us consider for simplicity a two-body reaction of the type k+l→i+jk+l\to i+j and its reverse reaction i+j→k+li+j\to k+l. From Eqs. (136) and (137) their contributions to the evolution of the abundance YiY_{i} take the form

Y˙i⊃Yk​Yl​ρn​NA​⟨σ​v⟩k​l→i​j−Yi​Yj​ρn​NA​⟨σ​v⟩i​j→k​l,\dot{Y}_{i}\supset Y_{k}Y_{l}\rho_{n}N_{A}\langle\sigma v\rangle_{kl\rightarrow{ij}}-Y_{i}Y_{j}\rho_{n}N_{A}\langle\sigma v\rangle_{ij\rightarrow{kl}}\,, (249)

with

ρn≡nbNA≡nb⋅u⁡(g/cm3).\rho_{\rm n}\equiv\frac{n_{\rm b}}{N_{A}}\equiv\;n_{\rm b}{\cdot}u\;\;\mathrm{(g/cm^{3})}. (250)

We see that ρn\rho_{\rm n} has the dimension of a mass density since uu is the atomic mass unit, that, by definition is related to Avogadro’s number by NA.uN_{A}.u=1g. By convention, NAN_{A} has been introduced in the definition of the reaction rate, hence what is tabulated for a given reaction is NA​⟨σ​v⟩N_{A}\langle\sigma v\rangle and one must multiply by ρn\rho_{\rm n} in order to build the rates (e.g. Γk​l→i​j\Gamma_{kl\to ij}) which appear in the general form Eq. (138). More generally for a reaction of the type i1+⋯+ip→j1+…​jqi_{1}+\dots+i_{p}\to j_{1}+\dots j_{q}, the contribution to the evolution of the species i1i_{1} is

Y˙i1⊃−Yi1​…​Yip​ρnp−1​NAp−1​γi1​…​ip→j1​…​jq.\dot{Y}_{i_{1}}\supset-Y_{i_{1}}\dots Y_{i_{p}}\rho_{\rm n}^{p-1}N_{A}^{p-1}\gamma_{i_{1}\dots i_{p}\to j_{1}\dots j_{q}}\,. (251)

Conventionally what is tabulated is NAp−1​γi1​…​ip→j1​…​jqN_{A}^{p-1}\gamma_{i_{1}\dots i_{p}\to j_{1}\dots j_{q}} 2222 22 More precisely, from (139) the factor is NA(Ni1+⋯+Nip)−1N_{A}^{(N_{i_{1}}+\dots+N_{i_{p}})-1} if the stoichiometric coefficients are not unity. and one must multiply by ρnp−1\rho_{\rm n}^{p-1} to build the reaction rate Γi1​…​ip→j1​…​jq\Gamma_{i_{1}\dots i_{p}\to j_{1}\dots j_{q}} appearing in Eq. (138). The method is similar for a reaction of the type j1+…​jq→i1+⋯+ipj_{1}+\dots j_{q}\to i_{1}+\dots+i_{p} which creates species i1i_{1}. See also appendix E of Serpico et al. [165] on this topic.

To summarize, in nucleosynthesis calculations (as in chemistry) we are concerned with number densities. However, it is convenient to normalize them to Avogadro’s number whose dimension can be considered2323 23 A subject of controversy, but irrelevant as soon as it is consistent with the definition of the reaction rate units. to be the inverse of a mass. The form (249) is purely conventional and ρn\rho_{\rm n} is just another manner to define a number density even though it has the dimension of a mass density.

C.2 Baryonic density and nucleonic density

In practice, except for BBN, the nucleonic density of Eq. (250) is usually identified with the atomic matter density, and the nuclear energy source is calculated independently as nuclear flow ×\times Q This corresponds to the approximation

A⋅u≈Z​mp+(A−Z)​mn−B⁡(A,Z)+Z​me,A{\cdot}u\;{\approx}\;Zm_{p}+(A-Z)m_{n}-B(A,Z)+Zm_{e}\,, (252)

i.e. an error of ≈\approx1%, completely negligible in stellar modeling. For BBN where D/H observations reach the percent level of uncertainty, it is worth considering the difference between nucleonic density and baryonic density.

The baryonic density Ωb⋅h2\Omega_{\mathrm{b}}{\cdot}h^{2} deduced from CMB observations is the atomic density i.e. taking into account the 4He binding energy and the mass of the electrons. Given that the fraction of baryons in the form of helium is YP≡4​YHe4Y_{\rm P}\equiv 4\,Y_{{}^{4}{\rm He}} and the rest is in the form of hydrogen, the average mass of baryons is [174]

mb\displaystyle m_{\rm b} ≡\displaystyle\equiv ξ​u\displaystyle\xi u (253)
ξ\displaystyle\xi ≡\displaystyle\equiv YP4​mHe4u+(1−YP)​mH1u\displaystyle\frac{Y_{\rm P}}{4}\frac{m_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He}}}{u}+(1-Y_{\rm P})\frac{m_{{}^{1}\mathrm{H}}}{u} (254)
=\displaystyle= mH1u​(1−1.75891×10−3​YP0.24709)\displaystyle\frac{m_{{}^{1}\mathrm{H}}}{u}\left(1-1.75891\times 10^{-3}\frac{Y_{\rm P}}{0.24709}\right)

where mHe4m_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He}} and mH1m_{{}^{1}\mathrm{H}} are the atomic masses (see appendix D). Using YP≃0.24709Y_{\rm P}\simeq 0.24709 for the final BBN Helium abundance (it is the most relevant abundance for CMB since stellar formation has not started during CMB formation) we get

ξ≃1.006052,ξ−1≃0.993984.\xi\simeq 1.006052\,,\quad\xi^{-1}\simeq 0.993984\,. (255)

Hence, from Eqs. (35) and (250), one should use in Eq. (249)

ρn=ξ−1​ρb,\rho_{\rm n}=\xi^{-1}\rho_{\rm b}\,, (256)

where ρb\rho_{\rm b} is obtained from Eq. (34). One can estimate the error introduced if we ignore this subtlety and use ξ=1\xi=1 in nuclear reaction. Numerically we found

ΔYP=5.6×10−4Δ(DH)=−2.4×10−7Δ(He3H)=3.7×10−8Δ(Li7H)=7.1×10−12.\Delta Y_{\rm P}&=5.6\times 10^{-4}\\ \Delta\left(\frac{{\rm D}}{{\rm H}}\right)=-2.4\times 10^{-7}\\ \Delta\left(\frac{{{}^{3}{\rm He}}}{{\rm H}}\right)=3.7\times 10^{-8}\\ \Delta\left(\frac{{{}^{7}{\rm Li}}}{{\rm H}}\right)=7.1\times 10^{-12}\,. (257)

Finally, since the abundances deduced from observations, other than 4He, are expressed as number ratios, hence, e.g. the observed D/H can be directly compared to the BBN YD/YH1Y_{\mathrm{D}}/Y_{\mathrm{{}^{1}H}} calculated ratio. The 4He (pseudo-)mass fraction, YPY_{\rm P} deduced from spectroscopic observations is defined as [146, 110]

YP≡4​y4​y+1Y_{\rm P}\equiv\frac{4y}{4y+1} (258)

with y≡nHe4/nH1≡YHe4/YH1y{\equiv}n_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He}}/n_{\mathrm{{}^{1}H}}{\equiv}Y_{{}^{4}\mathrm{He}}/Y_{\mathrm{{}^{1}H}} being the number ratio, resulting in a definition of YPY_{\rm P} identical to the BBN one.

Appendix D Numerical values

The values of cos⁡θC=Vud\cos\theta_{C}=V_{\rm ud} and gA=CA/CVg_{A}=C_{A}/C_{V} are taken from the Particle Data Group (PDG) [147]. The neutron decay rate τn=879.5​(±0.8)​s\tau_{n}=879.5(\pm 0.8)\,{\rm s} is from Serebrov et al. [164, Fig. 22] and includes only experiments after 2000. This value is slightly lower and with less experimental error than the previously admitted value τn=880.2​(1.1)​s\tau_{n}=880.2(1.1)\,{\rm s} of the PDG. We report errors on numerical parameters only if they are meaningful for BBN. Cosmological parameters are taken from Ade et al. [2].

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
